The pointer has thus done two incompatible things at once: it has named an exacting standard, and it has insisted that the standard is ordinary. The reader is left to resolve the contradiction by rising to the ordinary, which is the pointer's whole pedagogical point.

passage: 師謂僧曰、有時一喝如金剛王宝剣、有時一喝如踞地獅子、有時一喝如探竿影草、有時一喝不作一喝用。
notes: The locus classicus of Linji Yixuan's 四喝 (four shouts), in which the master distinguishes the pedagogical functions of the 喝 in explicit taxonomic terms. The literal sense: sometimes a shout is like the treasure-sword of the Vajra king; sometimes a shout is like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground; sometimes a shout is like a pole probing weeds with a shadow-grass on it; sometimes a shout is not used as a shout at all. The passage is doctrinally foundational as the first explicit Chan taxonomy of a non-verbal teaching device, and it rewards close reading. First, the taxonomic move — specifying four distinct functions for what could be heard as a single undifferentiated vocal event — insists that the 喝 is a technical instrument whose value depends on the calibration of its deployment. Linji is not expressing anger in four ways; he is distinguishing four pedagogical situations in which a shout performs a different kind of work. Second, the metaphors are not decorative but functional: the sword cuts cleanly through conceptual grasping; the crouching lion radiates presence without moving, testing whether the student is grounded; the probing pole tests the terrain before the teacher acts; and the fourth 'shout that is not a shout' marks the limit case where the shout appears in the situation without performing the function, either because the situation does not call for it or because the student is already in the position the shout would have established. Third, the phrase 不作一喝用 ('not used as a shout') is the structurally most demanding of the four: it names the shout's occasional self-withdrawal, the situation in which the master shouts and the shout is not a shout — a Chan figure that insists the meaning of the 喝 is not fixed by its acoustic form but by its function within the encounter. The four shouts together constitute the foundational Chan argument that non-verbal teaching devices are not expressive effusions but precisely calibrated instruments.

passage: 徳山示衆云、今夜不答話、問話者三十棒。
notes: A famous passage recording Deshan Xuanjian's use of the staff as a teaching method, preserved in the Chan lamp histories and cited throughout the commentarial tradition that stands behind the Gateless Gate's treatment of Deshan. The literal sense: Deshan addressed the assembly saying, 'Tonight I will not answer questions. Whoever asks a question gets thirty blows.' The passage compresses the doctrinal logic of 棒 into a few characters and rewards close reading. First, the prohibition 不答話 ('I will not answer questions') and the sanction 問話者三十棒 ('whoever asks gets thirty blows') establish a seemingly impossible pedagogical situation: the students have gathered to engage their teacher, and the teacher has foreclosed the standard mode of engagement. The apparent closure, however, is the whole teaching. The staff is not a penalty for asking questions in a context where asking is permitted; it is the teaching itself in a context where the discursive mode has been withdrawn. Second, the sanction applies symmetrically: anyone who asks receives the blow, regardless of the content or merit of the question. The axis of right-question and wrong-question has been collapsed, and the collapse is what the staff enforces. Third, Deshan's famous alternative formulation — 道得也三十棒、道不得也三十棒 ('whether you can say it or not, thirty blows') — extends the same logic to the answering side of the exchange: whether the student can produce the correct speech or cannot, the staff falls. The two sides of the discursive transaction — asking and answering, question and response — are both foreclosed by the staff, and the foreclosure is the demonstration that the teaching does not operate through the discursive transaction. The staff falls on the student at a location beneath the axis of speech altogether, and the claim embedded in Deshan's method is that the teaching is transmitted at that level.

passage: 師陞座、拈拂子示衆云、諸人還見麼。還聞麼。
notes: A representative formula preserved in the Blue Cliff Record and throughout the recorded-sayings genre: the master ascends the high seat, picks up the fly-whisk, shows it to the assembly, and asks — 'All of you, do you see? Do you hear?' The passage illustrates several features of the 拂子's role as a ceremonial and pedagogical implement. First, the sequence 陞座 (ascending the high seat) followed by 拈拂子 (picking up the fly-whisk) marks the fly-whisk as the implement appropriate to the master's speaking position: the act of ascending the seat is incomplete without the taking-up of the whisk, and the whisk in hand signals that what follows is formal dharma teaching rather than informal conversation. The 拂子 is thus not merely a prop but a structural component of the teaching situation. Second, the verb 拈 (to pick up delicately, to select between the fingers) is the same verb that names the commentarial acts of 拈古 and 拈提 — picking up an old case, picking up and presenting the essential point. The master picking up the fly-whisk is the physical analogue of picking up a case: both gestures select something delicate and hold it up for the assembly. Third, the two questions 還見麼 ('do you see?') and 還聞麼 ('do you hear?') frame the whisk's being held up as an event addressed to two senses at once — the visual event of the raised whisk and the acoustic event of the words being spoken — and the pairing asks the assembly whether they can receive both as a single teaching. The fly-whisk, the words, and the question together constitute one pedagogical act, and the assembly's task is to meet the whole.

passage: 千疑万疑、只是一疑。話頭上疑破、千疑万疑一時破。
notes: A compressed formulation widely transmitted through the Rinzai teaching tradition as the summary of Dahui Zonggao's doctrine of 疑団, compatible with and paraphrasing passages throughout his Letters on the practice of kànhuà chán. The literal sense: 'A thousand doubts, ten thousand doubts — they are only one doubt. When the doubt breaks through at the head of the critical phrase, the thousand and ten thousand doubts break at the same moment.' The formulation articulates the load-bearing logic of 疑団 in three moves, each of which rewards close attention. First, the equation 千疑万疑只是一疑 ('a thousand doubts, ten thousand doubts are only one doubt') is the doctrinal core: the scattered doubts that proliferate in the practitioner's discursive mind are not genuinely plural but a single underlying interrogation appearing in many instances, and the work of kànhuà is to let the apparent plurality collapse into the mass it always was. This is the phase transition the compound 疑団 names — the moment at which doubts-in-the-plural become the single 団 (bounded, consolidated mass) of doubt-in-the-singular. Second, 話頭上疑破 ('at the head of the critical phrase, the doubt breaks through') locates the resolution as an event rather than a process. The 疑団 does not gradually dissolve through analysis; it breaks through at a specific moment and at a specific location — on the 話頭 itself, the critical phrase the practitioner has been holding. Third, 一時破 ('broken at the same moment') closes the logic: because the thousand doubts were only one doubt, the one moment of breakthrough resolves them all simultaneously. The formulation compresses into two lines the entire Rinzai claim that consolidated doubt is the medium of awakening and that the practitioner's task is to consolidate rather than to analyze.

passage: 學道之人、須參箇本色老師、方得相應。若参邪師、被他引入鬼窟裏去。
notes: A representative formulation from Dahui's pastoral instructions to lay students, articulating the necessity of finding a properly authorized teacher. The literal sense: 'A student of the Way must practice under a genuine venerable teacher (老師) — only then can there be correspondence. If one practices under a false teacher, one will be led into the cave of demons.' The passage encapsulates the classical Chan doctrine that awakening is not achievable in isolation but requires the encounter with a specific, institutionally qualified teacher, and it rewards close reading for the register of the compound 老師. First, the qualifier 本色 ('of genuine color,' genuine in substance rather than in appearance) attached to 老師 performs important work: Dahui distinguishes the 老師 who is genuinely a 老師 — properly trained, properly authorized — from those who merely occupy the outward role. The compound 老師 already carries honorific weight, but 本色老師 intensifies it by specifying that the honor must correspond to actual realization. Second, the verb 參 (to practice with, to study under) governs the student's relation to the 老師 and marks that relation as an active, sustained engagement rather than a passive reception of teaching: the student participates in the office of the 老師 rather than merely receiving information from it. Third, the contrast with 邪師 (the false or heterodox teacher) and the striking figure of being drawn into 鬼窟裏 ('into the cave of demons') frame the stakes of the choice: practicing under an unqualified teacher is not merely ineffective but actively harmful, and the student's ability to distinguish a genuine 老師 from a false one is itself a question of practical discernment that the Chan tradition treats as load-bearing. The passage thereby articulates the institutional logic the compound 老師 encodes: the title marks an authorized office, the authorization is what makes the transmission possible, and the student's task is first to identify someone properly holding the office.

passage: 先師古佛、天童如淨禪師、常云、坐禪是身心脱落也、不用燒香禮拜念佛修懺看經。
notes: Dōgen's characteristic invocation of his Chinese master Rujing, drawing together the formal honorific 禅師 with his personal honorific 古佛 ('old Buddha') to name the figure whose teaching grounds Dōgen's own doctrinal program. The literal sense: 'My late teacher, the Old Buddha, Rujing Zenji of Tiantong, always used to say: zazen is the dropping-off of body-and-mind; there is no use for offering incense, bowing, reciting the Buddha's name, performing repentance, or reading sutras.' The passage illustrates several features of 禅師's role as a formal honorific within Dōgen's textual practice. First, the full honorific chain 先師古佛、天童如淨禪師 stacks four distinct markers of reverence: 先師 (my late teacher), 古佛 (Old Buddha — Dōgen's highest personal honorific), 天童 (the mountain of Rujing's monastery), and 禪師 (the formal Chan-master title). The layering is deliberate: the first three honorifics are personal and devotional, while the final 禪師 grounds them in the institutional office that gives the personal reverence its public warrant. The 禪師 title is what certifies that Rujing is an authorized ancestor whose teaching the living Sōtō community legitimately inherits, and the personal honorifics derive their doctrinal weight from being attached to a properly authorized 禅師. Second, the attribution formula 常云 ('always used to say') constructs Rujing's teaching as a continuous voice whose authority is transmitted through repetition across the master-disciple relation — Dōgen is not inventing the doctrine but receiving it from his 禅師, and the formula is the textual record of that reception. Third, the content of the saying — that zazen alone is shinjin datsuraku, without need for the other Buddhist practices — is one of the most doctrinally load-bearing claims in the Sōtō tradition, and its being attributed through the 禅師 honorific establishes the claim's lineage warrant. Dōgen's repeated use of this invocation throughout the Shōbōgenzō and the Eihei Shingi makes 禅師 specifically the title by which the living Sōtō community addresses the ancestor whose voice it inherits.

passage: 典座和尚、道心を発して、古来の徳行を慕うて、功夫力を尽くすべし。
notes: A representative formulation from Dōgen's Tenzo Kyōkun ('Instructions to the Cook,' one of the six texts composing the Eihei Shingi), addressing the tenzo in the register of the 和尚 compound. The literal sense: 'The tenzo-priest (典座和尚) should arouse the mind of the Way, emulating the virtuous conduct of the ancestors, and exhaust the power of sustained effort.' The passage illustrates several features of 和尚's institutional register within Sōtō monastic practice. First, the compound 典座和尚 attaches 和尚 to the office name 典座 (head cook), with the effect of framing the tenzo not as a functional position analogous to a secular cook but as a specifically ordained monastic office — the tenzo's work is the work of a 和尚, a fully ordained priest, and the cooking is therefore itself religious practice. This framing is the doctrinal core of Dōgen's Tenzo Kyōkun: the claim that the preparation of the community's meals is not a lower kind of work that the truly spiritual would avoid but is itself the expression of awakened practice. The 和尚 compound is what licenses the claim by establishing the tenzo as a preceptor whose daily work is on a continuum with ordination, sutra-chanting, and zazen. Second, the exhortation to 道心を発する (arouse the mind of the Way, hotsu bodaishin) addressed to the 和尚 places the tenzo's office within the framework of bodhicitta: the tenzo's work is structured by the same bodhi-aspiration that structures any monastic's work, and 和尚 specifies that this aspiration is held in the institutional register of the ordained preceptor rather than in any private or lay register. Third, the invocation of 古来の徳行 (the virtuous conduct of the ancestors from of old) attaches the individual tenzo-priest to a lineage of previous 和尚 figures who have held the office, extending the transmission logic of Sōtō monastic practice from the meditation hall and the dharma hall into the kitchen. The compound 和尚 is therefore doing precise institutional work in the passage: it specifies that the tenzo's office is a priestly office, that priestly offices are held within a lineage, and that the kitchen is therefore part of the lineage's transmission.

passage: 禅院に主事六人を立つ。皆な仏子なり、共に仏事を作す。中に就いて典座は衆僧の弁食を掌る。
notes: The opening lines of Dōgen's Tenzo Kyōkun ('Instructions to the Cook'), which establishes the institutional and doctrinal framing within which the rest of the text operates. The literal sense: 'In the Chan monastery six principal officers (主事) are established. All are children of the Buddha (仏子) and together perform the work of the Buddha (仏事). Among these the tenzo (典座) is in charge of the preparation of food for the assembly of monks (衆僧の弁食).' The passage rewards close attention for the way it positions 典座 within the institutional structure of the monastery and within the doctrinal frame of Dōgen's broader project. First, the enumeration 主事六人 ('six principal officers') situates the tenzo's office as one of a coordinated set — 都寺, 監寺, 副寺, 維那, 典座, 直歳 — whose responsibilities together cover the practical functioning of the entire monastery. The tenzo is not an isolated kitchen role but a structural counterpart to the offices governing administration (都寺, 監寺, 副寺), the meditation hall (維那), and longer-term stewardship (直歳); the kitchen is named alongside these as one of the six fundamental functions of monastic life. Second, the doctrinal claim 皆な仏子なり、共に仏事を作す ('all are children of the Buddha, together performing the Buddha's work') licenses the elevation of the tenzo's office that the rest of the text develops: if the kitchen work is itself 仏事 (the Buddha's work), then the tenzo's careful attention to ordinary tasks is not preliminary to practice but is itself the activity of awakened mind. Third, the specific phrasing 衆僧の弁食を掌る ('in charge of preparing food for the assembly') uses the verb 掌る (to hold in the hand, to be entrusted with) which echoes the 典 of 典座 itself: the tenzo holds, is entrusted with, the office of preparing food for the assembly, and the tenzo's office is a 掌, a holding, a formal entrustment that names the durability of the responsibility. The opening of the Tenzo Kyōkun therefore compresses into three short clauses the institutional position, the doctrinal frame, and the etymological logic of the office it goes on to articulate.

passage: 維那は綱紀を主り、衆僧を整理し、坐禅諷経の節度を司る。一切の犍稚を鳴らすこと、皆この職に属す。
notes: A representative formulation from the Chiji Shingi section of Dōgen's Eihei Shingi articulating the responsibilities of the ino. The literal sense: 'The ino (維那) takes charge of the regulating threads (綱紀), arranges the order of the assembly (衆僧), directs the timing and rhythm of zazen and sutra-chanting (坐禅諷経の節度). The sounding of all the bells, blocks, and signal instruments (一切の犍稚) belongs to this office.' The passage illustrates the precise scope of the ino's institutional work and the way the compound 維那 is doctrinally apt for that work. First, the phrase 綱紀を主り ('taking charge of the regulating threads') deploys the same binding-cord figure that 維 itself encodes: 綱 and 紀 are both threads of the woven fabric of monastic discipline, and the ino's office is to hold them — the ino binds the community to the schedule and the conduct it maintains together. The recurrence of the cord-and-binding figure in the verb governing the office is not coincidental but reflects the conceptual continuity between the office's name and its function. Second, the enumeration 坐禅諷経の節度 ('the timing-and-measure of zazen and sutra-chanting') specifies the two practical centers of the ino's institutional location: the meditation hall and the chanting services. These are the two activities whose conduct the ino directly supervises, and the office's identity is constructed around them — distinct from the tenzo (kitchen) and the chiji (administration), the ino's location is the zendō and the dharma hall during chanting. Third, the specification 一切の犍稚 ('all the bells, blocks, and signal instruments,' from Sanskrit ghaṇṭā) attaches to the ino the practical apparatus by which the rhythm of monastic life is communicated: the bells and blocks that signal the start and end of zazen, the wooden han struck before chanting, the densho rung for assemblies. The office is therefore named not abstractly but by the concrete sound-instruments through which its authority is exercised. The compound 維那 thereby names an office whose institutional logic is preserved across the passage: the binding of the community to its schedule (綱紀, 維), the supervision of zazen and chanting (the locations where binding is made audible), and the practical apparatus of bells and blocks (the means by which binding is signaled).

passage: 首座は一夏九旬の中、衆僧を率いて坐禅し、未だ参ぜざる者を勧めて参ぜしむべし。結制の終わるに及んで、堂頭和尚に代わりて陞座問答すべし。
notes: A representative formulation from the Eihei Shingi articulating the office of the shuso during the ango (practice period). The literal sense: 'During the ninety days of the summer practice period, the shuso (首座) leads the assembly in zazen and exhorts those who have not yet engaged in practice to do so. At the conclusion of the practice period (結制の終わる, the end of the binding), the shuso ascends the seat in place of the abbot (堂頭和尚に代わりて) and conducts the formal question-and-answer (陞座問答).' The passage illustrates several of the structural features of the shuso office that the compound 首座 encodes. First, the temporal frame 一夏九旬 ('one summer, ninety days') specifies the office as bounded by the practice period — the shuso is appointed for the duration of one ango and then relinquishes the office. The temporal limit is what makes the office function as a transitional stage in the longer training trajectory: the shuso is not promoted to a permanent rank but takes on the office for a specific period as a developmental marker. Second, the phrase 衆僧を率いて坐禅し ('leading the assembly in zazen') articulates the office's primary function during the practice period: the shuso is the senior practitioner whose presence and conduct organize the assembly's daily practice. The literal seating arrangement at the head of the meditation hall — the 首 of 首座 — is the spatial form this leadership takes. Third, the culminating phrase 堂頭和尚に代わりて陞座問答すべし ('ascending the seat in place of the abbot for the formal question-and-answer') articulates the hossenshiki (法戦式) function of the office: at the conclusion of the practice period the shuso publicly takes the abbot's high seat and responds to formal questions from the assembly, demonstrating the readiness to function as a respondent rather than a questioner that the practice period has cultivated. The substitution 代わりて ('in place of') is doctrinally significant: the shuso temporarily occupies the institutional position of the abbot, exercising for the duration of the ceremony a portion of the abbot's authority that is otherwise reserved. The compound 首座 therefore names an office whose three structural features — the temporal bounding, the leading-of-the-assembly during the period, and the ceremonial substitution at its conclusion — together constitute the office's specific work in the longer trajectory of monastic training.

passage: 上堂、僧堂前の直日、白槌して云く、法筵龍象衆、当に第一義を観ずべし。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the formal-talk (上堂) sections of the Record of Linji and the broader Linji-lineage convocation literature, illustrating the institutional role of the jikijitsu within the choreographed ritual of the dharma hall. The literal sense: 'At the formal convocation in the dharma hall, the jikijitsu (直日) standing before the monks' hall (僧堂前) sounds the white block (白槌) and announces: "Members of the dharma assembly (法筵), dragons and elephants of the host, you should observe the first principle (第一義)."' The passage illustrates the jikijitsu's institutional location within the choreography of the formal Chan convocation and the way the compound 直日 names the specifically practical-on-the-spot character of the office. First, the spatial location 僧堂前 ('before the monks' hall') situates the jikijitsu's position at the institutional threshold between the meditation hall and the dharma hall — the office is the practical hinge by which the assembly is moved from one ritual location to another, and the jikijitsu's authority is grounded in this transitional, on-the-spot positioning. Second, the implement 白槌 ('white block') names one of the practical tools of the office: the wooden block whose sounding signals the transition between phases of the convocation, whose authoritative use rests with the jikijitsu as the officer-of-the-day. The choice of 直 (on-the-spot) in the office name is doctrinally apt for an office whose authority is exercised through immediate, audible signaling: the jikijitsu's office is the office whose work is done in real time, in the moment, with the bell or block whose sounding cannot be postponed. Third, the formal pronouncement 法筵龍象衆、当に第一義を観ずべし ('members of the dharma assembly, dragons and elephants of the host, you should observe the first principle') is the standard convocation formula attributed to the white-block officer, and its delivery by the jikijitsu performs the office's institutional function: the formula opens the convocation by directing the assembly's attention to the dharma at hand, and the directing is done by the officer whose role is precisely to direct the assembly's attention through the practical choreography of the ritual. The compound 直日 therefore names an office whose specifically tactical-immediate character — what the jikijitsu does is done in the moment, with the implement-in-hand, on the spot — is preserved both etymologically (直 = on-the-spot, 日 = the day's rotation) and institutionally (the office's tools are immediate-signaling instruments wielded in real time).

passage: 侍者は、堂頭和尚に近侍して、進退を瞻視し、挙錯を奉行し、賓客を接送し、書状を呈通すべし。常に左右に在りて、和尚の旨を承け、衆僧に伝うべし。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the Chiji Shingi section of Dōgen's Eihei Shingi articulating the responsibilities of the jisha office. The literal sense: 'The jisha (侍者) attends closely on the abbot (堂頭和尚), watches over the abbot's movements (進退) and conduct (挙錯), receives and sees off guests (賓客), and conveys correspondence (書状). The jisha is constantly at the abbot's right and left, receives the abbot's intentions (旨), and conveys them to the assembly of monks (衆僧).' The passage illustrates several features of the institutional logic the compound 侍者 encodes. First, the verb 近侍 ('to attend closely') doubles down on the proximity dimension: 近 (close) is added to 侍 (to attend), and the reduplication marks the office as not merely an attendant role but specifically a close-attendant role whose institutional importance lies in the literal physical proximity to the abbot. The compound 近侍 is performing the same work that the 者 in 侍者 does — specifying the figure of the close-attending one — and the passage's choice of this verb is not redundant but emphatic. Second, the enumeration 進退を瞻視し、挙錯を奉行し、賓客を接送し、書状を呈通す ('watching the abbot's movements, attending the abbot's conduct, receiving and seeing off guests, conveying correspondence') articulates the office's practical scope as a coordinated cluster of tasks centered on the abbot's daily life: the jisha's work is not a single function but the integrated set of services that hold the abbot's institutional position in operating order. The cluster includes both inward-facing tasks (observing and supporting the abbot) and outward-facing tasks (mediating between the abbot and guests or correspondents), and the office's institutional function is precisely to absorb both. Third, the closing phrase 常に左右に在りて、和尚の旨を承け、衆僧に伝う ('constantly at the abbot's right and left, receiving the abbot's intentions and conveying them to the assembly of monks') articulates the office's mediating function in explicit terms: the jisha is the structural mediator between the abbot's intentions and the assembly's reception of them, and the office's institutional importance lies in the reliability of this mediation. The compound 侍者 therefore names an office whose three structural features — close physical proximity, integrated daily service, and reliable mediation between the principal and the assembly — together constitute the office's specific institutional work.

passage: 雲水の僧、行脚し参究する者、所到の処、必ず本師に事え、衆に随いて坐禅参問すべし。雲の出岫無心なるが如く、水の流澗自然なるが如し。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the Bendōhō and Shuryō Shingi sections of Dōgen's Eihei Shingi articulating the conduct expected of the unsui — the monks in formation. The literal sense: 'The unsui-monk (雲水の僧), the one who travels on foot (行脚) and inquires into the deepest matter (参究), must in every place where he arrives serve a primary teacher (本師) and follow the assembly in zazen and questioning. Like a cloud emerging from a mountain valley, no-mind; like water flowing in a brook, natural.' The passage illustrates several features of how the compound 雲水 operates in Dōgen's Sōtō articulation. First, the parallel construction 雲水の僧、行脚し参究する者 ('the unsui-monk, the one who travels on foot and inquires') glosses the compound 雲水 with the institutional realities it names: 行脚 (literally 'traveling on foot,' the practice of pilgrimage among monasteries) and 参究 ('deep inquiry,' the work of presenting one's understanding to a teacher and pressing through to deeper realization). The compound 雲水 is not abstract poetry but a name for these specific institutional practices, and Dōgen's parallel is what makes the institutional content of the poetic figure visible. Second, the prescription 所到の処、必ず本師に事え ('in every place where the unsui arrives, he must serve a primary teacher') articulates the structural feature that distinguishes the unsui from a simple wanderer: the cloud-and-water mode of life is conducted within the institutional structure of teacher-student relationships, and the unsui's mobility is mobility among teachers and assemblies, not mobility outside the institutional framework as such. Third, the closing simile 雲の出岫無心なるが如く、水の流澗自然なるが如し ('like a cloud emerging from a mountain valley, no-mind; like water flowing in a brook, natural') makes explicit the doctrinal content carried by the cloud-and-water figure. The cloud's unmindful emergence from the valley names the unsui's freedom from the calculative mind that would direct the journey toward an end-state; the water's natural flow names the unsui's conformity to the practice situation rather than the imposition of a preformed pattern. The figure 無心 (mushin, no-mind) is doctrinally load-bearing here: the unsui is not merely a young monk undergoing training but a figure whose mode of life is the practical analogue of the awakened mind's non-fixation, and the cloud-and-water simile is what makes this analogy concrete. The compound 雲水 therefore names an institutional office whose poetic-figural content is itself doctrinally articulated: to be an unsui is to live, for the duration of training, in the mode of practice that the awakened mind embodies.

passage: 禅堂は、衆僧の坐禅辦道の処なり。常住の節度、犍稚に依りて行ぜられ、退失すべからず。出入起居、皆な威儀を具すべし。
notes: A representative formulation from the Bendōhō section of Dōgen's Eihei Shingi articulating the institutional character of the 禅堂. The literal sense: 'The zendō (禅堂) is the place where the assembly of monks (衆僧) practices zazen and works at the Way (辦道). The constant schedule (節度) is conducted according to the bells and blocks (犍稚) and must not be departed from. Entries and exits, sitting and standing — all must be performed with proper deportment (威儀).' The passage illustrates several features of the institutional logic the compound 禅堂 encodes. First, the description 衆僧の坐禅辦道の処 ('the place where the assembly of monks practices zazen and works at the Way') articulates the hall's institutional function as a coordinate of two activities: 坐禅 (the sitting practice) and 辦道 (the broader work of practice-and-realization that bendō names). The hall is therefore not narrowly the place of zazen alone but the place where the comprehensive activity of practice — of which zazen is the central but not the only component — is conducted. The phrase carries doctrinal weight in Dōgen's framework: 辦道 is the verb of his foundational Bendōwa, and identifying the 禅堂 as the place of 辦道 ties the architectural space to the central activity of the Sōtō tradition. Second, the temporal phrase 常住の節度、犍稚に依りて行ぜられ ('the constant schedule, conducted according to the bells and blocks') articulates the institutional rhythm that makes the hall functional. The 犍稚 (Sanskrit ghaṇṭā, the bells and wooden signal instruments) are the practical apparatus by which the schedule is communicated to the assembly, and the office of the ino (維那) is responsible for their sounding. The hall's institutional life is therefore not free-form but tightly choreographed, and the choreography is what makes the integration of the assembly's activities possible. Third, the prescription 出入起居、皆な威儀を具すべし ('entries and exits, sitting and standing, all must be performed with proper deportment') articulates the doctrinal claim that the conduct of the body within the hall is itself part of the practice. The 威儀 (igi, the set of monastic forms governing posture, movement, and bearing) is not a peripheral matter of decorum but a structural component of practice-realization, and the hall's institutional character is constituted by the conduct of igi within it. The compound 禅堂 therefore names a space whose institutional function — the coordinated practice of the assembly under the discipline of the schedule and the conduct of igi — is doctrinally inseparable from the practice itself.

passage: 僧堂は、参禅辦道の場、衆僧の常住の処なり。一単に坐し、一単に臥し、一単に粥飯を喫す。これすなわち身心一如の処なり。
notes: A representative formulation from the Bendōhō section of Dōgen's Eihei Shingi articulating the institutional and doctrinal character of the 僧堂. The literal sense: 'The sōdō (僧堂) is the field of zazen and work-at-the-Way (参禅辦道の場), the constant dwelling (常住の処) of the assembly of monks. On a single tan position (一単) the monk sits in zazen, on a single tan position the monk lies down to sleep, on a single tan position the monk eats gruel and rice (粥飯). This is the very place of body-and-mind as one (身心一如).' The passage illustrates several features of the institutional logic the compound 僧堂 encodes and rewards close reading. First, the dual specification 参禅辦道の場、衆僧の常住の処 ('the field of zazen and work-at-the-Way, the constant dwelling of the assembly') articulates the hall's two integrated functions: it is the site of practice (the field of 参禅辦道) and the site of residence (the constant dwelling). The compound 僧堂 holds these two functions together as a single architectural and institutional reality, and the hall's specificity within Sōtō and Rinzai monasticism is precisely this integration. Second, the threefold 一単に坐し、一単に臥し、一単に粥飯を喫す ('on one tan position the monk sits, on one tan position the monk lies down, on one tan position the monk eats') compresses into three parallel clauses the architectural fact that gives the 僧堂 its institutional and doctrinal identity. The 単 (tan) is the single tatami-mat position assigned to each monk, and the doctrinal claim being articulated is that the same single space supports all three functions of the monk's daily life. The architectural integration is not a matter of efficiency or convenience but of doctrinal expression: meditation, sleep, and eating are not separate activities to be conducted in separate spaces but a single integrated practice that the architectural form of the hall makes concrete. Third, the closing phrase これすなわち身心一如の処なり ('this is the very place of body-and-mind as one') makes the doctrinal claim explicit. The Sōtō teaching of 身心一如 (shinjin ichinyo, the non-duality of body and mind) is not, in Dōgen's articulation, an abstract doctrinal proposition but a teaching whose institutional realization is the 僧堂 itself: the architectural space in which body and mind are integrated across the activities of meditation, sleep, and eating is the practical embodiment of the doctrine, and the doctrine is most concretely understood by living within the space. The compound 僧堂 therefore names a hall whose architectural integration is doctrinally articulated, and Dōgen's articulation of the hall's institutional character is one of the most direct instances of his consistent claim that doctrine and institutional form are not separable in Sōtō practice.

passage: 法堂は、住持上堂説法の処なり。朝夕の鐘鼓に随って衆を集め、住持高座に登りて宗旨を提唱す。一切の儀式、皆な威儀を具すべし。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the institutional regulations of the Eihei Shingi articulating the function of the 法堂 (hattō) within the monastic plan. The literal sense: 'The hattō (法堂) is the place where the abbot ascends the hall and preaches the dharma (上堂説法). According to the morning and evening bells and drums, the assembly is gathered, and the abbot ascends the high seat (高座) to formally present (提唱) the lineage's central teaching. All ceremonies must be conducted with full deportment (威儀).' The passage illustrates several features of the institutional logic the compound 法堂 encodes. First, the dual specification 住持上堂説法の処 ('the place where the abbot ascends the hall and preaches the dharma') articulates the hall's function not merely as a lecture space but as the architectural setting for two coordinated ritual acts: 上堂 (jōdō, ascending the hall) and 説法 (seppō, preaching the dharma). The compound 法堂 holds these two acts together as a single institutional reality, and the hall's specificity within Chan/Zen monasticism is precisely this integration. Second, the temporal-rhythmic phrase 朝夕の鐘鼓に随って衆を集め ('according to the morning and evening bells and drums, the assembly is gathered') articulates the institutional rhythm by which the hall's life is organized. The bells and drums (鐘鼓) are the practical signaling instruments; their sounding by the appropriate officers initiates the assembly's movement to the hall, and the hall's institutional life is therefore tightly choreographed rather than informal. Third, the architectural specification 住持高座に登りて宗旨を提唱す ('the abbot ascends the high seat and presents the lineage's central teaching') makes explicit the architectural embodiment of the abbot's teaching role. The 高座 (kōza, high seat) is the elevated throne that dominates the hall, and the act of 登る (climbing, ascending) is a physical-ritual gesture that materializes the institutional hierarchy. The compound 法堂 therefore names a hall whose architectural form, ritual choreography, and textual products are all integrated: the hall, the high seat, the ascent, the bells, the assembly, and the recorded sayings (語録) that preserve the abbot's discourse all constitute a single institutional reality.

passage: 三門は、衆生の解脱の入口なり。空・無相・無願、是れ三解脱門なり。一たび三門を入れば、世俗の塵を断ち、修行の道に入る。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the institutional and doctrinal articulation of the 三門 (sanmon) within the regulations and commentarial vocabulary of Sōtō monasticism. The literal sense: 'The sanmon (三門) is the entrance through which beings cross over to liberation. Emptiness (空), signlessness (無相), and wishlessness (無願) — these are the three gates of liberation (三解脱門). Once one has entered the sanmon, the dust of the worldly is severed, and one enters the path of practice.' The passage illustrates how the compound 三門 carries doctrinal symbolism in monumental architectural form. First, the opening identification 衆生の解脱の入口なり ('the entrance through which beings cross over to liberation') articulates the gate's function not as a mere architectural threshold but as a doctrinal threshold, and the gate's institutional weight is therefore inseparable from this symbolic content. Second, the threefold enumeration 空・無相・無願、是れ三解脱門なり ('emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness — these are the three gates of liberation') makes the doctrinal content of the three openings explicit. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā literature articulates these three as the three gates of liberation (三解脱門, sangedatsumon), and the architectural form of the sanmon is the monumental embodiment of this doctrinal structure: the three openings are the three gates given physical form. Third, the closing prescription 一たび三門を入れば、世俗の塵を断ち、修行の道に入る ('once one has entered the sanmon, the dust of the worldly is severed, and one enters the path of practice') articulates the institutional consequence of the threshold-crossing. The act of passing through the gate is not merely physical movement but a ritual transition from the lay world to the monastic life, and the gate's monumental form is calibrated to the weight of this transition. The compound 三門 therefore names a structure in which architectural form, doctrinal symbolism, and institutional function are integrated into a single threshold whose passage materializes the practitioner's entry into the path of liberation.

passage: 黄檗、師の手を執りて曰く、汝、即ち今、何処にか向かう。師曰く、河南に向かう。檗曰く、汝、即ち得たり。是れ、印可するの言なり。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the transmission narrative of the Record of Linji articulating the moment of inka. The literal sense: 'Huangbo took the master's [Linji's] hand and said: "Where will you go now?" The master said: "I will go to Henan." Huangbo said: "You have attained it." This is the speech of inka.' The passage compresses into a brief exchange the institutional and doctrinal logic of the compound 印可. First, the physical gesture 黄檗、師の手を執りて ('Huangbo took the master's hand') marks the encounter as one of intimate transmission rather than abstract certification. The compound 印可 in this passage is enacted through the bodily contact between master and disciple, and the gesture compresses into a single physical act the figure of the seal-impression: Huangbo's grasping of Linji's hand is itself a kind of seal-impression upon the disciple. Second, the brief verbal exchange — Huangbo asks where Linji will go, Linji answers, Huangbo affirms — illustrates the structurally unobtrusive form of the inka act. There is no formal ceremony in this passage, no elaborate ritual; the inka is enacted in the simplest possible exchange of question and affirmation, and yet the institutional weight of the act is fully present. The Chan tradition's literature is consistent in this regard: the institutional rigor of inka does not require external pomp, and the most institutionally significant inka acts are often the most apparently informal. Third, the closing identification 是れ、印可するの言なり ('this is the speech of inka') is the commentator's gloss that names the exchange as inka, and the gloss is doctrinally significant because it makes explicit what the encounter has been doing. Without the gloss the exchange might be read as a casual goodbye between teacher and student; with the gloss the institutional weight of the moment becomes legible. The compound 印可 therefore names an institutional act whose form can range from formal ceremony to apparently casual exchange, and the Record of Linji's preservation of this informal-but-weighty mode is one of the foundational textual articulations of the way inka actually operates in Chan practice.

passage: 嗣法は、師資親しく相見え、面授口決して、嗣書を授くるなり。一切の仏祖、皆な嗣法に依りて法を伝う。嗣法無くんば、仏法も亦た無し。
notes: A representative formulation drawn from the institutional articulation of dharma-succession in Dōgen's Sōtō monasticism, echoing the doctrinal logic of the Shōbōgenzō fascicle 嗣書 (Shisho). The literal sense: 'Shihō (嗣法) is conducted when master and disciple meet face-to-face in person (師資親しく相見え), the dharma is conferred mouth-to-mouth (面授口決), and the document of succession (嗣書) is bestowed. All Buddhas and patriarchs (一切の仏祖) transmit the dharma through shihō. Without shihō, the Buddha-dharma also is not.' The passage illustrates several features of the institutional and doctrinal logic the compound 嗣法 encodes. First, the requirement 師資親しく相見え、面授口決 ('master and disciple meet face-to-face in person, the dharma is conferred mouth-to-mouth') articulates the central Sōtō claim that dharma-succession requires direct embodied encounter. The compound 面授 (menju, face-to-face transmission) is invoked here as the structural form within which 嗣法 is enacted, and the two compounds together articulate the doctrinal claim that dharma cannot be transmitted at a distance, through documents alone, or through any form of mediated communication: only the direct encounter of master and disciple in person constitutes authentic shihō. Second, the documentary specification 嗣書を授くるなり ('the document of succession is bestowed') articulates the institutional weight of the documentary apparatus that accompanies the transmission. The 嗣書 (shisho) is the formal document of succession, and its bestowal upon the disciple is the institutional materialization of the dharma-succession. The document is doctrinally significant — Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō fascicle on the shisho is one of his most elaborate articulations of the institutional logic of transmission — and the document's physical transmission from master to disciple is part of how the act of shihō is institutionally constituted. Third, the closing claim 嗣法無くんば、仏法も亦た無し ('without shihō, the Buddha-dharma also is not') articulates the doctrinal weight of the institutional act in its strongest form. The claim is not merely that shihō is one mechanism by which dharma is transmitted but that the very existence of authentic dharma in the world depends on the institutional rigor of shihō. Without the unbroken chain of legitimate succession from Śākyamuni through the patriarchs to the present master and heir, the Buddha-dharma itself ceases to exist as an authentic transmission, and the institutional integrity of the lineage is therefore inseparable from the doctrinal integrity of the dharma. The compound 嗣法 therefore names an institutional act whose doctrinal weight is, in Dōgen's articulation, foundational: the dharma is what passes through shihō, and the lineage is the institutional reality of that passing.

passage: 薪は灰となる、さらにかへりて薪となるべきにあらず。しかあるを、灰はのち、薪はさきと見取すべからず。しるべし、薪は薪の法位に住して、さきありのちあり。前後ありといへども、前後際断せり。灰は灰の法位にありて、のちありさきあり。
notes: Dōgen's celebrated firewood-and-ash passage from the Genjōkōan fascicle, the foundational articulation of his distinctive reading of impermanence. The literal sense: 'Firewood becomes ash; it cannot return again to being firewood. Yet do not regard ash as later and firewood as earlier. Know: firewood abides in the dharma-position of firewood, and there is a before and an after. Although there is a before and an after, the before-and-after are cut off. Ash is in the dharma-position of ash, and there is an after and a before.' The passage is doing precise doctrinal work that depends entirely on the technical reading of 無常 the Shōbōgenzō articulates. Ordinary readings of impermanence treat firewood and ash as two states of a single underlying substance that persists across the transformation, with firewood becoming ash through a temporal process. Dōgen refuses this framing. Each phenomenon — firewood, ash — is fully its present condition without remainder, and the apparent temporal succession from firewood to ash is not a continuous flow but a discontinuous structure in which each 'dharma-position' (法位, hōi) is its own complete actuality. The phrase 前後際断 (zengo saidan, 'the before-and-after are cut off') is the doctrinal hinge: the ordinary reading of impermanence as a continuous flow of states is replaced by a reading in which each moment is its own complete arising-and-passing without temporal extension. This is what 無常 means in Dōgen's sense: not that things change but that each present condition is its own complete actuality, fully arisen and fully passing in the same moment, without the continuous temporal substrate that ordinary mind imagines. The passage is the locus classicus for the Sōtō reading of mujō and articulates in compact prose the philosophical move that the longer 'Busshō' fascicle elaborates as 無常仏性.

passage: ただ生死すなはち涅槃とこころえて、生死としていとふべきもなく、涅槃としてねがふべきもなし。このときはじめて、生死をはなるる分あり。
notes: The doctrinal hinge of Dōgen's brief Shōji fascicle, articulating the Sōtō refusal of the standard opposition between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. The literal sense: 'Just understand that birth-and-death (生死) is itself nirvāṇa, and there is nothing to be hated as birth-and-death, nothing to be desired as nirvāṇa. Only at this time is there a portion of release from birth-and-death.' The passage compresses into a few clauses the philosophical move that distinguishes the Sōtō position on 生死 from the standard Buddhist framing in which the cycle is the condition that liberation transcends. The doctrinal logic is precise. The opening identification 生死すなはち涅槃 ('birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa') uses the copula すなはち (sunawachi, 'precisely is, is identical with') to assert the non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa — paralleling the structure of 色即是空 (form is precisely emptiness) in the Heart Sutra and applying the same non-dual logic to the cycle of conditioned existence and the unconditioned. The middle clauses then derive the practical consequence: if 生死 is itself nirvāṇa, there is nothing to be hated about birth-and-death and nothing to be sought in nirvāṇa, and the practitioner's stance toward the cycle is neither aversion nor escape-seeking but full inhabitation. The closing clause このときはじめて、生死をはなるる分あり ('only at this time is there a portion of release from birth-and-death') is doctrinally subtle: release from 生死 is not the cessation of birth-and-death as a condition but the cessation of the practitioner's grasping at it as a problem. The passage is one of Dōgen's most concentrated articulations of the Sōtō position on saṃsāra and nirvāṇa and stands in productive tension with the Pure Land and earlier Buddhist framings of 生死 as the condition that liberation transcends.

passage: 迷時師度、悟了自度。度名雖一、用処不同。某甲生在邊方、語音不正、蒙師付法、今已得悟。只合自性自度。
notes: Huineng's response to Hongren in the transmission narrative of the Platform Sutra, articulating the relationship between the practitioner's ordinary condition of cyclic transmigration and the awakening that liberates from it. The literal sense: 'When deluded, the master ferries [the disciple] across; when awakened, one ferries oneself across. Although the name "ferrying" is one, its function differs. I was born in a border region and my speech is not standard; having received the dharma from the master, I have now attained awakening. It is only fitting that one's own self-nature ferry one's own self.' The passage uses the figure of 度 (du, ferrying-across) — the standard Buddhist metaphor for liberation as a crossing from the shore of saṃsāra to the shore of nirvāṇa — to articulate the relationship between the cyclic transmigration of 輪廻 and the awakening that liberates from it. The figure is doctrinally precise: 輪廻 is the condition the ferry crosses from, and the master's role is to ferry the deluded disciple across this cycle until the disciple has attained the awakening that allows self-ferrying. Huineng's distinctive contribution in the passage is the assertion that the ferrying ultimately must be self-ferrying — the awakened practitioner is the one who has recognized that 自性 (self-nature) is itself the means of crossing, and the master's earlier ferrying was preparatory to this recognition. The passage situates 輪廻 within the soteriological architecture of the Southern school: the cycle of transmigration is the condition that liberation addresses, but the means of addressing it is the recognition of self-nature rather than the cumulative effort of practice across lifetimes. The Sūtra's larger claim — that this recognition is sudden rather than gradual — gives the passage its polemical edge, but the doctrinal content of the figure of 輪廻 as the condition to be crossed is shared across schools.

passage: 正法千年、像法千年、末法万年。正法には教行証三つながら具す。像法には教行のみありて証無し。末法には教のみありて行証共に無し。
notes: The Mappō Tōmyōki's foundational articulation of the three dharma-ages and the doctrinal-practical content of mappō. The literal sense: 'The age of the true dharma (正法) is a thousand years; the age of the semblance dharma (像法) is a thousand years; the age of the latter dharma (末法) is ten thousand years. In the age of the true dharma, all three — teaching (教), practice (行), and realization (証) — are fully present. In the age of the semblance dharma, only teaching and practice remain; realization is absent. In the age of the latter dharma, only teaching remains; both practice and realization are absent.' The passage compresses into a few clauses the doctrinal architecture that shaped Kamakura Buddhist reform. The periodization of post-Buddha history into three eras of progressively diminishing dharma-efficacy is articulated with diagnostic precision: each era loses one of the three components that constitute the dharma's full operation, and the latter age is characterized by the survival of the teaching alone, without the practice and realization that would give the teaching its liberating effect. The doctrinal-practical consequence is severe: in mappō, the practitioner has access to the dharma's teachings (the sutras and treatises remain available) but the conditions of practice and realization are no longer adequate, and standard religious life — monastic ordination, ethical discipline, meditative cultivation, the attainment of awakening — is structurally impossible. This claim is the doctrinal warrant for the Kamakura reform movements: if the standard means are no longer adequate to mappō, new modes of practice fitted to the degenerate age must be developed, and Hōnen, Shinran, Nichiren, and others read the Mappō Tōmyōki passage as licensing their respective reformulations. The treatise's brief presentation of the periodization is therefore not a piece of antiquarian doctrinal history but a diagnostic of the contemporary religious condition that requires immediate practical response.

passage: 祇園精舎の鐘の声、諸行無常の響あり。沙羅双樹の花の色、盛者必衰の理をあらはす。おごれる人も久しからず、ただ春の夜の夢のごとし。たけき者も遂にはほろびぬ、ひとへに風の前の塵に同じ。
notes: The opening of the Heike Monogatari, one of the most recognized passages in all of Japanese literature and the locus classicus for the cultural-aesthetic register of 諸行無常 in Japanese tradition. The literal sense: 'The bell of Gion-shōja resounds the impermanence of all conditioned things (諸行無常). The color of the sāl trees' double flowers reveals the truth that the prosperous must decline (盛者必衰). The proud do not endure; they are like a dream on a spring night. The mighty fall in the end; they are no different from dust before the wind.' The passage compresses into four clauses the doctrinal-aesthetic frame within which the entire Heike Monogatari unfolds and articulates the position 諸行無常 occupies in Japanese cultural memory. The doctrinal precision is exact: the bell of Gion-shōja (Jetavana monastery, where the Buddha is said to have spent many of his retreats) resounds the universal claim of the first dharma seal, and the work's narrative of the rise and catastrophic fall of the Taira clan is presented as an extended demonstration of this universal teaching working out in human history. The compound 諸行無常 is paired with 盛者必衰 (jōsha hissui, the prosperous must decline), which is not a Buddhist canonical formula but a Chinese-classical proverb that the Heike's author has set alongside the dharma seal as a complementary articulation in a more historically and politically focused register. The pairing is doctrinally and rhetorically precise: the dharma seal 諸行無常 supplies the universal Buddhist frame, and the proverb 盛者必衰 specifies the political-historical application that the Heike's narrative will elaborate. The literary fabric of the passage — the bell, the sāl flowers, the spring-night dream, the dust before the wind — supplies the imagistic vocabulary through which mujō becomes accessible to the medieval Japanese imagination, and these images recur across the Heike and across centuries of subsequent Japanese literature as the standard imagistic register for impermanence. The passage is the moment in Japanese cultural history at which 諸行無常 ceased to be solely a piece of Buddhist doctrine and became a structuring principle of Japanese literary and cultural memory; the doctrinal claim and the literary topos are inseparable in the Japanese reception of the phrase from this passage onward.

passage: 五十四年、第一天を照らす。箇の趵跳をなして、大千を触破す。咦、渾身覓むるなく、活きながら黄泉に陥つ。
notes: Dōgen's death poem (辞世偈), composed in 1253 shortly before his death and preserved in the Eihei Kōroku as the final formal verse of his recorded sayings. The literal sense: 'Fifty-four years illuminating the first heaven. Making this somersault, I shatter the thousand-fold worlds. Ah! With my whole body seeking nothing, I plunge alive into the Yellow Springs.' The poem compresses into four lines a final articulation of Dōgen's distinctive Sōtō position on practice, realization, and the relationship between life and death. The opening clause names the temporal extent of Dōgen's life (he was fifty-four when he composed the poem) but immediately reframes it as a function of practice: the fifty-four years are not biographical duration but the time across which 'the first heaven' has been illuminated — practice as the activity of illumination across the span of a life. The middle clauses articulate the structural disposition of dying as a single decisive movement: 'making this somersault' (個の趵跳) names the moment of dying as a deliberate act, a single executed movement, not a passive undergoing; and 'shattering the thousand-fold worlds' (大千を触破す) names the cosmic-scale consequence of this single act, the death of the practitioner being not an event embedded in a larger world but an event that breaks the conceptual frame within which 'world' and 'death' are ordinarily understood. The closing clauses articulate the practitioner's relationship to death in a doctrinal register that is distinctively Dōgen's: 'with my whole body seeking nothing' (渾身覓むるなく) names the non-grasping disposition that Sōtō practice cultivates and that the moment of death tests; and 'I plunge alive into the Yellow Springs' (活きながら黄泉に陥つ) — 'Yellow Springs' (黄泉, kōsen) being the classical Chinese figure for the underworld of the dead — refuses the standard binary of life-and-death by asserting that the speaker plunges into death while still alive, the alive-and-the-dead being not-two in the doctrinal frame within which Dōgen's lifelong articulation of 生死 (shōji, birth-and-death) has unfolded. The poem is therefore not merely a final personal utterance but a final doctrinal articulation: Dōgen's death poem demonstrates in compressed verse the same Sōtō position on practice-realization, non-duality, and the inseparability of life and death that the Shōbōgenzō has articulated across thousands of pages, performing the position rather than merely stating it. The poem stands as one of the most celebrated examples of the jisei genre in the Zen monastic tradition and as a paradigmatic case of the genre's doctrinal-pedagogical function.

passage: 無無明、亦無無明尽、乃至無老死、亦無老死尽。
notes: The Heart Sutra's compressed denial of the twelve links of dependent origination (十二因縁), articulating the Mahāyāna position on the relationship between the Abhidharma analysis of 縁起 and the Prajñāpāramitā doctrine of emptiness. The literal sense: 'There is no ignorance, and no end of ignorance; up to no old-age-and-death, and no end of old-age-and-death.' The passage operates by naming the first and last links of the twelve-link chain (ignorance, 無明; old-age-and-death, 老死) and using the formula 乃至 ('up to' or 'as far as') to compress the intervening ten links into a single elided formulation. The negation 無 (no, without) is then applied twice to each of the named terms: there is no ignorance and no end of ignorance, no old-age-and-death and no end of old-age-and-death. The doctrinal logic of the doubled negation is precise. The Abhidharma analysis of 縁起 articulates the chain of conditions through which suffering arises (the twelve links from ignorance through old-age-and-death) and the corresponding analysis of how the chain can be unraveled by addressing its conditions (the cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of formations, and so on through to the cessation of old-age-and-death). The standard Buddhist soteriological frame is that practice cuts the chain by ending ignorance, and the cessation of suffering follows. The Heart Sutra's negation refuses both sides of this standard frame: it negates both the conditions and the cessation of the conditions, denying that the twelve-link analysis has ultimate purchase on reality at all. The doctrinal point is the Madhyamaka claim that pratītyasamutpāda is itself empty: the twelve-link chain articulates the relational structure of conditioned arising at the conventional level, but at the ultimate level even the chain itself lacks svabhāva and the doctrine of dependent origination must be deployed as a teaching tool rather than as a final ontological claim. The passage is one of the most concentrated articulations of the Madhyamaka position on the relationship between the Abhidharma scholasticism of conditioned arising and the Prajñāpāramitā doctrine of emptiness, and demonstrates the characteristic Mahāyāna move of refusing to let any doctrinal articulation — even the foundational doctrine of pratītyasamutpāda — settle as a final positive claim. For students approaching 縁起, the passage performs the doctrinal move that distinguishes the Mahāyāna inflection of the doctrine from the earlier Abhidharma articulation: pratītyasamutpāda is not a foundational theory of how things come into being but a teaching device that, having done its diagnostic work, must itself be released.

passage: 於是文殊師利問維摩詰、我等各自説已、仁者当説、何等是菩薩入不二法門。時維摩詰黙然無言。文殊師利歎曰、善哉善哉、乃至無有文字語言、是真入不二法門。
notes: The culminating exchange of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra's 'Dharma-gate of Non-duality' chapter, in which the highest articulation of 不二 is performed as silence. The literal sense: 'Thereupon Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "Each of us has spoken in turn. Now you, sir, must speak: what is the bodhisattva's entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality?" At that moment Vimalakīrti was silent and did not speak. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Even to the point of having no letters or words — this is the true entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality."' The passage operates as the culmination of an extended sequence in which thirty-two bodhisattvas have each articulated non-duality through specific negations of dualistic distinctions (production-and-cessation, defilement-and-purity, self-and-not-self, and so on), each demonstrating the doctrine through a particular dualistic frame they refuse. Mañjuśrī then offers a higher-order articulation: the true entry into non-duality is the absence of all such formulations, the recognition that every positive articulation of non-duality falls back into the dualistic frame the doctrine suspends. Vimalakīrti's silence is the next level of articulation: not the statement that non-duality cannot be stated but the actual performance of non-stating, the demonstration that non-duality is enacted in the suspension of articulation rather than in any propositional formulation about it. Mañjuśrī's praise then completes the structure: the recognition that the silence is the highest teaching is itself the recognition that what was being sought through articulation was always the suspension of articulation, and the silent moment becomes the dharma-gate that the entire chapter has been pointing toward. The passage is one of the most celebrated teaching moments in all of Mahāyāna literature and a foundational reference point for the entire Chan/Zen tradition's continued reliance on silence, gesture, paradox, and the koan as teaching devices that exceed propositional articulation. The doctrinal stake is precise: 不二 is not a piece of knowledge that can be transmitted as content but a structural disposition that can only be performed and recognized; the Vimalakīrti Sūtra's narrative-pedagogical staging of the doctrine through the sequence of bodhisattva articulations and the final silence is itself the teaching the passage gives, and the passage's enormous influence on East Asian Buddhism — including its repeated invocation in Chan/Zen texts as the warrant for non-discursive teaching methods — derives from this performative-pedagogical structure rather than from any doctrinal content the passage might be paraphrased as carrying.

passage: 自他一如にして、依正不二なり。修と証と一等にして、迷悟ひとつなり。仏祖の正伝は、この消息を見徹するにあり。
notes: A characteristic Dōgen-idiom articulation of the doctrinal logic that 一如 carries, in which the compound is paired across multiple registers with 不二 (not-two) and 一等 (one-as-equal) to assert the non-dual identity of self-and-other, of the sentient subject and its environing world (依正, eshō), of practice and realization, and of delusion and awakening. The literal sense: 'Self and other are one-as-suchness; the supporting and the supported are not-two. Practice and realization are one-as-equal; delusion and awakening are one. The right transmission of the buddhas and patriarchs lies in seeing through to this state of affairs.' The passage operates as a compact statement of the structural logic that runs through Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō, in which 一如 articulates the positive-affirmative side of the non-dual logic (oneness-as-suchness) while 不二 articulates the negative-theological side (refusal of the binary frame), and the two compounds together hold the doctrinal architecture that grounds Dōgen's distinctive Sōtō articulations: 身心一如 (body-mind as one), 修証一等 (practice and realization as one-equal), 自他一如 (self-and-other as one). The doctrinal stake of the passage is that the right transmission (正伝) does not consist in receiving a doctrinal content but in seeing through to the non-dual structure that 一如 names — a structure that is not a metaphysical claim about substantial unity but an articulation of how phenomena are not-two by virtue of their shared suchness, the bare thusness that holds across them without making them substantively identical. The passage is representative of Dōgen's broader use of 一如 across the Shōbōgenzō, where the compound is invoked across Bendōwa, Genjōkōan, Bukkyō, Sansuikyō, and other fascicles as the structural principle organizing his non-dual articulations.

passage: 舍利子、色不異空、空不異色、色即是空、空即是色。受想行識亦復如是。
notes: The Heart Sutra's celebrated chiastic formula in Xuanzang's 649 CE Chinese translation, the doctrinal pivot of the Prajñāpāramitā corpus's compression into 260 characters. The literal sense: 'Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is precisely emptiness; emptiness is precisely form. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise empty.' The passage operates as a four-stage chiastic articulation of the non-dual identity of form and emptiness, addressed in apostrophe to Śāriputra (the foremost of the Buddha's monastic disciples in wisdom, here positioned as the recipient of Avalokiteśvara's bodhisattva-instruction). The chiasmus moves through four logical stages. The first two stages assert non-difference (色不異空、空不異色, form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form), articulating the doctrinal claim through the negation 不異 (not different). The second two stages assert non-mediated identity (色即是空、空即是色, form is precisely emptiness, emptiness is precisely form), strengthening the claim from non-difference to identity through the copula 即是. The progression from non-difference to identity is doctrinally precise: the formula does not stop at the relatively weak claim that form and emptiness are not different but advances to the strong claim that they are precisely identical, with the immediacy of 即 forbidding any reading in which form and emptiness are two related things rather than one identical reality articulated under two registers. The passage then extends the formula across the four remaining aggregates ('feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise empty') through the elliptical 亦復如是 ('are likewise so'), generalizing the non-dual identification from form alone to the entire psychophysical complex of the five aggregates (五蘊, pañca-skandha) that the Abhidharma analysis takes as the constituents of the conventional self. The doctrinal stake of the passage is the Madhyamaka-Prajñāpāramitā middle way between the two extremes of eternalism (the reification of phenomena as ultimately real) and nihilism (the denial of phenomena as illusory), achieved by asserting the non-dual identity of phenomenal appearance and emptiness. The passage is the most-recited and most-commented passage in all of East Asian Buddhism, chanted daily across all Mahāyāna schools, and the structural model for non-dual identifications throughout the Chan/Zen tradition (修証一等, 定慧不二, 無常仏性) all draw on its logical architecture.

passage: 一即一切、一切即一。一中解無量、無量中解一。一一塵中、現一切法界。
notes: A canonical articulation of the dharma-realm cosmology that runs through the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and is condensed in the Huayan masters' commentary literature, expressing the structural claim that the totality of the dharma-realm is fully present in each particular phenomenon and that each particular phenomenon is fully expressive of the totality. The literal sense: 'One is precisely all; all is precisely one. Within one, the immeasurable is understood; within the immeasurable, one is understood. Within each particle of dust, the entire dharma-realm appears.' The passage operates through a sequence of mutually entailing identifications. The first stage (一即一切、一切即一) uses the copula 即 — the same non-mediated-identity copula that figures in the Heart Sutra's 色即是空 formula — to assert the non-dual identity of the one and the all, refusing both the reduction of the all to the one (which would be monistic) and the segregation of the one from the all (which would be pluralistic). The second stage (一中解無量、無量中解一) generalizes the structure across the relationship between unity and multiplicity, asserting that to understand the one is to understand the immeasurable and vice versa — the dharma-realm is a totality in which each register implies the others. The third stage (一一塵中、現一切法界) gives the cosmological-imagistic articulation: within each particle of dust, the entire dharma-realm appears, with the metaphor of the dust-particle (塵, jin) functioning as the smallest possible particular, the radically minimal phenomenon, in which the totality is nonetheless fully present. The doctrinal stake of the passage is the Huayan claim that the dharma-realm is a totality of mutually interpenetrating phenomena in which the whole is fully expressed in each part — the cosmological frame that Indra's Net (帝網) imagery dramatizes and the Fourfold Dharmadhātu doctrine systematizes. The passage establishes 法界 as not merely the sum of all phenomena but the structurally specific totality in which each particular contains and reflects the whole, and the Chan/Zen tradition's repeated invocations of the totality being expressed in each particular moment of practice draw on the dharma-realm cosmology that this passage articulates.

passage: 如帝釈宮殿、寶網覆上、一一寶珠、各現一切寶珠之影。一一影中、復現一切寶珠之影。如是重重無尽、事事無礙。
notes: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra's celebrated metaphor of Indra's Net (帝網, Indra-jāla), articulated in the Huayan masters' commentary literature as the imagistic ground for the doctrine of 事事無礙. The literal sense: 'Like Indra's palace, where a jewel-net covers above, and within each jewel each other jewel's reflection appears; and within each reflection, each other jewel's reflection appears again. In this way, in infinite recursion, phenomenon-and-phenomenon are without obstruction.' The passage operates through a sequence of cosmic-imagistic stagings of the doctrine. The first stage situates the metaphor in Indra's heavenly palace (帝釈宮殿), establishing the cosmological scope; the second stage describes the jewel-net (寶網) covering the palace; the third stage articulates the structural-recursive claim — within each jewel, each other jewel's reflection appears (一一寶珠、各現一切寶珠之影) — and immediately recurs the structure within each reflection (一一影中、復現一切寶珠之影), generating the infinite recursion that 重重無尽 ('layer after layer, without exhaustion') names. The metaphor's force is precisely structural: each jewel is fully itself, distinct from every other jewel, and each jewel reflects every other jewel and the reflection of every other jewel in every other jewel, in infinite recursion without confusion or obstruction. The metaphor stages the dual-register reality that 事事無礙 names in compact doctrinal form: each phenomenon remains fully itself in its concrete particularity, and each phenomenon is fully expressive of every other phenomenon in unobstructed mutual interpenetration, without the dual structure collapsing into either monistic unity or pluralistic separation. The doctrinal stake of the passage is the Huayan claim that the awakened dharma-vision sees the dharma-realm as Indra's Net — a totality in which each particular contains and reflects every other particular without obstruction. The passage's enormous influence on East Asian Buddhism extends well beyond the Huayan school proper: the imagery of Indra's Net is invoked across the Chan/Zen tradition as the cosmological background for claims about the totality of reality being expressed in each particular moment of practice, and the modern reception of Huayan thought in Western Buddhist studies has tended to focus on this image as the most accessible articulation of the dharmadhātu cosmology.

passage: 舎利子、是諸法空相、不生不滅、不垢不浄、不増不減。
notes: Shariputra — the nature of all dharmas is emptiness: not arising, not ceasing; not defiled, not pure; not increasing, not decreasing. The cascade of negations places 不生 first in the sequence through which the dharma-nature is articulated by sustained negation, giving the unborn the structural priority of opening the negative-theological articulation that the rest of the cascade extends across the binaries of purity and increase. The doctrinal grammar is precise: 不生 is not the assertion of a positive non-arisen substance but the active suspension of the conceptual frame of arising — paired immediately with 不滅 (not ceasing) so that neither pole of the arising-and-perishing structure is allowed to settle on the dharma-nature. The compound 不生不滅 thereby operates as the Heart Sutra's compact articulation of the unborn-and-undying that the rest of the cascade extends. The passage is recited daily in Japanese Buddhist practice and remains the canonical scriptural reference point for 不生 across the Mahāyāna tradition; Bankei's later teaching of the unborn presupposes this scriptural ground while shifting the register from scholastic negation to practical-existential pedagogy of the present functioning of awareness, but the compact scriptural articulation here remains the doctrinal anchor against which Bankei's pedagogy is calibrated.

passage: 執事元是迷、契理亦非悟。門門一切境、回互不回互。
notes: To grasp at phenomena (執事) is fundamentally delusion; to merge with principle (契理) is also not awakening. Each gate, each circumstance — interactive yet not interactive. The passage articulates the precise structural condition of the 理事 dialectic in compressed verse form: the doctrinal point is that grasping at either 事 or 理 in isolation misses the dialectic. To grasp at phenomena (執事) is the ordinary delusion of taking the differentiated particulars as self-sufficient realities; to merge with principle (契理) is the mirror-image delusion of taking the absolute pole as self-sufficient. Both are delusion because the truth of the dharma-nature lies in the structural relationship between the two poles rather than in either pole alone. Shitou's 'interactive yet not interactive' (回互不回互) names the precise structural condition: the two poles interpenetrate without collapsing into one, and the differentiated phenomena remain themselves without losing their saturation by principle. The passage gives 理 its precise doctrinal place: not a hidden absolute that the practitioner must reach by abandoning phenomena, but the absolute-universal pole whose dialectical relationship with phenomena structures the dharma-nature. The Sandōkai's articulation of the dialectic is the foundational doctrinal statement of the Caodong/Sōtō tradition's handling of 理 and is commented on continuously across the tradition from Dongshan and his successors through Dōgen and the modern Sōtō transmission.

passage: 事存函蓋合、理応箭鋒拄。承言須会宗、勿自立規矩。
notes: Phenomena fit together as a box and its lid (函蓋); principle responds as the points of two arrows meeting in mid-flight (箭鋒). To receive the words you must penetrate to the source; do not establish rules of your own. The passage articulates the precise structural relationship between 事 and 理 through two paired images that capture the dialectic in compact figural form. The image of the box and lid (函蓋合) names the way phenomena fit one another in the dharma-realm — each particular is fitted to every other particular without remainder, like a box and its lid that close perfectly without gap. The image of the arrow-points meeting (箭鋒拄) names the way principle responds — the absolute-universal pole meets each phenomenon as precisely as two arrows meeting point-to-point in mid-flight, with no margin for error or approximation. The doctrinal stake of 事 in this passage is its perfect mutual fitting: each phenomenon is fully itself in its concrete particularity, and yet is fitted to every other phenomenon without remainder, in the structural condition that the highest Huayan register names 事事無礙. The passage's closing instruction — receive the words but penetrate to the source, do not establish rules of your own — is the standard Caodong injunction against scholastic systematization of the dialectic, insisting that the 理事 vocabulary be received as a pointer to the structural condition rather than as a set of rules to be applied.

passage: 仏道をならふといふは、自己をならふ也。自己をならふといふは、自己をわするるなり。自己をわするるといふは、万法に証せらるるなり。万法に証せらるるといふは、自己の身心および他己の身心をして脱落せしむるなり。
notes: The celebrated passage from the Genjōkōan fascicle articulating the falling-away of body-mind as the structural moment in the unfolding of practice-realization. To study the buddha way is to study the self; to study the self is to forget the self; to forget the self is to be actualized by the myriad things; to be actualized by the myriad things is to cause the body-mind of self and the body-mind of others to fall away (脱落). The passage stages 身心脱落 as the culminating moment in a four-step structural articulation that proceeds from the self-study at the beginning of practice through the forgetting-of-self in the middle to the actualization-by-the-myriad-things and finally to the falling-away of body-mind in the structural completion. The doctrinal precision of the passage is in the calibrated grammar: the falling-away is not the result of practice but the structural condition that practice-realization is, and the inclusion of 'the body-mind of others' (他己の身心) in the falling-away makes clear that the compound names a structural condition rather than a private subjective event. The passage is the locus classicus of the Sōtō articulation of 身心脱落 across the Genjōkōan fascicle and is one of the most widely commented passages in the entire Shōbōgenzō. Modern Sōtō teachers from Sawaki Kōdō through Shunryu Suzuki and Uchiyama Kōshō have made the passage the central reference for their articulation of zazen as the activity in which body-mind falls away.

passage: いはゆる有時は、時すでにこれ有なり、有はみな時なり。
notes: The opening doctrinal claim of the Shōbōgenzō Uji fascicle: 'What is called being-time means that time is already being, and being is all of it time.' The passage articulates the structural identity of being and time in compact form across two parallel claims: time is already being (時すでにこれ有なり) and being is all of it time (有はみな時なり). The doctrinal precision is in the bidirectional claim: not just that beings exist in time or that time articulates beings, but that the two structures are mutually identical — every articulation of time is the being of that articulation, and every being is the timing of its being. The passage opens the fascicle's extended doctrinal argument and establishes the frame within which the rest of the fascicle's articulations operate: the mountain is time, the standing-on-the-summit is time, the monk passing through the marketplace is time, each particular being the temporal articulation through which it occurs. The compact bidirectional claim of this opening passage has been the object of continuous commentarial attention from Dōgen's immediate disciples through the modern Sōtō and Western philosophical reception, and the passage is taken across the tradition as the doctrinal anchor of the being-time articulation. Modern translators including Heine, Kim, Tanahashi, and Nishijima have given particular attention to this opening passage as the structural key to the rest of the fascicle.

passage: 諸法の仏法なる時節、すなはち迷悟あり、修行あり、生あり死あり、諸仏あり衆生あり。万法ともにわれにあらざる時節、まどひなくさとりなく、諸仏なく衆生なく、生なく滅なし。
notes: The celebrated opening passage of the Genjōkōan fascicle, articulating the dialectic of practice-realization across two paired registers. When all things are dharma (諸法の仏法なる時節), there is delusion and awakening, practice, birth-and-death, buddhas and sentient beings; when all things are without self (万法ともにわれにあらざる時節), there is neither delusion nor awakening, neither buddhas nor sentient beings, neither birth nor extinction.
