The passage stages the two registers as paired articulations of the same condition — the first register names the dimension in which differentiated phenomena are fully present in their dharmic articulation; the second register names the dimension in which the predicative grammar that distinguishes phenomena from one another has fallen away. The doctrinal stake of the passage is in its calibrated double-register articulation: 現成公案 names neither the first register alone (which would risk reifying the differentiated phenomena) nor the second register alone (which would risk collapsing the differentiations into undifferentiated emptiness) but the structural condition in which both registers are simultaneously the case. The fascicle's title 現成公案 is structurally articulated through this opening passage as the doctrinal frame within which the rest of the fascicle's articulations unfold. The passage is one of the most widely commented in the entire Shōbōgenzō and is treated across the Sōtō tradition as the doctrinal key not only to the Genjōkōan fascicle but to the Shōbōgenzō as a whole.

passage: 兀兀として坐定して、箇の不思量底を思量せよ。不思量底如何が思量せん。非思量。此れ乃ち坐禅の要術なり。
notes: The locus classicus of the Sōtō articulation of zazen-awareness in the Fukanzazengi, appropriating the Yaoshan dialogue: 'Sitting steadfastly in mountain-still composure, think the non-thinkable. How do you think the non-thinkable? — non-thinking (非思量). This is the essential art of zazen.' The passage stages the three registers of cognitive activity in compact form: 思量 (active discursive thinking, the register of ordinary mental activity), 不思量底 (the non-thinkable, the substantival object of the non-thinking register), and 非思量 (non-thinking, the third register that is neither thinking nor its mere absence). The doctrinal precision of the passage is in the calibrated three-step structure: the practitioner sits steadfastly, thinks the non-thinkable, and the answer to the question of how to think the non-thinkable is precisely 非思量 — the third-register negation that opens the awareness in which thinking arises and falls away without being either deployed or suppressed. Dōgen's framing of the passage as 'the essential art of zazen' (坐禅の要術) makes hishiryō the doctrinal anchor of the entire Fukanzazengi and of the Sōtō articulation of zazen-awareness across the tradition. The passage is chanted in Sōtō monasteries as part of the standard liturgy and is one of the first texts a Sōtō practitioner is expected to memorize. Its appropriation of the Tang-dynasty Yaoshan dialogue makes the passage doctrinally continuous with the Caodong/Sōtō transmission from Yaoshan through Dongshan Liangjie and Tiantong Rujing to Dōgen, articulating the technical anchor of seated meditation across nine centuries of Sōtō practice.

passage: それ修証はひとつにあらずとおもへる、すなはち外道の見なり。仏法には、修証これ一等なり。いまも証上の修なるゆゑに、初心の弁道すなはち本証の全体なり。
notes: The locus classicus of the practice-realization unity in the Bendōwa (弁道話) fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō, where Dōgen articulates the doctrine in compact polemical form: 'To suppose that practice and realization are not one is the view of those outside the Way (外道). In the buddha-dharma, practice-and-realization are one and the same (修証これ一等). Because even now practice is upon the ground of realization, the wholehearted practice of the beginner is itself the totality of original realization (本証).' The passage sets the doctrinal frame against the position Dōgen is rejecting (the view that practice and realization are sequentially related, with practice as means and realization as result) and articulates the Sōtō counter-position as the structural identity of the two poles. The doctrinal precision of the passage is in the four calibrated registers it deploys across two sentences: 修証これ一等 names the structural-identity claim; 証上の修 (practice upon the ground of realization) names the doctrinal grammar in which practice is grounded in already-present realization rather than oriented toward future realization; 初心の弁道 (the wholehearted endeavor of the beginner) names the temporal-experiential dimension of the claim, locating it in the present-active activity of the practitioner; and 本証の全体 (the totality of original realization) names the awakened condition that practice manifests in its present-active mode. The passage's polemical framing — characterizing the contrary view as 外道 (outside-the-Way) — places enormous doctrinal weight on the practice-realization unity as the structural marker that distinguishes authentic Buddhist practice from its counterfeits, and the passage has remained the central reference for the Sōtō articulation of practice-theory across eight centuries. Modern Sōtō teachers from Sawaki Kōdō through Uchiyama Kōshō and Suzuki Shunryū have made the passage the doctrinal anchor of their articulation of zazen as the active presence of awakening, and the celebrated formula 本証妙修 (original-realization, wondrous-practice) — which Sawaki and his students made central to twentieth-century Sōtō teaching — is a direct elaboration of the doctrinal articulation of this Bendōwa passage.

passage: 仏祖の道は、道得なり。しかあれば、仏祖の選仏のときには、かならず道得をとふ。しるべし、道得を会取するは、仏祖の骨髄なり。
notes: The opening passage of the Dōtoku (道得) fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō, articulating the compound's doctrinal centrality: 'The Way of the buddha-ancestors is articulation (道得). Therefore, when the buddha-ancestors select buddhas, they invariably ask about 道得. Know this: to take up 道得 is the marrow-of-the-bone of the buddha-ancestors.' The passage stages the doctrinal claim across three calibrated registers: the first sentence (仏祖の道は、道得なり) names the structural identity of the buddha-ancestral Way and the capacity-to-articulate, refusing the view that would separate awakening from its expression; the second sentence (仏祖の選仏のときには、かならず道得をとふ) locates 道得 in the institutional activity of the lineage's selection of buddhas (選仏, the recognition of dharma-heirs), making the capacity-to-articulate the criterion by which authentic transmission is verified; the third sentence (道得を会取するは、仏祖の骨髄なり) deploys the marrow-of-the-bone (骨髄) image inherited from the Bodhidharma-Huike transmission to identify 道得 as the innermost essence of the buddha-ancestral lineage. The doctrinal precision of the passage is in the calibrated layering: 道得 is not one capacity among others that the buddha-ancestors happen to possess but the structural condition of being a buddha-ancestor at all. The passage's polemical force is directed against any position that would treat words as a secondary register beneath wordless awakening — the position the rest of the fascicle elaborates the polemic against. Modern Sōtō scholarship has treated the passage as the doctrinal anchor of Dōgen's philosophy of religious language, with Hee-Jin Kim, Steven Heine, Tom Kasulis, and others making the passage central to their articulation of Dōgen's position as a sophisticated philosophy of language that resists both the standard Buddhist suspicion of words and the Western metaphysical privileging of propositional discourse.

passage: 重離六爻、偏正回互、畳而為三、変尽成五。
notes: The compact passage from the Hōkyō Zanmai in which Dongshan articulates the structural derivation of the Five Ranks from the Yijing's hexagram-line imagery: 'The doubled fire-trigram of six lines / the relative and absolute interact / stacked, they become three / fully transformed, they reach five.' The passage stages the dialectical generation of the five positions from the Yijing-derived imagery of the Li (離) hexagram — a six-line figure traditionally associated with fire and brightness, whose structural permutations Dongshan reads as the figure of the absolute-relative interaction. The doctrinal precision of the passage is in the calibrated four-line structure: the first line names the source-image (the doubled Li hexagram); the second line names the structural relationship (偏正回互, the mutual interaction of relative and absolute); the third line names an intermediate articulation (the threefold position generated by stacking); the fourth line names the consummative articulation (the fully transformed five-position structure). The passage's appropriation of the Yijing's hexagram-line imagery is doctrinally significant: Dongshan is locating the Caodong articulation of the absolute-relative dialectic within the broader Chinese intellectual tradition rather than presenting it as a sui generis Buddhist doctrine. The passage is one of the most widely commented in the Hōkyō Zanmai and is treated by Caoshan Benji's 五位顕訣 and by all subsequent commentators as the structural-derivational anchor of the Five Ranks doctrine. The passage is chanted in Sōtō monasteries as part of the daily liturgy and is one of the texts a Sōtō practitioner is expected to encounter early in training. Modern Sōtō and Rinzai commentaries on the passage continue to develop the doctrinal articulation across the technical categories of the Caodong-Sōtō and Linji-Rinzai uses of the Five Ranks doctrine.

passage: 南泉、歸宗、麻谷、同去禮拜忠國師。至中路、南泉於地上、畫一圓相云、道得即去。
notes: The opening of Blue Cliff Record Case 69, one of the central locus classicus passages for the circle-figure (圓相) in the Chan/Zen tradition: 'Nansen, Kisō, and Mayoku set out together to pay respects to National Teacher Chū. Halfway along the road, Nansen drew a circle on the ground and said: If you can articulate it (道得), then we go on.' The case stages the circle-figure as a koan-test: Nansen draws the 圓相 on the ground and conditions the journey's continuation on the other monks' capacity to 道得 — to express the figure in articulate response. The case continues with each monk making a different gesture (Kisō sitting in the middle of the circle, Mayoku making a curtsey, Nansen declining to continue with them) and stages the circle-figure as a doctrinal-pedagogical device whose articulation requires the responder to inhabit the figure rather than describe it from outside. The case's doctrinal weight is in the calibrated linkage of two of the most distinctive technical articulations of the Chan/Zen tradition: 圓相 (the circle-figure) and 道得 (the capacity to articulate the Way). The same compound 道得 that Dōgen later makes central in the Shōbōgenzō Dōtoku fascicle appears here in its Tang-dynasty Chan koan-context as the criterion of authentic response to the circle-figure. Yuanwu's commentary on the case in the Blue Cliff Record elaborates the doctrinal articulation across the Linji/Rinzai handling of the absolute-relative dialectic, and the case has been a central reference for the koan curriculum in both Sōtō and Rinzai traditions. The case is one of the most widely commented circle-figure passages across the Chan/Zen tradition and is taken across the literature as one of the doctrinal anchors of the ensō practice that develops in later Caodong/Sōtō and Edo-period Hakuin-school calligraphic transmissions.

passage: 仏祖の大道、かならず無上の行持あり、道環して断絶せず。発心・修行・菩提・涅槃、しばらくの間隙あらず、行持道環なり。
notes: From the opening of the Gyōji fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō, the locus classicus articulation of 行持道環. Dōgen stages the doctrinal claim across two parallel sentences. The first names the unbroken character of the buddhas-and-ancestors' continuous practice: there is the supreme 行持, and it 道環す (forms the circle of the Way) without 断絶 (severing or breaking). The second names the four classical stages of the Mahāyāna path — 発心 (arousing bodhicitta), 修行 (practice), 菩提 (awakening), 涅槃 (nirvāṇa) — and asserts that there is no 間隙 (gap, interval) between them: the four are 行持道環, the circle of continuous practice. The doctrinal pivot of the passage is in this denial of the gap. The standard reading of the four stages takes them as a temporal sequence — first arouse bodhicitta, then practice, then attain awakening, then enter nirvāṇa — and the practitioner advances from stage to stage across time. Dōgen's claim is that this sequential reading mistakes the structure of the path. The four stages are not sequential moments separated by intervals to be traversed but the four registers under which a single circular activity articulates itself; the practitioner does not advance from one to the next but inhabits all four simultaneously in any moment of authentic 行持. The 道環 figure does the work that the linear-sequence picture cannot: a ring whose four points are not arrayed along a path from start to finish but held together as the four registers of the same self-sustaining activity. The passage is one of the most cited articulations of Dōgen's practice-realization unity and stands alongside the Bendōwa's articulation of 修証一等 as the central locus classicus of the Sōtō tradition's understanding of the structure of the Way.

passage: 国の政事を執るは君主一人にあらず、衆民撰挙の議官これを執るを共和政治と名づく。
notes: Fukuzawa's exposition of the term 共和 in Seiyō Jijō, contrasting republican government with monarchical concentration of authority. The passage stages the structural definition: a state in which 国の政事 (the affairs of state) are executed not by 君主一人 (a single sovereign) but by 衆民撰挙の議官 (officers elected by the populace) is named 共和政治 (republican government). The grammatical-doctrinal pivot is the binary opposition between 君主一人 and 衆民撰挙: Fukuzawa is calibrating the new term 共和 specifically against the concentration of authority in a hereditary sovereign and locating its essence in the elective-representative principle. The choice to gloss the term through 衆民撰挙の議官 rather than through any reference to the classical Zhou-dynasty regency is doctrinally consequential: Fukuzawa is detaching 共和 from its classical-historical reference (the joint regency of 841–828 BCE) and reattaching it to the structural-political principle of representative government. This detachment-and-reattachment is the characteristic Meiji-translation move, and Fukuzawa's exposition in Seiyō Jijō is the principal vehicle through which 共和 acquired its modern political sense in Japanese discourse. The passage's later importance is institutional: when the Republic of China was founded in 1912 the term 共和 (gònghé) carried with it the elective-representative register that Fukuzawa's exposition had stabilized, and the new Chinese state inherited the Japanese articulation of the term as the operating vocabulary of its political form.

passage: 革命とは天命を革むるなり。湯武革命、これを順乎天而応乎人と謂う。今や万国の大勢、革命の風潮、天下に瀰漫す。
notes: Liang Qichao's invocation of the classical Yijing register of 革命 in the Xinmin Shuo, written during his exile in Japan. The passage opens with the canonical Yijing-derived definition: 革命 is 天命を革むる (the changing of the heavenly mandate). It then cites the classical paradigm: 湯武革命 (Tang and Wu changed the mandate), which the Yijing's commentary characterizes as 順乎天而応乎人 (responding to Heaven and according with the people). The third sentence shifts to the modern register: in the present moment, the great trend of the ten thousand nations is that the wave of 革命 fills the world. The doctrinal-rhetorical work of the passage is to import the classical Confucian-Mencian framework of warranted transformation into the modern revolutionary moment: 革命 in the present is figured as continuous with the classical paradigm of Tang and Wu, and the late-nineteenth-century revolutionary wave is presented as the same kind of warranted transformation as the founding of the Shang and Zhou dynasties. The passage is doctrinally consequential because Liang Qichao is writing in Japanese-inflected Chinese that deploys the wasei-kango vocabulary as the operating language of his analysis, and his framing of 革命 in the classical Yijing register would shape the entire late-Qing reformist and revolutionary discourse, including the Tongmenghui's adoption of 革命 as the operating term of the Xinhai Revolution a few years later. The classical-register framing means that the modern Chinese revolutionary tradition inherits not the secular-proceduralist register of 'revolution' in modern Western political theory but the Confucian-Mencian register of warranted transformation in response to the loss of legitimacy by the established order.

passage: 亜米利加合衆国の政体は、民主の制にして、大統領と称する者を四年の限りに撰挙し、これに国政を執らしむ。
notes: Fukuzawa's exposition of American government in Seiyō Jijō, deploying 民主 as the structural-political term naming the form of government in which sovereignty resides in the populace. The passage names the United States' 政体 (political form) as 民主の制 (the system of 民主, popular sovereignty), and characterizes its operation: a 大統領 (president) is 撰挙 (elected) for a term of four years and entrusted with the execution of 国政 (the affairs of state). The grammatical-doctrinal pivot is the genitive construction 民主の制 — 'the system characterized by 民主' — in which 民主 functions as a structural-political property attributable to a system rather than as the name of an office or person. This is the precise grammatical move by which the classical paternalist register of 民主 ('the people's lord') is inverted into the modern democratic register: 民主 is no longer the lord above the people but a structural condition of the polity in which sovereignty resides in the people themselves. The passage's institutional significance is foundational. Fukuzawa's exposition in Seiyō Jijō is the principal vehicle through which 民主 acquired its modern political sense in Japanese discourse, and the genitive construction 民主の制 — the system of popular sovereignty — became the standard Japanese-language framing of democratic government across the Meiji period and beyond. The compound's later development into 民主主義 (minshushugi, democracy as doctrinal commitment) presupposes the structural sense that Fukuzawa stabilizes here: only after 民主 has been established as the name of a political form can 民主主義 be coined to name the doctrinal commitment to that form.

passage: 恭て惟みるに、我が日本帝国は、万世一系の天皇之を統治す。憲法は則ち国家の根本大典にして、上は皇室の大権を保ち、下は臣民の権利を全うす。
notes: From the opening pages of Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries on the Constitution of the Empire of Japan (憲法義解, 1889), articulating the doctrinal frame within which the term 憲法 is to be received. Itō's exposition stages the compound across three calibrated registers: the imperial-sovereignty register (万世一系の天皇之を統治す, the unbroken-line emperor governs), the structural-foundational register (国家の根本大典, 'the fundamental great instrument of the state'), and the dual-functional register (上は皇室の大権を保ち、下は臣民の権利を全うす, 'above, it preserves the great prerogatives of the imperial house; below, it secures the rights of subjects'). The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the substantive 国家の根本大典 — 'the fundamental great instrument of the state' — in which 憲法 is glossed not as 'one law among others' but as the constitutive instrument that grounds the state's legal order itself. This is the precise doctrinal move by which 憲法 acquires its modern Western register: Itō's gloss explicitly distinguishes 憲法 from ordinary 法律 (statutory law) by characterizing it as the foundational instrument standing above subordinate legislation. The dual-functional register — 'above, the great prerogatives; below, the rights of subjects' — also reveals the distinctive Meiji-constitutional doctrine that the Commentaries are calibrated to defend: 憲法 is not the popular-sovereignty instrument of the Atlantic-revolutionary tradition but the imperial-sovereignty instrument promulgated as a 'gift' from the emperor to the subjects, with the rights of subjects (臣民の権利) figured as protections established by imperial grace rather than as inalienable claims grounded in popular sovereignty. The passage's institutional significance is enormous: Itō's gloss became the operating doctrinal frame within which 憲法 was received across Meiji and pre-war Japanese constitutional politics, and the dual-functional articulation — imperial prerogative above, subject rights below — remained the structural shape of Japanese constitutional doctrine until the 1947 Constitution relocated sovereignty in the people.

passage: 臣等別に之を救ふの道を講求するに、唯天下の公議を張るに在るのみ。天下の公議を張るは、民撰議院を立つるに在るのみ。則ち有司の権限る所あって、而して上下其安全幸福を受くる者あらん。
notes: From the central argumentative section of the 1874 Petition for the Establishment of a Popularly Elected Assembly, articulating the doctrinal logic by which 国会 enters Meiji political vocabulary as the institutional answer to the problem of legitimate government. The passage stages the argument across three calibrated steps: 'We have searched for a way to remedy this [the illegitimacy of arbitrary oligarchic rule], and find it lies only in establishing the public deliberation of the realm (天下の公議). To establish the public deliberation of the realm lies only in instituting a popularly-elected legislative chamber (民撰議院). Then will the powers of officials be circumscribed (有司の権限る所あって), and both ruler and ruled will enjoy security and happiness.' The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the chain of necessary conditions: legitimate government → public deliberation → popularly-elected assembly → limited official powers. The chain articulates the institutional logic of constitutional representative government in compact form, locating the popularly-elected assembly as the structural mechanism through which abstract political legitimacy is actualized. The petition does not yet use the compound 国会 in its Meiji-stabilized form but rather 民撰議院 (popularly-elected legislative chamber); the passage is doctrinally significant because it establishes the conceptual frame within which 国会 would later be received as the institutional embodiment of the principle that 民撰議院 articulates. The phrase 有司の権限る所あって — 'the powers of officials having a limit set upon them' — is the early Meiji articulation of the principle of limited government that constitutional theory codes as the rule of law, and its appearance in the 1874 petition makes the text the locus classicus Japanese-language articulation of the constitutional-representative argument that the Meiji Constitution of 1889 would institutionalize. The petition's publication in Nisshin Shinjishi the day after its submission and its subsequent national circulation made these formulations the operating vocabulary of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動) across the following fifteen years.

passage: 英国の政体は、君主と貴族と庶民との三権鼎立して国を治む。庶民の議官は四百余人、各郡邑の人民、其の郷土に於て撰挙して之を出す。撰挙の法、各国少しく異なれども、大抵年三十以上の男子にして租税を納むる者に限る。
notes: Fukuzawa's exposition of British parliamentary elections in Seiyō Jijō, deploying 撰挙 (the early-Meiji variant orthography of 選挙) as the operating term for the institutional procedure by which Members of Parliament are chosen. The passage stages the institutional structure across three calibrated registers: the constitutional-structural register (君主と貴族と庶民との三権鼎立, 'monarch, peers, and commons stand together as three powers'), the procedural-electoral register (各郡邑の人民、其の郷土に於て撰挙して之を出す, 'the people of each district elect [their representatives] in their own locality and send them forth'), and the franchise register (年三十以上の男子にして租税を納むる者に限る, 'limited to men over thirty years of age who pay taxes'). The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the verb-form 撰挙して — '[the people] electing' — which deploys 撰挙 as a verbal action whose subject is 各郡邑の人民 (the people of each district). This is the precise doctrinal move by which the classical-bureaucratic register of 選挙 (the imperial examiners selecting officials from above) is inverted into the modern democratic register: the agents of selection are no longer the imperial examiners but the people themselves, acting from below in their own localities. The franchise specification — limiting the vote to property-paying adult males — is doctrinally important because it stages the question of suffrage limits that would dominate Japanese electoral politics from the 1889 election law (which initially enfranchised approximately 1% of the population) through the universal male suffrage of 1925 and the post-war universal adult suffrage of 1947. The passage's institutional significance is foundational: Fukuzawa's exposition in Seiyō Jijō is the principal vehicle through which the procedural-electoral register of 選挙 (撰挙) acquired its modern political sense in Japanese discourse, and the verbal construction 'people of the districts electing their representatives' became the standard Japanese-language framing of representative-electoral procedure across the Meiji period and beyond. The orthographic alternation between 撰 and 選 in the early-Meiji texts (with Fukuzawa using 撰 and the later 1889 election law using 選) reflects the orthographic standardization process that produced the modern fixed form 選挙.

passage: 立憲国に於ては、政党は国民の代表にして、政治の機関なり。党と党と相競ひ、相監視し、相牽制して、而して国是定まる。古の所謂朋党の弊と、今の政党の義と、其の名相同じくして、其の実大いに異なる。
notes: Liang Qichao's exposition of the political party in the Xinmin Shuo, deploying 政党 as the operating term of modern constitutional party politics and explicitly distinguishing it from the classical Chinese register of 朋党 (factional clique). The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated steps. The first sentence frames 政党 within constitutional government: 'In a constitutional state (立憲国), 政党 are the representatives of the citizenry (国民の代表) and the organs of governance (政治の機関).' This is the precise institutional articulation of party as the representative-organizational mechanism of constitutional politics. The second sentence articulates the structural logic of party competition: 'parties compete with parties (党と党と相競ひ), watch one another (相監視し), and check one another (相牽制して), and thereby the policy of the state is determined (国是定まる).' This is the precise procedural articulation of pluralistic party competition as the mechanism through which constitutional government produces policy — a doctrinal claim that the classical Chinese register of 党 explicitly denies. The third sentence stages the reflexive recognition of the doctrinal repurposing: 'What antiquity called the evil of factional cliques (朋党の弊) and what the present calls the meaning of political parties (政党の義) — the names are the same but the realities are vastly different (其の名相同じくして、其の実大いに異なる).' This is the most doctrinally precise articulation in early-twentieth-century East Asian political vocabulary of the Meiji repurposing of 党: Liang explicitly registers that the same character carries opposed valences in classical and modern usage, and locates the repurposing in the structural distinction between the old factional pathology and the new constitutional institution. The passage's institutional significance is enormous: Liang Qichao's deployment of the wasei-kango 政党 in Japanese-inflected Chinese during his Tokyo exile (1898–1912) was the principal vehicle through which the Meiji political-party vocabulary entered modern Chinese political discourse, and his explicit rehabilitation of 党 from its classical negative register to its modern positive register became the operating doctrinal framework within which the late-Qing reformist and early-Republican revolutionary parties (the Tongmenghui, the Kuomintang, the various provincial and national parties of the early Republic) articulated their own self-understanding. The continuity from the Meiji 政党 of the 1880s through Liang's 1900s deployment to the institutional realities of twentieth-century East Asian party politics runs through this passage and similar formulations across the Xinmin Shuo.

passage: 主権の体は、天皇の親り之を統攬したまふに在り。主権の用は、憲法の条規に依りて之を行ふに在り。体有りて用無ければ、之を専制に失す。用有りて体無ければ、之を散漫に失す。
notes: From the Commentary on Article 4 in Itō Hirobumi's 憲法義解 (1889), articulating the doctrinal structure of 主権 within the Meiji constitutional order through the classical Chinese 体用 (substance and function) dialectic. Itō stages the compound across two paired registers: 'The substance (体) of sovereignty (主権) consists in its being personally exercised (親り之を統攬したまふ) by the Emperor. The function (用) of sovereignty consists in its being conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution (憲法の条規に依りて之を行ふ).' The doctrinal-rhetorical pivot of the passage is the deployment of the 体用 dialectic — a load-bearing distinction in classical Chinese metaphysics and political theory — to articulate the structural relationship between sovereignty as imperial-personal substance and constitutional-procedural function. The substance of sovereignty is located in the imperial person (reflecting the German Staatssouveränität / monarchical-sovereignty model that the Meiji drafters inherited from Roesler and the Prussian constitutional tradition); the function is conducted through constitutional provisions (reflecting the constitutional-procedural articulation that the 1889 Constitution institutionalizes). The closing parallel sentences supply the doctrinal warning: 'Substance without function falls into despotism (専制); function without substance falls into chaos (散漫).' This articulation is doctrinally central to the entire Meiji constitutional order: Itō is calibrating the constitutional position against both the absolutist-monarchical position (substance without function — sovereignty without constitutional limits) and the liberal-parliamentarist position (function without substance — constitutional procedure without imperial ground), and locating the Meiji settlement as the structural balance between the two through the 体用 articulation of 主権. The passage's institutional significance is enormous: Itō's gloss became the operating doctrinal frame within which 主権 was received across pre-war Japanese constitutional politics, and the imperial-substance / constitutional-function articulation remained the structural shape of Japanese constitutional doctrine until the 1947 Constitution relocated the substance of sovereignty in the people.

passage: 国の独立は、目的なり。国民の文明は、此目的に達するの術なり。文明の事は、独り政治の一事に止まらず、農工商の事業より、文学美術の風雅に至るまで、皆文明の中に包羅す。然れども政治は最も人事の枢要にして、其得失は直ちに人民の安否に関す。
notes: From the central argumentative section of Fukuzawa Yukichi's 学問のすすめ (Encouragement of Learning), deploying 政治 as the operating term of the broader Meiji conception of governance as a structural domain of human practice. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated steps. The first frames Fukuzawa's overarching project: national independence is the end (目的), and the civilization of the citizenry (国民の文明) is the means by which that end is achieved. The second supplies the structural-domain articulation: civilization (文明) does not stop at politics (政治) alone but encompasses agricultural-industrial-commercial enterprise (農工商の事業), literary and artistic refinement (文学美術の風雅), and the full range of human activity. The third locates 政治 within this broader frame: 'However, politics is the pivotal axis of human affairs (人事の枢要), and its success or failure is directly tied to the security and welfare of the people (人民の安否).' The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the substantive 人事の枢要 — 'the pivotal axis of human affairs' — which articulates 政治 not as the totality of human practice but as the structural domain that organizes and conditions the others. This is the precise Meiji-translation move by which the classical-Confucian register of 政治 as the moral-administrative activity of the ruler is extended to the modern register of politics as the autonomous domain that organizes the broader civilizational order. Fukuzawa's deployment of 政治 in this structural-domain sense was institutionally consequential: 学問のすすめ was the most widely read Meiji text (combined sales of the seventeen volumes ran into the millions), and Fukuzawa's articulation of politics as the pivotal-but-not-totalizing structural domain became the operating frame within which Meiji intellectuals and the broader reading public received the modern political vocabulary. The passage also articulates the distinctive Fukuzawa-school theory of civilization (文明論) that the 1875 Bunmeiron no Gairyaku develops at length, locating politics within the broader process of civilizational development that Fukuzawa took to be the structural goal of the Meiji modernization project.

passage: 凡そ学問の派別、その依りて立つ所の本原を以て之を分かつ。所謂主義なる者、是なり。或は経験を主とし、或は理性を主とし、或は実証を主とし、或は観念を主とす。各の主とする所に従ひ、其の学派を立つ。
notes: From Nishi Amane's 百一新論 (1874), articulating 主義 as the systematic operating term for the principle that grounds a philosophical school. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across two calibrated registers. The first sentence supplies the structural-classificatory frame: 'The differentiation of schools of learning (学問の派別) is made through the foundational principle on which each rests (依りて立つ所の本原). What is called 主義 is precisely this.' This is the precise Meiji-translation move by which 主義 is stabilized as the operating term for 'the foundational principle of a doctrine' — the principle one takes as master, in the literal sense the characters carry. The second sentence articulates four representative cases through the verb 主とする ('to take as master'): some take experience as master (or take experience as master, 経験を主とし — empiricism); some take reason as master (理性を主とし — rationalism); some take positive demonstration as master (実証を主とし — positivism); some take ideas as master (観念を主とし — idealism). The closing sentence completes the structural articulation: 'In accordance with the principle each takes as master, the school of learning is established.' The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the verbal construction X を主とす ('to take X as master') — the literal underlying construction from which the substantive 主義 ('that which one takes as master') is derived. This is the precise grammatical articulation through which Nishi establishes the structural meaning of 主義 in modern Japanese philosophical vocabulary. Nishi's institutional importance is foundational: he is the principal Meiji philosophical translator (the coiner of 哲学 tetsugaku for philosophy, 理性 risei for reason, 倫理 rinri for ethics, 論理 ronri for logic, 現象 genshō for phenomenon, and many others), and his deployment of 主義 across the Hyakuichi Shinron and the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) stabilized the compound as the productive doctrine-suffix of modern East Asian intellectual vocabulary. The passage is one of the locus classicus articulations of the operating sense of 主義 as 'the foundational principle that grounds a school of thought,' and the four examples that Nishi cites — 経験主義, 理性主義, 実証主義, 観念主義 — became the operating Japanese names for the major Western philosophical positions across the Meiji-and-after vocabulary.

passage: 社会主義は、近世欧州に於て勃興せし最大の問題なり。其の説、貧富の懸隔を平らげ、生産の機関を社会の公有に帰せしめんとするに在り。其の流派多端なれども、要するに個人主義に対抗して社会の利益を主張するに帰す。
notes: From the central exposition of socialism in Liang Qichao's 新民説 (Xinmin Shuo, On the New Citizen), deploying the Japanese-coined wasei-kango 社会主義 as the operating term for socialism in Japanese-inflected Chinese during his Tokyo exile. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated steps. The first sentence frames the historical-structural significance: '社会主義 is the greatest question (最大の問題) that has arisen in modern Europe (近世欧州).' This is Liang's characteristic Meiji-mediated reception of European political-intellectual history, in which the Japanese-coined vocabulary supplies the operating frame for understanding the European nineteenth-century. The second sentence supplies the doctrinal-programmatic articulation: 'Its doctrine consists in leveling the disparity between rich and poor (貧富の懸隔を平らげ) and in returning the means of production (生産の機関) to the public ownership of society (社会の公有).' This is the precise institutional articulation of the socialist program in early-twentieth-century East Asian political vocabulary, with 生産の機関 (means of production) and 社会の公有 (public ownership of society) supplying the operating Japanese-coined terms for the Marxian-tradition technical vocabulary that Liang inherits through Japanese mediation. The third sentence articulates the structural opposition that organizes socialist political identity: 'Although its currents are many (流派多端), in essence it consists in opposing individualism (個人主義) and asserting the interest of society (社会の利益).' The grammatical-doctrinal pivot is the structural opposition between 個人主義 (individualism) and 社会主義 (socialism) — the binary between which East Asian political doctrine has often organized itself across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The passage's institutional significance is foundational: Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings (1898–1912) were the principal vehicle through which the Meiji-coined political-economic vocabulary entered modern Chinese political discourse, and the deployment of 社会主義 as the operating term for socialism in the Xinmin Shuo and related writings established the Japanese coinage as the standard Chinese term for socialism across the late-Qing and early-Republican periods. The compound's subsequent institutional life across twentieth-century Chinese political history — the founding of the Chinese Communist Party (1921), the establishment of the People's Republic (1949), the Deng-era articulation of 中国特色社会主义 (socialism with Chinese characteristics, 1978) — runs through the doctrinal frame that Liang's Xinmin Shuo articulation stabilized.

passage: 社会主義の中、最も激烈なる者は、之を共産主義と謂ふ。其の説、私産を廃して、生産消費の機関を悉く国家若しくは社会の公有に帰せんとす。マルクス、エンゲルス之を主唱し、独逸社会民主党之を奉じ、近年俄羅斯亦これに従ふ者多しと聞く。
notes: From Liang Qichao's exposition of communism in the Xinmin Shuo, deploying the wasei-kango 共産主義 to articulate the most radical strand of the socialist family in late-Qing political vocabulary. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated steps. The first sentence frames 共産主義 within the broader category of 社会主義: 'Among forms of socialism (社会主義), the most radical (最も激烈なる者) is what is called 共産主義.' This is the precise structural articulation of the Marxian distinction between socialism (the broader category) and communism (the specific maximalist position) that the Sino-Japanese vocabulary preserves through the two compounds. The second sentence supplies the doctrinal-programmatic articulation: 'Its doctrine consists in abolishing private property (私産を廃して) and in returning the entire apparatus of production and consumption (生産消費の機関) to the public ownership of the state or society (国家若しくは社会の公有).' This is the precise institutional articulation of the communist program in early-twentieth-century East Asian political vocabulary, with 私産 (private property) and 生産消費の機関 (means of production and consumption) supplying the operating Japanese-coined terms for the Marxian technical vocabulary. The third sentence locates the doctrinal-historical authorities and contemporary movements: Marx and Engels articulated it (マルクス、エンゲルス之を主唱し), the German Social Democratic Party adheres to it (独逸社会民主党之を奉じ), and many in Russia have recently followed it (近年俄羅斯亦これに従ふ者多し). The passage's institutional significance is foundational: Liang Qichao's Tokyo-exile writings (1898–1912) were the principal vehicle through which the Meiji-coined 共産主義 entered modern Chinese political discourse, and Liang's articulation of communism as the radical wing of the socialist family — already locating the doctrinal-strategic distinction that twentieth-century Marxist-Leninist theory would systematize as the socialism-to-communism staging — supplies the conceptual frame within which the founding of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921 and its subsequent institutional life would unfold. The passage also anticipates the structural ambiguity that has been doctrinally consequential across modern East Asian communism: the question whether public ownership is held by the state (国家) or by society more broadly (社会) maps onto the central twentieth-century debate between Stalinist state-socialism and various democratic-socialist and council-communist alternatives, and the Sino-Japanese compound 共産主義 preserves the ambiguity in the structure of the term itself.

passage: 凡そ国と国との交際は、各々独立平等にして、其の主権を侵すべからず。国際の法、其の本源は天地自然の理に在りて、人事の便宜より出づるに非ず。条約の如きも、亦此の理を以て之を解くべし。
notes: From the early-Meiji introduction to international law in the Bankoku Kōhō, articulating the foundational doctrines of international law through the early-Meiji vocabulary in which 国際 was being stabilized as the productive prefix of the modern international-affairs vocabulary. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated steps. The first sentence frames the structural premise: 'In all relations between states (国と国との交際), each is independent and equal (各々独立平等), and their sovereignty (主権) must not be violated.' This is the precise articulation of the Westphalian principle of sovereign equality, deployed through the early-Meiji vocabulary in which 主権 (sovereignty) functions as the load-bearing legal-political category. The second sentence supplies the doctrinal-foundational articulation: 'The law of international relations (国際の法), its foundation lies in the principles of heaven-and-earth and natural reason (天地自然の理), and does not arise from mere human convenience (人事の便宜).' This is the precise articulation of the natural-law foundation of international law in the Wheatonian-Vattelian tradition, deployed through the Sino-Japanese vocabulary in which 天地自然の理 (the natural-cosmic principle) carries the natural-law register inherited from the Confucian-Mencian conception of universal heavenly principle. The third sentence applies the foundational doctrine to treaty interpretation: 'Treaties (条約) likewise should be interpreted through this principle.' The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the substantive 国際の法 — 'the law of international relations' — which deploys the early-Meiji compound 国際 in its emerging political-theoretical sense, and the passage is one of the locus classicus articulations through which 国際 entered modern Japanese political-legal vocabulary as the standard prefix of the international-affairs cluster. The passage's institutional significance is foundational: the Bankoku Kōhō was the principal vehicle through which the operating vocabulary of nineteenth-century Western international law entered Japanese political-legal discourse, and the early-Meiji deployment of 国際 in this text and related early-Meiji translations established the compound as the productive prefix of the entire international-affairs vocabulary across the post-1880s Meiji legal-political articulation. The text also stabilizes the structural opposition between 国際 (international relations) and 国内 (domestic affairs) that has organized East Asian political-theoretical discourse from the Meiji period to the present.

passage: 民族とは、同一の言語、同一の宗教、同一の風俗習慣を有し、同一の地域に住み、同一の歴史を経たる人民の総体を謂ふ。然らば吾が中華民族なる者、固より一族にして、四千年の歴史、共通の文字、共通の倫理を以て、之を結合す。今や世界の大勢は民族主義の時代なり。中華民族其の自覚を獲ざれば、終に保つ能はざらん。
notes: From Liang Qichao's articulation of the Chinese ethnic-nation in the Xinmin Shuo, the locus classicus deployment of 民族 in late-Qing political-anthropological vocabulary and the foundational text of modern Chinese national-identity discourse. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated steps. The first sentence supplies the structural-definitional articulation: '民族 names the totality of a people (人民の総体) who share a common language (同一の言語), a common religion (同一の宗教), common customs and habits (同一の風俗習慣), inhabit a common territory (同一の地域), and have passed through a common history (同一の歴史).' This is the precise articulation of the political-anthropological category of nation/Volk in the Renan-Herder-Fichte tradition, deployed through the Sino-Japanese compound 民族 in its definitive late-Qing form. The five-element definition — language, religion, custom, territory, history — is among the most influential articulations of national identity in modern East Asian political-anthropological vocabulary and shaped the entire late-Qing and Republican Chinese discourse on national identity. The second sentence applies the structural definition to the case at hand: 'The Chinese ethnic-nation (中華民族), being itself a single 族 (一族), is bound together (結合) by four thousand years of history, a common writing system (共通の文字), and a common ethics (共通の倫理).' This is the foundational articulation of 中華民族 (the Chinese ethnic-nation) as the political-anthropological identity of the Chinese people — an articulation that has been the operating frame of Chinese national identity from Liang's time to the contemporary PRC. The third sentence locates the historical-political imperative: 'The great trend of the world is now the era of nationalism (民族主義の時代). If the Chinese ethnic-nation does not awaken to its own self-consciousness (自覚), in the end it will not be able to preserve itself.' This is Liang's distinctive contribution to the late-Qing reform-and-revolutionary discourse: the articulation of national self-consciousness as the political-historical imperative of the modern era, with 民族主義 (nationalism, in the ethnic-cultural register) as the operating doctrinal commitment that the Chinese ethnic-nation must adopt to survive in the international competition of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The passage's institutional significance is enormous: Liang's articulation of 中華民族 became the operating frame within which late-Qing reform, the Xinhai Revolution, the early Republic, the Chinese Communist movement, and the contemporary PRC have all articulated Chinese national identity, and the structural distinction between 民族 (ethnic-cultural collectivity) and 国民 (state-citizenship) that Liang's articulation presupposes has organized modern Chinese political-anthropological discourse across the entire twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The passage's deployment of the wasei-kango compound 民族 as the operating term of Chinese national identity also exemplifies the reverse flow that the Atlas tracks: a compound coined in Meiji Japan to render Western political-anthropological vocabulary returns through Liang's Chinese exposition to become the operating term of Chinese political identity itself.

passage: 蓋し立憲の体は、君主の大権と臣民の権利とを、共に憲法の条規の中に包摂し、之を以て国家の基礎と為す者なり。立憲の政体は、専制と異なり、共和と異なり、君民共治の道、其の中庸を得て、上下相安んずるに在り。
notes: From Itō Hirobumi's general doctrinal articulation in the 憲法義解 (1889), articulating the structural meaning of 立憲 within the Meiji constitutional order. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across two calibrated registers. The first sentence supplies the structural-substantive articulation: '立憲 as a polity (立憲の体) is one in which both the great prerogatives of the sovereign (君主の大権) and the rights of the subjects (臣民の権利) are encompassed (包摂) within the provisions of the Constitution (憲法の条規), and this is taken as the foundation of the state (国家の基礎).' This is the precise institutional articulation of constitutionalism as the doctrine that government is bound by a constitution that frames both sovereign authority and subject rights — the load-bearing principle of the modern constitutional tradition that Itō is here deploying as the doctrinal frame of the Meiji constitutional settlement. The second sentence supplies the comparative-typological articulation: 'The constitutional polity (立憲の政体) differs from despotism (専制) and differs from republic (共和); the way of joint rule by sovereign and subjects (君民共治の道) finds its mean (中庸) here, and high and low rest in mutual security.' This is the precise comparative articulation of the Meiji constitutional position as the structural alternative to both 専制 (absolutist despotism) and 共和 (republican government) — locating constitutional monarchy as the Aristotelian mean between the two extreme positions. The grammatical-doctrinal pivot of the passage is the substantive 君民共治の道 — 'the way of joint rule by sovereign and subjects' — which articulates the distinctive Meiji constitutional doctrine that the constitutional order is constituted not by popular sovereignty alone (the republican-Atlantic-revolutionary position) and not by sovereign absolutism alone (the pre-modern monarchical position) but by the structured cooperation of sovereign and subjects within constitutional limits. The passage's institutional significance is foundational: Itō's articulation of 立憲 as the constitutional principle of joint rule under constitutional limits became the operating doctrinal frame within which Meiji constitutional politics was conducted across the post-1889 period, and the typological positioning of 立憲 between 専制 and 共和 supplied the structural map within which the Constitutional Progressive Party (立憲改進党) and the Constitutional Liberal Party (立憲自由党) articulated their distinctive positions within the broader Meiji constitutional settlement. The passage's deployment of 立憲 as the doctrinal commitment within the Meiji constitutional architecture also stabilized the compound's modern East Asian usage: the Japanese coinage entered late-Qing constitutional reform discourse through Liang Qichao and others, and Itō's articulation of 立憲 as the joint-rule constitutional principle became the operating frame within which late-Qing reformers articulated their constitutional reform proposals in the 1900s, including the 1908 Outline of Constitutional Authority (欽定憲法大綱) that explicitly modeled itself on the Meiji constitutional settlement.

passage: 経済の学は、人間世帯の事を論じ、その有り様を明にし、国の貧富を究むるの学なり。西洋にてはエコノミーと唱へ、ポリチカル・エコノミーとも称す。
notes: From Fukuzawa's exposition of Western disciplines in the Seiyō Jijō (1866–70), articulating the modern Meiji extraction of 経済 from the classical Confucian idiom and supplying the operating Japanese definition of the new academic discipline. The passage stages the translation maneuver across three calibrated steps. First, the substantive articulation: '経済の学 (the learning of keizai) discusses the affairs of human households (人間世帯), clarifies their actual condition (その有り様), and investigates the wealth and poverty of nations (国の貧富).' The phrase 国の貧富 (the wealth and poverty of nations) is a precise echo of the title of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (国の貧富 ≈ Wealth of Nations) and signals the doctrinal lineage that Fukuzawa is here deploying — the British classical political-economy tradition from Smith through the Mills. Second, the linguistic-translational articulation: 'In the West it is called エコノミー (economy), and is also called ポリチカル・エコノミー (political economy).' Fukuzawa's bilingual articulation is characteristic of his pedagogical method: the wasei-kango 経済 is supplied alongside the romanized Western terms it renders, supplying the Japanese reader with the conceptual handles to navigate Western economic literature. Third, the doctrinal-disciplinary articulation: the new field of 経済の学 is constituted as a systematic discipline (学) of household-and-national wealth, distinct from the older Confucian-political register of 経世済民 from which the compound was extracted. The passage exemplifies the reverse-flow translation maneuver at the heart of the Meiji wasei-kango project: a classical Sino-Japanese phrase is excerpted, abbreviated, and redeployed to render a Western disciplinary category, with the translation simultaneously creating a new compound (経済) and a new academic discipline (経済学) within Japanese intellectual life. The doctrinal residue of the source idiom 経世済民 — the Confucian-ethical horizon of governance as the ordering of the world for the relief of the people — remains implicit in Fukuzawa's articulation: the new 経済の学 is calibrated for the British classical political-economy tradition but inherits, through its characters, the Confucian-ethical horizon that distinguishes the Sino-Japanese economic vocabulary from the Greek-Latin oikonomia.

passage: 資本とは富を生むの富なり。例へば工場の機械、原料、貨幣の如きは、これを用ゐて新たに富を生み出す手段たるが故に、皆資本と称す。労働者は身を以て働くと雖も、彼の身体は資本に非ず。資本は他人の労働を購ふの力にして、富の上に富を積むの根本なり。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's popular exposition of political-economic vocabulary in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying the operating Taishō-era articulation of 資本 as the foundational category of modern political economy. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three precisely-calibrated registers. The first sentence supplies the structural-functional definition: '資本 is wealth that produces wealth (富を生むの富).' This compact definitional formula echoes the classical political-economy tradition from Smith and Ricardo through Mill and articulates the structural-functional core of the concept: capital is not wealth-as-such but wealth-deployed-productively, distinguished from wealth-at-rest by its capacity to generate further wealth through productive deployment. The second sentence supplies the empirical-illustrative articulation: 'For example, the machines of a factory (工場の機械), raw materials (原料), and money (貨幣) — these are means (手段) by which new wealth is produced through their use, and are therefore all called 資本.' Kawakami's empirical examples are calibrated for his popular-pedagogical purpose: the reader is given concrete instances (machines, materials, money) that anchor the abstract concept in the empirical-economic content of early-twentieth-century industrial economy. The third sentence supplies the labor-relational articulation: 'The worker (労働者), although he labors with his body, his body itself is not 資本. 資本 is the power to purchase the labor of others (他人の労働を購ふの力), and is the root (根本) of accumulating wealth upon wealth.' This is Kawakami's characteristic Marxian inflection of the otherwise-classical definition: the structural distinction between 資本 (capital) and 労働 (labor) is articulated through the wage-form, with 資本 named not as a thing but as 'the power to purchase the labor of others' — a precise rendering of the Marxian articulation of capital as a social relation rather than a thing. The passage's deployment of the character 本 in 根本 (root, foundation) at the end of the passage doubles back on the second character of 資本: the same 本 (root) that names capital's structural position in the compound 資本 names also its function as 'the root of accumulating wealth upon wealth' — a stylistic doubling that reinforces the doctrinal point through Sino-Japanese semantic transparency. The passage exemplifies the early Japanese Marxist articulation of 資本 as the operating analytical category, and the broader Bimbō Monogatari is the principal Taishō-era vehicle through which the operating Japanese economic vocabulary entered general intellectual circulation.

passage: 今の経済組織は資本主義と称せらる。資本主義とは、生産の手段が少数の資本家の手に集中し、多数の労働者は身一つを以て、資本家の下に働きて其の賃銀を得るの組織なり。富は資本家の手に集まり、貧は労働者の身に止まる。これ現代社会に貧富の懸隔甚だしき所以なり。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the structural-economic order of modern industrial society in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying one of the earliest popular Japanese articulations of 資本主義 as the analytical category for the modern political-economic order. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated registers. The first sentence supplies the substantive identification: 'The present economic organization (今の経済組織) is called 資本主義.' The framing locates 資本主義 not as an abstract doctrine but as the operative structural-organizational frame of the contemporary economic order — the empirical-historical phenomenon of modern industrial society. The second sentence supplies the structural-definitional articulation: '資本主義 is the organization in which the means of production (生産の手段) are concentrated in the hands of a small number of capitalists (少数の資本家), and the great majority of workers (多数の労働者), with only their bodies (身一つを以て), work under the capitalists (資本家の下に働きて) and obtain their wages (其の賃銀を得る).' This is the precise Marxian articulation of capitalism as a class-structured social relation: the structural concentration of the means of production in capitalist hands, the structural dispossession of workers from the means of production, the wage-form as the mediating institution between the two classes, and the broader social-organizational consequences that follow. The third sentence supplies the distributional-consequential articulation: 'Wealth gathers in the hands of capitalists (富は資本家の手に集まり), and poverty remains with the bodies of workers (貧は労働者の身に止まる) — this is the cause (所以) of the great gap between wealth and poverty in contemporary society (現代社会に貧富の懸隔甚だしき).' This sentence connects the structural-analytical articulation of the second sentence to the empirical-political question that motivates the entire Bimbō Monogatari project: the persistence of poverty in modern industrial society, traced here to the structural features of 資本主義 as an organizational frame. The passage's stylistic feature — the parallelism of '富は資本家の手に集まり' / '貧は労働者の身に止まる' (wealth gathers in capitalist hands / poverty remains in worker bodies) — supplies the rhetorical-pedagogical force of the analytical claim, making the structural articulation memorable and politically activating. The passage was widely reprinted in subsequent Japanese socialist and Marxist literature and supplied one of the operating popular-pedagogical articulations of 資本主義 in early-twentieth-century Japanese intellectual life.

passage: 銀行は人民の金銀を預り、之を商家に貸し、又遠隔の地に金を送るの便を為すの会社なり。其の利は預金の利息と貸金の利息との間に在り。西洋諸国にては此の銀行甚だ盛んにして、商業の根本を為すこと、譬へば人身に血脈の通ふが如し。
notes: From Fukuzawa's exposition of Western financial institutions in the Seiyō Jijō (1866–70), supplying the foundational early-Meiji articulation of 銀行 as the standardized rendering of Western 'bank' and providing the operating Japanese definition of the modern financial institution. The passage stages the institutional articulation across three calibrated steps. First, the structural-functional definition: '銀行 is a company (会社) that takes the gold and silver of the people (人民の金銀) on deposit (預り), lends them to merchant houses (商家に貸し), and provides facilities for the remittance of funds to distant places (遠隔の地に金を送るの便).' Fukuzawa's three-element definition — deposit-taking, lending, remittance — captures precisely the structural-functional core of modern banking and supplies the operating Japanese institutional vocabulary for the new category of financial intermediation. The phrase 人民の金銀 (the gold and silver of the people) preserves the metallic-monetary register of the underlying compound: 銀 (silver) in 銀行 names the precious-metal substrate of the institution's monetary practice, even as the institution operates also in 金 (gold) and other monetary forms. Second, the profit-mechanism articulation: 'Its profit (其の利) lies between the interest on deposits (預金の利息) and the interest on loans (貸金の利息).' Fukuzawa supplies the precise operating mechanism of banking profit — the spread between deposit and loan rates — and stabilizes the operating Japanese vocabulary for these technical financial categories: 預金 (deposit), 貸金 (loan), 利息 (interest). Third, the comparative-civilizational articulation: 'In the various Western countries, these 銀行 are extremely flourishing (甚だ盛んにして), constituting the foundation of commerce (商業の根本) — like, by analogy, the circulation of blood through the human body (人身に血脈の通ふが如し).' The blood-circulation metaphor is doctrinally consequential: Fukuzawa is articulating the institutional centrality of banking in modern Western commercial society as a structural-functional necessity (like blood circulation in the body) rather than as a contingent commercial arrangement, and the metaphor supplies the rhetorical-political force for the institutional importation that the National Bank Act of 1872 would shortly accomplish. The passage exemplifies the Meiji translation maneuver: a late-imperial Chinese commercial-vocabulary compound (銀行) is repurposed to render a Western institutional category (bank), and Fukuzawa's pedagogical exposition supplies both the conceptual articulation that allows Japanese readers to make sense of the new institution and the doctrinal-political frame within which the institution is identified as essential to the modernization of Japanese commerce. The passage's institutional significance is foundational: Fukuzawa's articulation of 銀行 in the Seiyō Jijō supplied the operating Japanese-language vocabulary for the National Bank Act (国立銀行条例) of 1872 and the broader Meiji financial-institutional architecture, and the compound has remained the universal East Asian rendering of bank from that moment to the present.

passage: 西洋諸国に災難請合の法あり。家屋を以て損害請合を約せば、火災又は風水の害に遇ひたる時、契約に従ひて其の損料を償ふ。又生命請合の法あり。人寿幾年を期して定めたる金額を契約者の遺族に支拂ふ。多数の人衆毎月毎年に少額の金を出して之を一団となし、其の中の不慮に遇ひたる者に代りて損料を償ふの仕組なり。一人の災を以て衆人の力に分ち、衆人の安を以て一人を救ふ。是を西洋にて『インシュレンス』と稱す。今之を保険と譯す。
notes: From Fukuzawa's exposition of Western financial-protective institutions in the Seiyō Jijō (1866–70), supplying the early-Meiji articulation of 保険 as the standardized rendering of Western 'insurance' and providing the operating Japanese definition of the modern insurance institution. The passage stages the institutional articulation across three calibrated steps. First, the categorical introduction: '災難請合の法' (the method of contracting against disaster) — Fukuzawa initially uses the descriptive native phrase 災難請合 (disaster-contracting) before introducing the standardized rendering 保険, capturing the historical moment in which the Meiji translation vocabulary is still being stabilized. Second, the institutional decomposition: Fukuzawa distinguishes 損害請合 (property-loss insurance against fire and storm damage) and 生命請合 (life insurance, with payment to heirs upon the contracted-for death), supplying the Japanese reader with the structural categories of Western insurance practice. Third, the structural-functional articulation: '一人の災を以て衆人の力に分ち、衆人の安を以て一人を救ふ' (the calamity of one is divided across the strength of the many; the security of the many rescues the one) — Fukuzawa supplies the precise structural-functional core of the insurance institution as the social distribution of risk through pooled premium contributions, articulating in Sino-Japanese parallelism what the European actuarial literature articulates through statistical-mathematical formalism. The closing sentence ('是を西洋にて『インシュレンス』と稱す。今之を保険と譯す') performs the explicit translation moment: the Western institution is named in transliterated katakana ('インシュレンス'), and the Japanese rendering 保険 is then established as the operating term. The passage exemplifies the Meiji translation maneuver and supplies the foundational Japanese-language articulation of the insurance institution that subsequent Meiji and Taishō commercial-legal discourse — the 1879 founding of the Tokio Marine Insurance Company, the 1881 founding of Meiji Life, the 1899 Commercial Code — would inherit and elaborate.

passage: 西洋諸国に大事業を起すには、其の費用甚だ多し。一人の力にては成すべからず。是に於て会社を結びて多数の人衆共に出資し、其の出資の額に応じて株式を分つ。株式は譲渡すべく、又之を売買すべし。事業の利益は株式の数に応じて分配せらる。是を株式会社と稱す。鉄道、工場、銀行皆是の如き仕法を以て成る。
notes: From Fukuzawa's exposition of Western corporate-commercial institutions in the Seiyō Jijō (1866–70), supplying the early-Meiji articulation of 株式 as the standardized rendering of Western 'shares' and providing the operating Japanese definition of the joint-stock corporation. The passage stages the institutional articulation across four calibrated steps. First, the structural problem: '大事業を起すには、其の費用甚だ多し。一人の力にては成すべからず' (to undertake a great enterprise the costs are enormous; one person's strength cannot accomplish it) — Fukuzawa frames the joint-stock corporation as the institutional solution to the structural problem of large-scale capital aggregation, situating the corporate form within a functional rather than legal-formal articulation. Second, the institutional architecture: '会社を結びて多数の人衆共に出資し、其の出資の額に応じて株式を分つ' (a company is formed; many persons together contribute capital; according to the size of the contribution, 株式 are divided) — Fukuzawa supplies the operating Japanese-language vocabulary for the corporate-equity structure, with 株式 stabilized as the term for the proportional ownership unit. Third, the transferability articulation: '株式は譲渡すべく、又之を売買すべし' (株式 may be transferred and may be bought and sold) — the passage articulates the structural-functional feature of corporate shares as transferable financial instruments, the institutional innovation that distinguishes the modern joint-stock corporation from earlier partnership forms. Fourth, the proportional-distribution articulation and the institutional consolidation: '事業の利益は株式の数に応じて分配せらる。是を株式会社と稱す' (the profits of the enterprise are distributed in proportion to the number of 株式; this is called 株式会社) — the passage stabilizes the compound 株式会社 (joint-stock company) as the standardized Japanese institutional category. The closing enumeration ('鉄道、工場、銀行皆是の如き仕法を以て成る' — railways, factories, and banks are all formed by this method) supplies the empirical-institutional anchoring that connects the abstract corporate-legal category to the concrete institutional landscape of Western industrial society. The passage exemplifies the Meiji translation maneuver — extending the Tokugawa-commercial vocabulary of kabu (the registered, transferable membership-rights of the kabunakama) to render the Western corporate-share institution — and supplies the foundational Japanese-language articulation that subsequent Meiji commercial-legal discourse would inherit and elaborate through the 1872 National Bank Act, the 1893 and 1899 Commercial Codes, and the broader institutional architecture of modern Japanese corporate law.

passage: 近代の経済組織に於ては、金融の機関甚だ重要なり。銀行は預金者より金を預り、之を企業家に貸付け、其の利息を以て利を得。生産の事業を起さんとする者は、自己の資本のみを以て足らざる時、銀行より金を借り、又は株式を発行して市場より資を集む。金融の仕組は、社会の各所に蓄へられたる資本を生産の場に流れ込ましむるの装置にして、資本主義経済の血脈を為すなり。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the structural-functional architecture of modern financial systems in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying one of the principal Taishō-era articulations of 金融 as the analytical category for the institutional sphere of monetary-credit intermediation in modern industrial society. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across three calibrated registers. First, the institutional-categorical assertion: '近代の経済組織に於ては、金融の機関甚だ重要なり' (in the modern economic organization, the institutions of 金融 are of paramount importance) — Kawakami frames 金融 not as an abstract financial-theoretical category but as the operating institutional sphere whose structural centrality to modern economic life requires explicit pedagogical exposition. Second, the structural-functional articulation: '銀行は預金者より金を預り、之を企業家に貸付け、其の利息を以て利を得' (the bank takes money on deposit from depositors, lends it to entrepreneurs, and obtains profit through interest) — Kawakami supplies the precise operating mechanism of financial intermediation, with the productive Japanese-language vocabulary 預金 (deposit), 貸付 (lending), 利息 (interest), 企業家 (entrepreneur) deployed in calibrated articulations. The passage continues with the corporate-financial articulation: '生産の事業を起さんとする者は、自己の資本のみを以て足らざる時、銀行より金を借り、又は株式を発行して市場より資を集む' (one who would undertake a productive enterprise, when his own 資本 is insufficient, borrows money from the bank, or issues 株式 to gather capital from the market) — Kawakami articulates the structural relations between 資本 (capital), 株式 (shares), 銀行 (banks), and 金融 (finance) as a unified institutional architecture. Third, the cosmological-analogical articulation: '金融の仕組は、社会の各所に蓄へられたる資本を生産の場に流れ込ましむるの装置にして、資本主義経済の血脈を為すなり' (the institutional architecture of 金融 is the apparatus that causes the 資本 accumulated in various locations of society to flow into the sites of production, constituting the blood-vessels of the capitalist economy) — Kawakami's blood-vessel metaphor doctrinally echoes Fukuzawa's earlier metaphor for 銀行 as the blood-circulation of commerce in the Seiyō Jijō, supplying the structural-functional articulation through which the financial sphere is identified as the circulatory system of the capitalist political-economic order. The passage's stylistic and conceptual sophistication — the precision of the operating vocabulary, the structural articulation of the institutional architecture, the cosmological scope of the blood-vessel metaphor — exemplifies Kawakami's pedagogical-analytical method and the broader Bimbō Monogatari project of stabilizing the operating Taishō-era Japanese economic vocabulary for general intellectual circulation.

passage: 近代の社会に於ては、生産は個人の手仕事に非ず、企業の組織を以て営まる。企業とは、資本を投じて労働を雇ひ、商品を製造して市場に売り、其の差額を以て利潤を得るの組織なり。大企業は機械を備へ、多数の労働者を集め、大規模に生産を行ふ。其の利潤は資本家の手に集まり、賃銀は労働者の身に止まる。企業の発達と共に、富と貧との懸隔愈々甚だしく、社会問題愈々深刻なり。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the structural-organizational character of modern productive activity in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying one of the principal Taishō-era articulations of 企業 as the analytical category for the institutional unit of capitalist productive enterprise. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across four calibrated steps. First, the structural-historical assertion: '近代の社会に於ては、生産は個人の手仕事に非ず、企業の組織を以て営まる' (in modern society, production is not the handicraft of individuals but is conducted through the organization of 企業) — Kawakami frames 企業 as the structural-historical category that distinguishes modern industrial production from pre-modern artisanal production, supplying the analytical apparatus through which the modern productive order is rendered visible. Second, the definitional articulation: '企業とは、資本を投じて労働を雇ひ、商品を製造して市場に売り、其の差額を以て利潤を得るの組織なり' (an 企業 is an organization that invests 資本, hires 労働, manufactures commodities, sells them in the market, and obtains 利潤 through the differential) — Kawakami supplies the precise structural-functional definition of the capitalist enterprise as the institutional unit organized around the systematic conversion of capital and labor into commodity-production for profit, deploying the productive Japanese-language vocabulary of modern political economy. Third, the scale-articulation: '大企業は機械を備へ、多数の労働者を集め、大規模に生産を行ふ' (the great 企業 is equipped with machinery, gathers many laborers, and conducts production at large scale) — Kawakami specifies the empirical-historical conditions of large-scale industrial enterprise, articulating the structural features (machinery, labor concentration, large-scale production) that distinguish modern industrial capitalism from earlier commercial-capitalist forms. Fourth, the distributional-political articulation: '其の利潤は資本家の手に集まり、賃銀は労働者の身に止まる' (the profits gather in the hands of the capitalist; the wages remain on the bodies of the workers) — Kawakami connects the structural-organizational analysis of the 企業 to the distributional-political question that motivates the entire Bimbō Monogatari project, with the parallelism of 利潤/賃銀 (profits/wages) and 資本家の手/労働者の身 (capitalist's hands/worker's bodies) supplying the rhetorical-political force of the structural analysis. The passage's stylistic and analytical sophistication exemplifies Kawakami's articulation of the productive Taishō-era Japanese economic vocabulary, with 企業 stabilized as the analytical category for the institutional-organizational unit of modern industrial production within the broader cluster of compounds (資本, 労働, 利潤, 資本家, 賃銀, 商品, 市場) that together constitute the operating vocabulary of modern Japanese political economy.

passage: 労働とは、人の身体を以て富を生み出すの活動なり。資本主義の世に於ては、労働者は身一つを以て、其の労働力を資本家に売り、賃銀を得て生活す。労働は富の根本なり。一切の財貨は、労働の力を経ずして産み出さるるものなし。然るに、労働の生み出したる富は、労働者の手に止まらず、多くは資本家の手に流れ込む。是れ近代社会の貧富懸隔の根因にして、社会問題の出づる所以なり。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the foundational political-economic category of labor in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying the principal Taishō-era articulation of 労働 as the analytical anchor of the modern political-economic vocabulary. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across four calibrated steps. First, the definitional articulation: '労働とは、人の身体を以て富を生み出すの活動なり' (labor is the activity by which a person produces wealth through the body) — Kawakami supplies the basic anthropological-economic definition of labor as the bodily-productive activity that generates wealth, articulating the foundational human-economic category that the broader structural analysis will deploy. Second, the wage-labor articulation: '資本主義の世に於ては、労働者は身一つを以て、其の労働力を資本家に売り、賃銀を得て生活す' (in the capitalist world, the worker, with only his body, sells his 労働力 [labor power] to the capitalist and obtains wages [賃銀] to live) — Kawakami articulates the precise Marxian distinction between 労働 (labor as activity) and 労働力 (labor power as the commodity sold), with the wage-form mediating the structural relation between worker and capitalist. The deployment of 労働力 as a calque of Marx's Arbeitskraft preserves the structural-analytical pivot of Capital with Sino-Japanese transparency. Third, the value-source articulation: '労働は富の根本なり。一切の財貨は、労働の力を経ずして産み出さるるものなし' (labor is the root of wealth; no good or commodity is produced without passing through the power of labor) — Kawakami articulates the labor theory of value through the classical political-economy register inherited from Smith and Ricardo and elaborated by Marx, with the foundational claim that labor is the substance and source of all economic value. Fourth, the distributional-political articulation: '労働の生み出したる富は、労働者の手に止まらず、多くは資本家の手に流れ込む' (the wealth produced by labor does not remain in the hands of the worker, but flows for the most part into the hands of the capitalist) — Kawakami articulates the surplus-value extraction at the heart of the Marxian critique of capitalism, with the structural-distributional consequence connected to the Bimbō Monogatari's central question about the persistence of poverty in modern industrial society. The passage's deployment of the productive cluster 労働 / 労働者 / 労働力 / 賃銀 / 資本家 across calibrated articulations exemplifies Kawakami's pedagogical-analytical method and supplies one of the foundational Taishō-era stabilizations of the operating Japanese political-economic vocabulary.

passage: 経済の循環は、生産と消費との二大作用より成る。生産は富を作り出し、消費は之を費やす。一国の経済の盛衰は、生産と消費との均衡如何に依る。消費は人の生活の必須にして、衣食住より始まり、教育、娯楽、医療に至るまで、皆消費の項目なり。然れども、貧者の消費は生存の最低限度に止まり、富者の消費は奢侈に流る。同じく消費と称すれども、其の質は天地の如く異なる。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the macroeconomic-circuit category of consumption in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying the principal Taishō-era articulation of 消費 as the analytical counterpart of 生産 (production) in the modern economic-circuit vocabulary. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across four calibrated steps. First, the macroeconomic-circuit articulation: '経済の循環は、生産と消費との二大作用より成る' (the circulation of the economy is composed of the two great functions of production and consumption) — Kawakami articulates the structural-circuit framework of modern political economy, in which 生産 (production) and 消費 (consumption) constitute the two principal aggregates whose interaction sustains the economic circulation; the framework derives from the Physiocratic and classical-political-economy tradition through Quesnay, Smith, and the nineteenth-century elaborations. Second, the structural-functional articulation: '生産は富を作り出し、消費は之を費やす' (production creates wealth; consumption expends it) — Kawakami supplies the precise structural-functional definition of consumption as the using-up counterpart of the production-creates side of the economic circuit, with the verb 費やす (tsuiyasu, to spend, to expend) reinforcing the spending-register of 費 in the compound 消費. Third, the empirical-categorical articulation: '消費は人の生活の必須にして、衣食住より始まり、教育、娯楽、医療に至るまで、皆消費の項目なり' (consumption is the necessity of human life, beginning with clothing-food-shelter and extending to education, entertainment, medical care — all are categories of consumption) — Kawakami specifies the empirical content of consumption across a categorical taxonomy that anticipates the modern consumer-expenditure classifications of national-income accounting (with 衣食住, the classical clothing-food-shelter triad of basic-necessity consumption, supplemented by the modern categories of education, entertainment, and health care). Fourth, the distributional-political articulation: '貧者の消費は生存の最低限度に止まり、富者の消費は奢侈に流る' (the consumption of the poor halts at the bare minimum of subsistence, while the consumption of the rich flows into luxury) — Kawakami connects the structural-categorical analysis of consumption to the distributional-political question that motivates the entire Bimbō Monogatari project, with the parallelism of 貧者 / 富者 (the poor / the rich) and 生存の最低限度 / 奢侈 (the bare minimum of subsistence / luxury) supplying the rhetorical-political force of the analytical claim. The closing articulation '同じく消費と称すれども、其の質は天地の如く異なる' (though both are called consumption, their quality differs as heaven from earth) drives home the Bimbō Monogatari's central theme: the structural-categorical homogeneity of 'consumption' as an economic category masks the radical inequality of its distributional content, and the structural-political analysis must descend from the aggregate to the distribution to render the question of poverty visible.

passage: 近代の経済の特色は、工業の発達に在り。蒸気の力、電気の力を借りて、機械を以て大量の商品を製造するの仕組、是を工業と称す。古代に於ては、農業を以て国の本と為したれども、近代に至りては、工業の発達と共に、国の富は工業より生じ、人口の多数は工場に集まる。英国は世界に先んじて工業国と成り、独逸、米国、日本、之に次ぐ。工業の発達は、富と便利とを齎せしと同時に、労働者を機械の傍らに繋ぎ、貧と労苦とを生み出したり。是れ近代の二面性なり。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the structural-historical character of modern industrial production in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying the principal Taishō-era articulation of 工業 as the analytical category through which the structural transformation of modern economic life is rendered visible. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across four calibrated steps. First, the structural-historical claim: '近代の経済の特色は、工業の発達に在り' (the distinctive feature of the modern economy lies in the development of industry) — Kawakami frames 工業 as the structural-historical category that defines modern economic modernity, supplying the analytical apparatus through which the contrast between modern and pre-modern economic life is articulated. Second, the technological-definitional articulation: '蒸気の力、電気の力を借りて、機械を以て大量の商品を製造するの仕組、是を工業と称す' (the system of borrowing the power of steam and electricity to manufacture commodities in great quantity through machinery — this is called industry) — Kawakami supplies the precise technological-economic definition of industry as the machine-aided, energy-intensive, large-scale production-system that distinguishes modern industrial production from pre-modern artisanal manufacture. Third, the historical-comparative articulation: '古代に於ては、農業を以て国の本と為したれども、近代に至りては、工業の発達と共に、国の富は工業より生じ、人口の多数は工場に集まる。英国は世界に先んじて工業国と成り、独逸、米国、日本、之に次ぐ' (in ancient times, agriculture was made the foundation of the nation, but on reaching modern times, with the development of industry, the wealth of the nation arises from industry, and the majority of the population gathers in factories. Britain became an industrial nation ahead of the world; Germany, the United States, and Japan follow) — Kawakami articulates the structural-historical succession from agricultural to industrial economic order and supplies the comparative-international ranking of industrial development that frames the late-Meiji and Taishō Japanese self-understanding as a late-developing industrial economy catching up to the Western leaders. Fourth, the distributional-political articulation: '工業の発達は、富と便利とを齎せしと同時に、労働者を機械の傍らに繋ぎ、貧と労苦とを生み出したり。是れ近代の二面性なり' (the development of industry has brought wealth and convenience, while at the same time chaining workers to the side of the machine and producing poverty and toil — this is the two-sidedness of modernity) — Kawakami articulates the dialectical-double character of industrial development that the Bimbō Monogatari's central question requires: industry produces both the abundance that makes modern life possible and the structural conditions of working-class poverty that the work seeks to analyze. The passage's deployment of the productive cluster 工業 / 工業国 / 工場 / 機械 / 労働者 across calibrated articulations exemplifies the operating Taishō-era Japanese industrial-economic vocabulary.
