passage: 資本家は其の資本を消費に費やすこと無く、却て之を生産の場に投ずるなり。是を投資と称す。投資の道は数多あり。或は工場を建て、機械を備へ、自ら事業を起すあり。或は他人の事業に資を出だし、株式を買ひて配当を受くるあり。或は銀行に金を預けて利息を得、又は国債社債を買ひて利を取るあり。投資の利は、生産の場に於て労働の生み出したる剰余価値より来る。資本主義の根本は、此の投資と剰余価値との連環に在り。
notes: From Kawakami Hajime's exposition of the financial-economic category of investment in the Bimbō Monogatari (1917), supplying the principal Taishō-era articulation of 投資 as the analytical category for the directed deployment of capital toward productive return. The passage stages the doctrinal articulation across four calibrated steps. First, the structural-definitional articulation: '資本家は其の資本を消費に費やすこと無く、却て之を生産の場に投ずるなり。是を投資と称す' (the capitalist does not spend his capital in consumption, but on the contrary casts it forth into the place of production. This is called 投資) — Kawakami articulates the structural-categorical distinction between 消費 (consumption, present using-up) and 投資 (investment, future-oriented productive deployment), supplying the analytical contrast that organizes the modern macroeconomic-aggregate vocabulary. The verb 投ずる (tōzuru, to cast forth) preserves the casting-and-committing register of the 投 character with structural transparency. Second, the categorical-typological articulation: '投資の道は数多あり。或は工場を建て、機械を備へ、自ら事業を起すあり。或は他人の事業に資を出だし、株式を買ひて配当を受くるあり。或は銀行に金を預けて利息を得、又は国債社債を買ひて利を取るあり' (there are many ways of investment: one may build a factory, equip it with machinery, and start one's own enterprise; one may put capital into another's enterprise, buy 株式 and receive dividends; one may deposit money in a bank to obtain interest, or buy government and corporate bonds to take profit) — Kawakami supplies the empirical-categorical typology of investment forms that anticipates the modern financial-economic taxonomy: direct investment (one's own enterprise), equity investment (株式 share-purchase with dividend return), bank deposits (with interest return), and bond investment (with bond-coupon return). The typology stabilizes the operating vocabulary across the modern Japanese financial-investment landscape. Third, the value-source articulation: '投資の利は、生産の場に於て労働の生み出したる剰余価値より来る' (the profit of investment comes from the surplus value that labor produces at the place of production) — Kawakami articulates the Marxian theory of profit-source through 剰余価値 (jōyō kachi, surplus value, calquing Mehrwert), connecting the financial-investment vocabulary to the structural-analytical apparatus of Capital. The articulation rejects the marginalist-neoclassical treatment of investment-return as derived from the productivity of capital itself and locates the source of investment-return in the labor-substance that is realized in the production-process. Fourth, the structural-systemic articulation: '資本主義の根本は、此の投資と剰余価値との連環に在り' (the root of capitalism lies in this circuit of investment and surplus value) — Kawakami articulates the structural pivot of the capitalist mode of production as the M-C-M' circuit of investment-and-surplus-value-extraction, with the productive cluster 投資 / 剰余価値 / 資本主義 articulating the analytical apparatus through which the structural-systemic character of capitalism is rendered visible. The passage exemplifies Kawakami's articulation of the productive Taishō-era Japanese financial-economic vocabulary, with 投資 stabilized as the analytical category for the directed-deployment-of-capital within the broader Marxian-economic apparatus.

passage: 凡ソ人ハ皆民事ノ権利ヲ享有ス。其ノ享有スル権利ハ法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ之ヲ行使スルコトヲ得。所有ノ権利ハ最モ完全ナル権利ナリ。然レドモ法律又ハ規則二於テ禁ズル所ノ用法ヲ以テ之ヲ行使スルコトヲ得ズ。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Civil Code (民法, c. 1870–1874), in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 権利 across the three structural moves that the French Code's Title I (Of Persons) and Title II (Of Property) contributed to the modern Japanese legal vocabulary. First, the universal-subjective articulation: '凡ソ人ハ皆民事ノ権利ヲ享有ス' (every person enjoys civil rights) — Mitsukuri renders the foundational French Civil Code Article 8 ('Tout Français jouira des droits civils,' every Frenchman enjoys civil rights), with the calibration toward universal personhood (人, person rather than 'Frenchman') reflecting the doctrinal generalization through which the Civil Code's national-civic-rights articulation was extended in the early-Meiji rendering toward the universal-juridical-subject register. The verb 享有 (kyōyū, to enjoy as a possession) preserves the structural register of the French jouir as the active-possessive enjoyment of legal status that is constitutive of the modern legal subject. Second, the law-bounded articulation: '其ノ享有スル権利ハ法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ之ヲ行使スルコトヲ得' (the rights one enjoys may be exercised in accordance with what the law prescribes) — Mitsukuri articulates the structural relation between 権利 and 法律 by which the legal subject's rights are exercisable only within the scope that the statutory law defines, calibrating the French Code's articulation of the law-bounded character of subjective rights for the modern Japanese legal vocabulary. Third, the property-rights articulation: '所有ノ権利ハ最モ完全ナル権利ナリ。然レドモ法律又ハ規則二於テ禁ズル所ノ用法ヲ以テ之ヲ行使スルコトヲ得ズ' (the right of ownership is the most complete right; nevertheless it may not be exercised in any manner prohibited by law or regulation) — Mitsukuri renders the French Civil Code Article 544's articulation of ownership ('La propriété est le droit de jouir et disposer des choses de la manière la plus absolue, pourvu qu'on n'en fasse pas un usage prohibé par les lois ou par les règlements') with the structural calibration toward the modern Japanese vocabulary of 所有権 (shoyūken, property right) as one species within the broader genus of 権利. The passage's institutional significance is foundational: the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus was operating under intense institutional pressure from the unequal-treaty negotiations with the Western powers, who demanded the establishment of a modern Western-style legal system in Japan as a condition for revising the consular jurisdictions in the treaty ports. Mitsukuri's translations of the French Codes supplied the operating doctrinal-vocabulary apparatus through which the modern Japanese legal vocabulary was stabilized, with 権利 emerging from this translation work as the operating term for subjective right within the modern continental civil-law register that the Meiji legal system adopted.

passage: 日本臣民ハ法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ兵役ノ義務ヲ有ス。又法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ納税ノ義務ヲ有ス。蓋シ兵役ト納税ハ臣民ノ二大義務ニシテ国家ノ存立ハ此二者ノ上二在リ。権利ハ恩賜ノ憲法二依リテ之ヲ享ケ、義務ハ忠誠ノ赤心二出デテ之ヲ尽クス。権利義務相俟チテ始メテ国家ノ秩序成ル。
notes: From the section of Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries on the Constitution (憲法義解, 1889) glossing Articles 20 and 21 of the Meiji Constitution — the articles articulating the duties of military service and tax-paying as the two great obligations of imperial subjects. The passage stages the foundational Meiji-constitutional articulation of 義務 across four calibrated moves. First, the dual articulation of the principal subject-duties: '日本臣民ハ法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ兵役ノ義務ヲ有ス。又法律ノ定ムる所二従ヒ納税ノ義務ヲ有ス' (Japanese subjects, in accordance with what the law prescribes, have the duty of military service. Likewise, in accordance with what the law prescribes, they have the duty of paying taxes) — Itō articulates the two compulsory subject-duties that the Constitution institutes, with the structural calibration toward the law-bounded character of the duties: 義務 is enforceable only within the scope that 法律 (statutory law) defines, with the statute supplying the operational specification of the constitutional duty. Second, the structural-functional articulation: '蓋シ兵役ト納税ハ臣民ノ二大義務ニシテ国家ノ存立ハ此二者ノ上二在リ' ('truly, military service and taxation are the two great duties of subjects, and the existence of the state rests upon these two') — Itō articulates the structural-functional ground of the duties: the state cannot exist without the resources (men and money) that subjects supply through these duties, and 義務 is calibrated as the operational mechanism through which subjects discharge their structural contribution to the state. Third, the asymmetric articulation of the rights-and-duties relation: '権利ハ恩賜ノ憲法二依リテ之ヲ享ケ、義務ハ忠誠ノ赤心二出デテ之ヲ尽クス' (rights are received through the Constitution as imperial gift, while duties are discharged through the sincere heart of loyalty) — Itō articulates the doctrinally-distinctive Meiji-constitutional asymmetry between 権利 and 義務: rights derive from the imperial-grant register of the Constitution (恩賜, imperial bestowal), while duties derive from the loyalty-relational register of the subject's structural relation to the sovereign (忠誠ノ赤心, the sincere heart of loyalty). The asymmetry is doctrinally consequential — it locates rights as gifts of imperial grace rather than as inalienable claims, and duties as expressions of subject-loyalty rather than as the structural correlate of right within a relation of legal equality. Fourth, the structural-completing articulation: '権利義務相俟チテ始メテ国家ノ秩序成ル' ('only when rights and duties stand together is the order of the state achieved') — Itō articulates 権利義務 (rights-and-duties) as the paired axis through which legal subjecthood is structured within the Meiji-constitutional order. The passage exemplifies the Meiji-constitutional articulation of 義務 as the deontological correlate of 権利 within the imperial-subject framework, with the doctrinal asymmetry between the imperial-grant register of rights and the loyalty-relational register of duties supplying the structural shape of the pre-war Japanese constitutional vocabulary.

passage: 凡ソ法律ハ帝国議会ノ協賛ヲ経ルヲ要ス。法律ハ憲法ノ範囲二於テ之ヲ制定スベシ。憲法二抵触スル法律ハ其ノ効力ヲ生ゼズ。法律ハ天皇之ヲ裁可シ公布シ其ノ施行ヲ命ズ。法律ハ国民ノ権利義務ヲ規律スル根本ノ準則ニシテ憲法ハ之ヲ統括スル至高ノ大典ナリ。
notes: From the section of Itō Hirobumi's Commentaries on the Constitution (憲法義解, 1889) glossing Articles 5, 6, and 37 of the Meiji Constitution — the articles articulating the procedure of statutory enactment and the structural relation between 法律 and 憲法 within the Meiji-constitutional framework. The passage stages the foundational Meiji-constitutional articulation of 法律 across four calibrated moves. First, the procedural-legislative articulation: '凡ソ法律ハ帝国議会ノ協賛ヲ経ルヲ要ス' (all laws require the consent of the Imperial Diet) — Itō articulates the constitutional principle that statutory law is the product of the legislative process within the bicameral assembly, with the verb 協賛 (kyōsan, to give consent / to assist by approval) calibrating the Diet's role as cooperatively-consensual rather than independently-sovereign within the imperial-constitutional framework. Second, the structural-hierarchical articulation: '法律ハ憲法ノ範囲二於テ之ヲ制定スベシ。憲法二抵触スル法律ハ其ノ効力ヲ生ゼズ' (laws shall be enacted within the scope of the Constitution; laws that conflict with the Constitution shall have no effect) — Itō articulates the structural-hierarchical principle of constitutional supremacy by which 法律 (statutory law) is positionally subordinate to 憲法 (constitutional law), with the legitimacy of any 法律 depending on its consistency with the 憲法. The articulation imports into the Meiji-constitutional vocabulary the German Rechtsstaat principle of constitutional supremacy that the Meiji constitutional drafters inherited from the German constitutional-theoretical tradition through Hermann Roesler and the broader 1880s constitutional-drafting process. Third, the imperial-sanction articulation: '法律ハ天皇之ヲ裁可シ公布シ其ノ施行ヲ命ズ' (laws are sanctioned, promulgated, and ordered into effect by the Emperor) — Itō articulates the Meiji-constitutional doctrine of imperial sanction by which the Emperor's approval is the structural-completing element of statutory enactment, calibrating 法律 within the German-monarchical-constitutional rather than the Atlantic-popular-sovereignty register. Fourth, the structural-functional articulation: '法律ハ国民ノ権利義務ヲ規律スル根本ノ準則ニシテ憲法ハ之ヲ統括スル至高ノ大典ナリ' (statutory law is the foundational standard that regulates the rights and duties of the people; the Constitution is the supreme great instrument that governs it) — Itō articulates the structural-functional relation between 法律 (statutory law) as the operational layer that regulates 権利 (rights) and 義務 (duties) and 憲法 (constitutional law) as the foundational layer that governs the body of statutory law itself. The passage exemplifies the Meiji-constitutional calibration of 法律 within the structural-hierarchical Rechtsstaat framework, with the compound stabilized as the operational category of statute below the constitutional layer of 憲法 in the modern Japanese legal-constitutional vocabulary.

passage: 裁判ハ法律ノ範囲二於テ之ヲ行フ。判事ハ法律以外二権限ヲ有セズ。凡ソ訴訟ハ其ノ管轄ヲ有スル裁判所二於テ之ヲ受理シ、其ノ判決ハ法ノ定ムル所二従ヒ之ヲ言渡ス。裁判ハ公開ヲ原則トス。然レドモ風俗又ハ国安二害アリト認ムル時ハ之ヲ秘密二行フコトヲ得。判決ハ宣告ノ後速ニ書面ヲ以テ之ヲ作成シ判事之二署名捺印スベシ。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Criminal Instruction (治罪法 / 民事訴訟法, c. 1870–1874), in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 裁判 across five calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese judicial vocabulary was stabilized. First, the law-bounded articulation: '裁判ハ法律ノ範囲二於テ之ヲ行フ。判事ハ法律以外二権限ヲ有セズ' (trials are conducted within the scope of the law; judges have no authority outside the law) — Mitsukuri articulates the structural principle of judicial subordination to law that the Napoleonic Code institutionalized as the foundational doctrine of the modern continental civil-law tradition: the judge applies the law rather than making it, and the trial is the structured procedure within which legal questions are resolved through the application of statutory and code-based rules. The principle calibrates 裁判 within the continental civil-law inquisitorial register rather than the common-law adversarial register. Second, the jurisdictional articulation: '凡ソ訴訟ハ其ノ管轄ヲ有スル裁判所二於テ之ヲ受理シ' (all litigations shall be received at the court that has jurisdiction over them) — Mitsukuri articulates the jurisdictional structure of the modern court system, calibrating the operating vocabulary 訴訟 (litigation, the litigant's bringing of claim), 裁判所 (court, the institutional locus of trial), and 管轄 (jurisdiction, the territorial-subject-matter scope of judicial authority) within the modern Japanese judicial vocabulary. Third, the law-application articulation: '其ノ判決ハ法ノ定ムル所二従ヒ之ヲ言渡ス' (the verdict shall be pronounced in accordance with what the law prescribes) — Mitsukuri articulates the structural relation between 法 (law) and 判決 (verdict) by which the judicial determination derives its authority from the statute it applies. Fourth, the publicity articulation: '裁判ハ公開ヲ原則トス。然レドモ風俗又ハ国安二害アリト認ムル時ハ之ヲ秘密二行フコトヲ得' (trials are public as a general principle; however, where they are deemed harmful to public morals or state security, they may be conducted in secret) — Mitsukuri articulates the modern principle of judicial publicity (the open court, principe de publicité) that the French Revolution institutionalized as a structural reform of the secret pre-revolutionary judicial procedure, with the qualified exception preserving the ancien-régime category of secret procedure for limited cases of public morals and state security. The articulation introduces the modern Western judicial-procedural principle of publicity into the Japanese judicial vocabulary as one of the structural features of the modern judicial system. Fifth, the formal-procedural articulation: '判決ハ宣告ノ後速ニ書面ヲ以テ之ヲ作成シ判事之二署名捺印スベシ' (after pronouncement, the verdict shall be promptly drawn up in writing and the judge shall sign and seal it) — Mitsukuri articulates the formal-procedural requirements for the documentary record of the judicial determination, calibrating the operating vocabulary 宣告 (pronouncement), 書面 (written instrument), 署名捺印 (signature and seal) within the modern Japanese judicial-procedural vocabulary. The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental civil-law judicial system in early-Meiji Japan, with 裁判 stabilized as the operating term for the structured procedure of judicial trial and the broader cluster 訴訟 / 裁判所 / 判事 / 判決 / 管轄 / 宣告 articulating the institutional-procedural apparatus of the modern Japanese judicial system.

passage: 夫レ人民ノ天賦人権ハ天ノ与フル所二シテ君主ノ恩賜二非ズ。生命ヲ全ウシ財産ヲ守リ意見ヲ表シ集会ヲ為スハ凡ソ人タル者ノ固有スル権利ナリ。政府ハ此ノ権利ヲ保護スルガ為メ二設ケラルル者二シテ若シ之ヲ侵スコトアラバ其ノ正当ナル根拠ヲ失フ。今我国ノ政体ハ上帝室二在リ下人民二在ラズ。有司専権ヲ恣ニシ法律一定ノ準縄ナク賞罰愛憎二出デ言路壅塞シテ困苦ヲ告グルニ由ナシ。是レ人権ヲ保ツノ道二非ズ。臣等以為ラク之ヲ救フノ道タダ天下ノ公議ヲ張ルニ在ルノミ。
notes: From the foundational textual articulation of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動) in the milieu of the Itagaki Petition for the Establishment of a Popularly Elected Assembly (民撰議院設立建白書, January 1874) and the broader argumentative apparatus that surrounded the petition's submission and circulation. The passage stages the foundational late-Meiji articulation of 人権 across four calibrated doctrinal moves. First, the natural-law articulation: '夫レ人民ノ天賦人権ハ天ノ与フル所二シテ君主ノ恩賜二非ズ' (the heaven-endowed human rights of the people are given by heaven and are not the gift of the sovereign) — the passage articulates the load-bearing late-Meiji doctrinal claim that human rights are pre-political natural-law entitlements grounded in the structure of human nature itself, calibrated explicitly against the imperial-grant register that would later be institutionalized in the 1889 Meiji Constitution's articulation of 臣民の権利 (rights of subjects) as imperial bestowal. The compound 天賦人権 (tenpu jinken, heaven-endowed human rights) is the principal late-Meiji liberal articulation of natural-law rights, with 天 (heaven, the cosmological-ethical order), 賦 (to bestow, to apportion), and 人権 (human rights) combined to articulate rights as the structural endowment of human beings by the cosmological-ethical order rather than the conditional gift of political authority. Second, the typological articulation: '生命ヲ全ウシ財産ヲ守リ意見ヲ表シ集会ヲ為スハ凡ソ人タル者ノ固有スル権利ナリ' (the preservation of life, the protection of property, the expression of opinion, and the holding of assembly are rights inherent in everyone who is a human being) — the passage supplies the empirical-typological listing of natural-rights protections, calibrated explicitly through the Lockean-French triad of life-property-liberty supplemented by the assembly-and-expression rights that the 1789 French Declaration of the Rights of Man articulated. The articulation deploys 凡ソ人タル者 (everyone who is a human being) as the universal-anthropological subject of rights, calibrating the rights-bearer at the universal-human-nature level rather than the citizen-of-a-nation or imperial-subject level. Third, the social-contract-doctrinal articulation: '政府ハ此ノ権利ヲ保護スルガ為メ二設ケラルル者二シテ若シ之ヲ侵スコトアラバ其ノ正当ナル根拠ヲ失フ' (the government is established for the protection of these rights, and if it violates them it loses its legitimate ground) — the passage articulates the foundational Lockean-revolutionary doctrine of legitimate political authority as derived from and limited by the natural rights it is established to protect, calibrating the modern Japanese political vocabulary toward the social-contract-theoretical framework that supplied the doctrinal foundation of the late-Meiji liberal-democratic movement. Fourth, the institutional-reformist articulation: '是レ人権ヲ保ツノ道二非ズ。臣等以為ラク之ヲ救フノ道タダ天下ノ公議ヲ張ルニ在ルノミ' (this is not the path of preserving human rights; we humbly submit that the path of remedy lies only in establishing public deliberation under heaven) — the passage articulates the institutional-reformist demand for a popularly-elected legislative assembly (民撰議院 minsen giin) as the structural-political mechanism through which 人権 (human rights) and 公議 (kōgi, public deliberation) can be institutionally realized. The passage exemplifies the foundational late-Meiji liberal-natural-rights articulation of 人権, with the compound calibrated specifically toward the natural-law-grounded universal-anthropological register that distinguishes the Freedom and People's Rights Movement vocabulary from the imperial-grant register that the 1889 Meiji Constitution would subsequently institutionalize.

passage: 契約ハ二人若ハ数人ノ間二於テ合意ヲ以テ成立スル者ナリ。其ノ要素ハ第一二当事者ノ承諾、第二二能力、第三二確定セル目的、第四二適法ナル原因二在リ。適法二成立シタル契約ハ之ヲ為シタル当事者ノ間二於テ法律ト同一ノ効力ヲ有ス。契約ハ合意又ハ法律ノ認ムル原因二依ルニ非ザレバ之ヲ取消スコトヲ得ズ。契約ハ信義ヲ以テ之ヲ履行スベシ。当事者ハ其ノ表示シタル所ノミナラズ事ノ性質、慣習、衡平ノ要求スル所ノ一切ノ義務二拘束セラル。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Civil Code's Title III (Of Contracts and of Conventional Obligations in General, Articles 1101–1369), in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 契約 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese contract-law vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: '契約ハ二人若ハ数人ノ間二於テ合意ヲ以テ成立スル者ナリ' (a contract is that which is formed between two or more persons by mutual agreement) — Mitsukuri renders the foundational French Civil Code Article 1101 ('Le contrat est une convention par laquelle une ou plusieurs personnes s'obligent...') with the calibration of 合意 (gōi, mutual agreement) as the structural foundation of the contract. The articulation imports into modern Japanese legal vocabulary the continental Willensdogma — the doctrine that the parties' free declaration of will is the structural foundation of contractual obligation — that distinguishes the continental civil-law contract tradition from the Anglo-American common-law consideration-based apparatus. Second, the formal-elements articulation: '其ノ要素ハ第一二当事者ノ承諾、第二二能力、第三二確定セル目的、第四二適法ナル原因二在リ' (its essential elements are: first, the consent of the parties; second, capacity; third, a definite object; fourth, a lawful cause) — Mitsukuri renders the French Civil Code Article 1108's articulation of the four essential elements of a valid contract (consentement, capacité, objet certain, cause licite), calibrating the modern Japanese contractual-formation vocabulary toward the continental civil-law four-element apparatus. The classical Roman-canon-law cause doctrine (cause licite, the lawful cause that grounds the obligation) is one of the doctrinally-distinctive features of the French civil-law contract tradition that the early-Meiji translations imported into modern Japanese legal vocabulary, although the subsequent Japanese Civil Code of 1898 substantially recalibrated the doctrinal apparatus toward the German Pandectist articulation through the Willenserklärung (declaration of will) framework. Third, the legal-effect articulation: '適法二成立シタル契約ハ之ヲ為シタル当事者ノ間二於テ法律ト同一ノ効力ヲ有ス。契約ハ合意又ハ法律ノ認ムル原因二依ルニ非ザレバ之ヲ取消スコトヲ得ズ' (a contract lawfully formed has the same effect between the contracting parties as the law itself; a contract may not be revoked except by mutual agreement or for the causes that the law recognizes) — Mitsukuri renders the French Civil Code Article 1134's celebrated articulation ('Les conventions légalement formées tiennent lieu de loi à ceux qui les ont faites'), one of the most doctrinally-load-bearing articulations of modern continental contract law: the contract has between the parties the force of law itself, and the principle of contractual sanctity (pacta sunt servanda) is the structural foundation of the modern obligation-system. Fourth, the good-faith-and-equity articulation: '契約ハ信義ヲ以テ之ヲ履行スベシ。当事者ハ其ノ表示シタル所ノミナラズ事ノ性質、慣習、衡平ノ要求スル所ノ一切ノ義務二拘束セラル' (contracts shall be performed in good faith; the parties are bound not only to what they have expressly declared but to all the obligations that the nature of the matter, custom, and equity require) — Mitsukuri renders the French Civil Code Articles 1134(3) and 1135's good-faith articulation, calibrating the operating vocabulary 信義 (shingi, good faith), 慣習 (kanshū, custom), 衡平 (kōhei, equity) within the modern Japanese contract-law vocabulary. The good-faith principle (信義則, shingisoku) became one of the doctrinally-load-bearing principles of modern Japanese contract law, with the Japanese Civil Code's Article 1(2) explicitly articulating the principle and the post-WWII Japanese contract-law jurisprudence developing a substantial doctrinal apparatus around the good-faith requirement. The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental civil-law contract system in early-Meiji Japan, with 契約 stabilized as the operating term for contract and the broader cluster 合意 / 承諾 / 能力 / 目的 / 原因 / 信義 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of contractual formation, validity, and performance within the modern Japanese civil-law tradition.

passage: 凡ソ犯罪ハ法律ノ明文ヲ以テ之ヲ定ムルニ非ザレバ之ヲ罰スルコトヲ得ズ。法律ノ規定スル所二非ザル行為ハ犯罪二非ズ。犯罪ハ其ノ重キヲ重罪ト為シ其ノ軽キヲ軽罪ト為シ其ノ更二軽キヲ違警罪ト為ス。重罪ハ身体ノ刑及ビ恥辱ノ刑ヲ以テ之ヲ罰シ、軽罪ハ拘禁及ビ罰金ヲ以テ之ヲ罰シ、違警罪ハ科料ヲ以テ之ヲ罰ス。何人ト雖モ犯罪ノ時二於テ既二法律ノ定メタル刑ヲ加フルコトヲ得。但シ其ノ後新タナル法律ノ刑ヲ軽クスル時ハ被告人二有利ナル方ヲ適用ス。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Code Pénal (1810) and the Code d'Instruction Criminelle, in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 犯罪 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese criminal-law vocabulary was stabilized. First, the nulla-poena-sine-lege articulation: '凡ソ犯罪ハ法律ノ明文ヲ以テ之ヲ定ムルニ非ザレバ之ヲ罰スルコトヲ得ズ。法律ノ規定スル所二非ザル行為ハ犯罪二非ズ' (no crime may be punished unless it is defined by the express text of the law; an act not provided for by the law is not a crime) — Mitsukuri renders the foundational principle of modern criminal law articulated in the French Code Pénal's preliminary article and the German Feuerbachian formula nulla poena sine lege (no penalty without prior law), calibrating the modern Japanese criminal-law vocabulary toward the Beccarian-Enlightenment doctrinal foundation of the rule-of-law-grounded criminal-law tradition. The principle became foundational to the modern Japanese criminal-law tradition, with the compound 罪刑法定主義 (zaikei hōteishugi, the principle of nulla poena sine lege) articulated through the Boissonade Penal Code of 1880 and entrenched in Article 31 of the post-war 1947 Constitution. Second, the typological articulation: '犯罪ハ其ノ重キヲ重罪ト為シ其ノ軽キヲ軽罪ト為シ其ノ更二軽キヲ違警罪ト為ス' (crimes are classified as serious offenses, lesser offenses, and police infractions according to their gravity) — Mitsukuri renders the French Code Pénal's tripartite classification of offenses (crime, délit, contravention) into the modern Japanese criminal-law typology of 重罪 (jūzai, felony / serious crime), 軽罪 (keizai, misdemeanor / lesser crime), and 違警罪 (ikeizai, police infraction / petty offense). The tripartite typology was institutionalized through the Boissonade Penal Code of 1880 but was substantially restructured by the German-influenced Penal Code of 1907 toward a binary 罪 / 罰 (crime / punishment) framework, with the French tripartite typology partially preserved in the modern distinction between 刑事犯 (criminal offense) and 行政犯 (administrative offense). Third, the proportional-punishment articulation: '重罪ハ身体ノ刑及ビ恥辱ノ刑ヲ以テ之ヲ罰シ、軽罪ハ拘禁及ビ罰金ヲ以テ之ヲ罰シ、違警罪ハ科料ヲ以テ之ヲ罰ス' (serious crimes are punished by corporal and infamy penalties, lesser crimes by detention and fines, and petty offenses by minor monetary penalties) — Mitsukuri articulates the modern proportional-punishment apparatus of the French Code Pénal, calibrating the modern Japanese punishment vocabulary 身体ノ刑 (corporal punishment), 恥辱ノ刑 (infamy punishment), 拘禁 (detention), 罰金 (fine), 科料 (minor monetary penalty) within the rule-of-law-grounded criminal-sanction framework that the Beccarian-Enlightenment tradition supplied. Fourth, the lex-mitior articulation: '何人ト雖モ犯罪ノ時二於テ既二法律ノ定メタル刑ヲ加フルコトヲ得。但シ其ノ後新タナル法律ノ刑ヲ軽クスル時ハ被告人二有利ナル方ヲ適用ス' (no person may be punished except by the penalty that the law had established at the time of the crime; however, if a subsequent law lessens the penalty, the more favorable provision shall apply to the defendant) — Mitsukuri articulates the modern principle of non-retroactivity of criminal law combined with the lex mitior principle (the application of the more lenient subsequent law), supplying the operating doctrinal apparatus of modern continental criminal-law temporal application that the modern Japanese Penal Code's Article 6 inherits. The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental criminal-law system in early-Meiji Japan, with 犯罪 stabilized as the operating term for crime and the broader cluster 重罪 / 軽罪 / 違警罪 / 罰金 / 科料 / 罪刑法定 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of the modern Japanese criminal-law tradition.

passage: 凡ソ訴訟ハ原告ト被告ト二人ノ当事者ヲ以テ成立ス。原告ハ其ノ請求ノ理由及ビ証拠ヲ陳述シ被告ハ之二答弁スルコトヲ得。被告人ハ法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ弁護人ヲ選任スルノ権利ヲ有ス。被告人ハ自己二不利ナル供述ヲ強ヒラルルコト無シ。判決ノ確定スルマデハ被告人ハ無罪ノ推定ヲ受ク。被告人ハ証人ト対質シ反対尋問ヲ為スコトヲ得。被告人ノ防御ハ其ノ正当ナル権利ニシテ之ヲ妨グルコトヲ得ズ。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Code of Civil Procedure and the Code d'Instruction Criminelle, in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 被告 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese procedural-defense vocabulary was stabilized. First, the procedural-opposition articulation: '凡ソ訴訟ハ原告ト被告ト二人ノ当事者ヲ以テ成立ス。原告ハ其ノ請求ノ理由及ビ証拠ヲ陳述シ被告ハ之二答弁スルコトヲ得' (a litigation is constituted by two parties, the plaintiff and the defendant; the plaintiff sets forth the grounds and evidence of his claim, and the defendant may answer to the same) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational structural-procedural opposition between 原告 (plaintiff, the active-charging side) and 被告 (defendant, the passive-receiving side) of the litigation, with the structural symmetry of the 原 / 被 prefix-pattern (the original-charging vs. the receiving-charged) preserving in the Sino-Japanese compound a doctrinal precision that the asymmetric English plaintiff / defendant pair does not foreground. The articulation supplies the foundational procedural-vocabulary of modern Japanese litigation. Second, the right-to-counsel articulation: '被告人ハ法律ノ定ムル所二従ヒ弁護人ヲ選任スルノ権利ヲ有ス' (the accused has, in accordance with the provisions of the law, the right to appoint defense counsel) — Mitsukuri articulates the criminal defendant's right to counsel, calibrating the operating vocabulary 弁護人 (bengonin, defense counsel) and 被告人 (hikokunin, the criminally accused, distinguished from the broader civil-procedural 被告) within the modern Japanese criminal-procedural vocabulary. The right-to-counsel principle would be substantially elaborated through the post-war 1948 Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 37 of the 1947 Constitution under American Occupation influence, but the foundational articulation enters modern Japanese legal vocabulary through the early-Meiji French-procedural-code translations. Third, the privilege-against-self-incrimination and presumption-of-innocence articulation: '被告人ハ自己二不利ナル供述ヲ強ヒラルルコト無シ。判決ノ確定スルマデハ被告人ハ無罪ノ推定ヲ受ク' (the accused shall not be compelled to make statements unfavorable to himself; until the verdict is final, the accused enjoys the presumption of innocence) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational due-process protections of the modern criminal defendant: the privilege against self-incrimination (the structural protection against compelled self-incrimination, codified as a constitutional right in Article 38 of the post-war Constitution) and the presumption of innocence (the structural-procedural rule that the prosecution bears the burden of proof and the accused is treated as innocent until proven guilty, articulated as 無罪推定 muzai suitei in modern Japanese criminal-procedural vocabulary). The articulation imports into modern Japanese legal vocabulary the foundational due-process apparatus of modern continental criminal procedure, calibrating the operating vocabulary 被告人 toward the constitutional-rights-bearing register that the post-war Japanese criminal-procedural tradition would substantially elaborate. Fourth, the confrontation-and-defense articulation: '被告人ハ証人ト対質シ反対尋問ヲ為スコトヲ得。被告人ノ防御ハ其ノ正当ナル権利ニシテ之ヲ妨グルコトヲ得ズ' (the accused may confront witnesses and conduct cross-examination; the defense of the accused is his legitimate right and may not be impeded) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational defense-rights apparatus of the modern criminal defendant: the right to confront witnesses (対質, taishitsu, the structural-procedural right to face the accuser), the right to conduct cross-examination (反対尋問, hantai jinmon), and the structural-procedural protection of the defense as a legitimate right that the prosecution may not impede. The articulation supplies the foundational defense-rights vocabulary that the modern Japanese criminal-procedural tradition inherits, with the post-war Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 37 of the 1947 Constitution substantially elaborating the apparatus under American Occupation influence. The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental procedural-defense system in early-Meiji Japan, with 被告 / 被告人 stabilized as the operating term for the procedural defendant and the broader cluster 原告 / 弁護人 / 答弁 / 対質 / 反対尋問 / 防御 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of modern Japanese procedural-defense within the civil and criminal litigation systems.

passage: 原告ハ訴訟ヲ提起スル者ナリ。其ノ請求ハ書面ヲ以テ裁判所二提出スベシ。原告ハ其ノ請求ノ理由及ビ事実ヲ明確二陳述シ其ノ証拠ヲ示スベシ。訴訟ヲ提起セントスル者ハ法律ノ定ムル利益ヲ有スルニ非ザレバ之ヲ提起スルコトヲ得ズ。原告ハ訴訟ノ進行二必要ナル一切ノ行為ヲ為スノ権利ヲ有スルト共二其ノ義務ヲ負フ。原告ハ其ノ請求ヲ証スル責任ヲ負フ。原告ハ判決ノ確定スルマデ其ノ請求ヲ取下グルコトヲ得。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Code de procédure civile (1806), in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 原告 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese civil-plaintiff vocabulary was stabilized. First, the originating-action articulation: '原告ハ訴訟ヲ提起スル者ナリ。其ノ請求ハ書面ヲ以テ裁判所二提出スベシ' (the plaintiff is the one who initiates the litigation; his claim shall be submitted to the court in writing) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational structural definition of the plaintiff function as the originating-active party of civil litigation, with 提起 (teiki, to initiate / to bring forward) supplying the operating procedural verb for the lodging of the formal claim. The articulation imports into modern Japanese civil-procedural vocabulary the continental civil-procedure articulation of plaintiff-initiated litigation that descends from the Roman-law actio doctrine through the medieval and modern continental procedural traditions. Second, the standing-and-interest articulation: '訴訟ヲ提起セントスル者ハ法律ノ定ムル利益ヲ有スルニ非ザレバ之ヲ提起スルコトヲ得ズ' (one who would initiate a litigation may not do so unless he holds an interest provided for by law) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational procedural-doctrinal requirement of plaintiff standing (原告適格, genkoku tekikaku — the structural requirement that the plaintiff have a legally-cognizable interest in the matter, descending from the French intérêt à agir doctrine and parallel to the German Klagebefugnis). The articulation imports into modern Japanese civil-procedural vocabulary the foundational doctrine that distinguishes legally-cognizable claims from mere general grievances, with the doctrinal apparatus subsequently elaborated through the modern Japanese civil-procedure jurisprudence. Third, the burden-of-proof articulation: '原告ハ訴訟ノ進行二必要ナル一切ノ行為ヲ為スノ権利ヲ有スルト共二其ノ義務ヲ負フ。原告ハ其ノ請求ヲ証スル責任ヲ負フ' (the plaintiff has the right and the obligation to undertake all acts necessary for the progress of the litigation; the plaintiff bears the responsibility of proving his claim) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational doctrinal allocation of the burden of proof to the plaintiff (立証責任, risshō sekinin, descending from the Roman-law principle ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat — the burden of proof rests on the one who asserts, not on the one who denies), one of the structurally-load-bearing principles of modern continental civil procedure. The articulation supplies the operating vocabulary 立証 (risshō, to prove / to bring evidence) and 責任 (sekinin, responsibility / liability — itself a structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern Japanese legal vocabulary) within the modern Japanese civil-procedural framework. Fourth, the disposition-of-claim articulation: '原告ハ判決ノ確定スルマデ其ノ請求ヲ取下グルコトヲ得' (the plaintiff may withdraw his claim until the judgment becomes final) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational doctrinal principle of the plaintiff's procedural autonomy over the disposition of the claim — the principle of party-disposition (処分権主義, shobun-ken shugi) that grounds the modern continental civil-procedure articulation of the parties' control over the scope and continuation of the litigation. The articulation supplies the operating procedural vocabulary 取下 (torisage, withdrawal of claim) within the modern Japanese civil-procedural framework. The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental civil-plaintiff system in early-Meiji Japan, with 原告 stabilized as the operating term for the civil plaintiff and the broader cluster 提起 / 請求 / 立証 / 取下 / 原告適格 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of modern Japanese civil-procedural plaintiff-function within the civil litigation system.

passage: 刑法ハ犯罪及ビ其ノ刑罰ヲ定ムル法律ナリ。何人モ法律ノ明文ヲ以テ予メ定メラレタル犯罪ノ外其ノ行為ヲ罰セラルルコト無シ。何人モ犯罪ノ時二施行セラレタル法律二非ザレバ之二依リテ罰セラルルコト無シ。刑法ハ凡テノ人二平等二適用セラル。刑法ハ其ノ施行後二行ハレタル行為二限リテ之ヲ適用ス。但シ被告人二有利ナル新法ハ既往二遡リテ之ヲ適用ス。刑法ハ犯罪ヲ重罪・軽罪・違警罪ノ三種二区別シ各其ノ性質二応ジテ刑罰ヲ定ム。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Code Pénal (1810) — specifically the preliminary articles and the foundational provisions on the application of the criminal law — in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 刑法 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese criminal-law-as-codified-domain vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: '刑法ハ犯罪及ビ其ノ刑罰ヲ定ムル法律ナリ' (the criminal law is the law that defines crimes and their penalties) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational structural definition of 刑法 as the systematically-codified domain that articulates the offense-and-punishment relation, with the dual-element structure 犯罪 + 刑罰 (crime and penalty) supplying the foundational doctrinal articulation that descends from the Beccarian-Feuerbachian criminal-law tradition. The articulation imports into modern Japanese legal vocabulary the systematic-codified articulation of criminal law as a doctrinal-domain that is structurally distinguished from the broader penal-administrative apparatus of the classical-imperial tradition. Second, the nulla-poena-sine-lege articulation: '何人モ法律ノ明文ヲ以テ予メ定メラレタル犯罪ノ外其ノ行為ヲ罰セラルルコト無シ。何人モ犯罪ノ時二施行セラレタル法律二非ザレバ之二依リテ罰セラルルコト無シ' (no person shall be punished for any act other than crimes defined in advance by the express text of the law; no person shall be punished except on the basis of the law that was in force at the time of the crime) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational principle of nulla poena sine lege (no penalty without prior law) and its temporal-application corollary of non-retroactivity, the foundational doctrinal principles of modern continental criminal law that the Beccarian-Feuerbachian tradition supplies. The principle would be subsequently institutionalized in the modern Japanese criminal-law tradition through the Boissonade Penal Code of 1880, the current Penal Code of 1907, and Article 31 of the post-war 1947 Constitution, with the operating doctrinal compound 罪刑法定主義 (zaikei hōteishugi) supplying the systematic articulation of the principle. Third, the equality-of-application and lex-mitior articulation: '刑法ハ凡テノ人二平等二適用セラル。刑法ハ其ノ施行後二行ハレタル行為二限リテ之ヲ適用ス。但シ被告人二有利ナル新法ハ既往二遡リテ之ヲ適用ス' (the criminal law applies equally to all persons; the criminal law applies only to acts committed after its entry into force; however, a new law that is more favorable to the accused shall be applied retroactively) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational equality-before-the-criminal-law principle and the lex mitior corollary of the temporal-application doctrine, supplying the operating doctrinal apparatus that grounds the modern continental criminal-law tradition's articulation of equal-and-proportionate criminal-state authority within the rule-of-law framework. The articulation institutionalizes in modern Japanese legal vocabulary the foundational liberal-democratic principles that distinguish modern criminal law from the classical-imperial penal apparatus of personalized-and-status-graduated punishment. Fourth, the typological-classification articulation: '刑法ハ犯罪ヲ重罪・軽罪・違警罪ノ三種二区別シ各其ノ性質二応ジテ刑罰ヲ定ム' (the criminal law classifies crimes into the three categories of serious crimes, lesser crimes, and police infractions, and prescribes punishments according to the nature of each) — Mitsukuri renders the French Code Pénal's tripartite classification (crime, délit, contravention) into the modern Japanese criminal-law typology, supplying the operating vocabulary 重罪 (jūzai), 軽罪 (keizai), 違警罪 (ikeizai) that institutionalizes the French-Beccarian typological articulation. The tripartite typology was substantially restructured by the German-influenced Penal Code of 1907 toward a binary structure, with the French tripartite typology partially preserved in the modern distinction between 刑事犯 (criminal offense) and 行政犯 (administrative offense). The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental criminal-law-as-systematically-codified-domain in early-Meiji Japan, with 刑法 stabilized as the operating term for the codified criminal law and the broader cluster 罪刑法定 / 平等 / 不遡及 / lex mitior / 重罪・軽罪・違警罪 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of modern Japanese criminal law within the rule-of-law-grounded continental criminal-law tradition.

passage: 民法ハ人ノ身分及ビ財産二関スル一切ノ私法的関係ヲ定ムル法律ナリ。民法ハ人ヲ以テ凡テノ私法的関係ノ主体ト為ス。総テノ人ハ法律ノ前二平等ニシテ其ノ権利ヲ享有ス。所有ハ最モ完全ナル仕方二於テ物ヲ使用シ収益シ及ビ処分スルノ権利ナリ。但シ法律及ビ命令ノ禁ズル所二非ザル場合二限ル。契約ハ当事者ノ間二於テ法律ト同一ノ効力ヲ有シ其ノ合意ハ之ヲ遵守スベシ。何人モ他人二損害ヲ加ヘタル者ハ其ノ過失二依ル時ハ之ヲ賠償スル義務ヲ負フ。婚姻、親子、相続二関スル事項ハ別二之ヲ定ム。
notes: From Mitsukuri Rinshō's translation of the French Code civil (1804) — specifically the preliminary provisions and the foundational articulations of legal personality, property, contract, and tort — in the calibrated bungo register of early-Meiji legal translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 民法 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese civil-law-as-codified-domain vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: '民法ハ人ノ身分及ビ財産二関スル一切ノ私法的関係ヲ定ムル法律ナリ。民法ハ人ヲ以テ凡テノ私法的関係ノ主体ト為ス' (the civil law is the law that defines all private-legal relations concerning persons' status and property; the civil law treats the person as the subject of all private-legal relations) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational structural definition of 民法 as the systematically-codified domain of private-legal relations centered on the person as the legal subject, with the operating vocabulary 私法的関係 (shihōteki kankei, private-legal relations) and 主体 (shutai, subject — itself a structurally-load-bearing wasei-kango of modern Japanese philosophical and legal vocabulary) supplying the foundational doctrinal articulation. The articulation imports into modern Japanese legal vocabulary the modern continental civil-law tradition's articulation of the legal-subject as the structural foundation of the private-law domain, descending from the Pandectist-doctrinal apparatus of subjektive Rechte (subjective rights). Second, the equality-and-rights articulation: '総テノ人ハ法律ノ前二平等ニシテ其ノ権利ヲ享有ス' (all persons are equal before the law and enjoy their rights) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational principle of equality before the law that grounds the modern continental civil-law tradition's articulation of the legal subject, supplying the operating vocabulary 平等 (byōdō, equality) that institutionalizes in modern Japanese legal vocabulary the foundational liberal-democratic principle of equal legal personality. The articulation marks a substantial doctrinal recalibration from the classical-imperial Japanese legal tradition's status-graduated articulation of legal capacity, with the post-Meiji-Restoration abolition of the formal status-distinctions and the broader Meiji liberalization of legal personality supplying the institutional context within which the principle was articulated. Third, the property-and-contract articulation: '所有ハ最モ完全ナル仕方二於テ物ヲ使用シ収益シ及ビ処分スルノ権利ナリ。但シ法律及ビ命令ノ禁ズル所二非ザル場合二限ル。契約ハ当事者ノ間二於テ法律ト同一ノ効力ヲ有シ其ノ合意ハ之ヲ遵守スベシ' (ownership is the right to use, to enjoy the fruits of, and to dispose of property in the most complete manner, except where prohibited by law or regulation; a contract has between the parties the effect of law itself, and the agreement shall be observed) — Mitsukuri articulates the foundational principles of the modern civil-law property-and-contract apparatus, supplying the operating vocabulary 所有 (shoyū, ownership), 使用 (shiyō, use), 収益 (shūeki, enjoyment of fruits / usufruct), 処分 (shobun, disposition), 契約 (keiyaku, contract), 合意 (gōi, agreement) — the foundational vocabulary of modern Japanese property-and-contract law. The articulation imports into modern Japanese legal vocabulary the foundational French-Code-civil articulations of Article 544 (the absolute-property doctrine) and Article 1134 (pacta sunt servanda, the contractual-sanctity principle) that supply the doctrinal foundation of the modern continental civil-law private-property-and-contract apparatus. Fourth, the tort-and-family-law articulation: '何人モ他人二損害ヲ加ヘタル者ハ其ノ過失二依ル時ハ之ヲ賠償スル義務ヲ負フ。婚姻、親子、相続二関スル事項ハ別二之ヲ定ム' (anyone who causes damage to another, when it is due to his fault, bears the obligation of compensation; matters concerning marriage, parent-and-child relations, and inheritance are provided for separately) — Mitsukuri renders the French Code civil Article 1382's foundational tort-doctrine articulation (the fault-based liability principle that grounds the modern continental tort-law tradition) and references the broader civil-code-articulated regulation of family and inheritance, supplying the operating vocabulary 過失 (kashitsu, fault / negligence), 賠償 (baishō, compensation), 婚姻 (kon'in, marriage), 親子 (oyako / shinshi, parent-child), 相続 (sōzoku, inheritance / succession) — the foundational vocabulary of modern Japanese tort-and-family-law. The articulation imports into modern Japanese legal vocabulary the foundational French-Code-civil articulation of fault-based delictual liability (the Article 1382 / current 1240 articulation that supplies the foundational tort-doctrine of the modern continental civil-law tradition). The passage exemplifies Mitsukuri's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern continental civil-law-as-systematically-codified-domain in early-Meiji Japan, with 民法 stabilized as the operating term for the codified civil law and the broader cluster 主体 / 平等 / 所有 / 契約 / 過失 / 賠償 / 婚姻 / 相続 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of modern Japanese civil law within the continental civil-law tradition that the subsequent 1898 Civil Code substantially recalibrated toward the German Pandectist-doctrinal apparatus.

passage: Subject 主観。認識ノ主体即チ我ヲ謂フ。客観二対シ我ヨリ事物ヲ見ル方ヲ主観ト称ス。Kant二於テハ主観即チ純粋我ハ凡テノ経験ヲ統一スル先験的綜合ノ根原ナリ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register that the Meiji philosophical translators developed for the systematic transposition of Western philosophical terminology into Japanese. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 主観 across three calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese subject-vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: 'Subject 主観。認識ノ主体即チ我ヲ謂フ' (Subject — 主観. It signifies the cognitive subject, namely the I) — Inoue articulates the foundational structural definition of 主観 as the cognitive I that is the bearer of experience, with the operating compound 認識ノ主体 (the cognitive subject) supplying the doctrinal coupling that the subsequent Japanese philosophical vocabulary inherits. The articulation imports into modern Japanese vocabulary the post-Cartesian and Kantian articulation of the cognitive subject as the centered I from which knowing proceeds. Second, the perspectival-relational articulation: '客観二対シ我ヨリ事物ヲ見ル方ヲ主観ト称ス' (the side from which I view things, in opposition to the objective, is called 主観) — Inoue articulates the dialectical-perspectival structure of the subject-object pair, with 主観 named as the side from which the view proceeds and 客観 as the side that stands over against it. The articulation institutionalizes the host-and-guest 主 / 客 dialectic of classical Sino-Japanese vocabulary as the operating Japanese frame for the Kantian Subjekt-Objekt structure, with 観 as the perspectival suffix that the dialectical pairing modifies. Third, the Kantian-transcendental articulation: 'Kant二於テハ主観即チ純粋我ハ凡テノ経験ヲ統一スル先験的綜合ノ根原ナリ' (in Kant, 主観 — the pure I — is the source of the transcendental synthesis that unifies all experience) — Inoue articulates the strict Kantian register of the Subjekt as the unity of apperception, with 純粋我 (junsui ga, the pure I) supplying the operating Japanese rendering of Kant's reines Ich and 先験的綜合 (sengenteki sōgō, transcendental synthesis) supplying the rendering of transzendentale Synthesis. The passage exemplifies the Tetsugaku Jii's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the Kantian and post-Kantian subject-object structure in modern Japanese philosophical translation, with 主観 stabilized as the operating rendering of Subjekt and the broader cluster 認識主体 / 純粋我 / 先験的綜合 supplying the doctrinal apparatus that subsequent Japanese philosophical writing inherits.

passage: Object 客観。主観二対シ認識セラルル所ノ事物ヲ謂フ。我ノ外二存スル一切ノ対象即チ客観ナリ。Kant二於テハ客観ハ感性ノ多様ガ悟性ノ範疇ヲ以テ統一セラレタル時始メテ成立スル者ナリ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 客観 across three calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese object-vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: 'Object 客観。主観二対シ認識セラルル所ノ事物ヲ謂フ' (Object — 客観. It signifies the things that are cognized in opposition to the subjective) — Inoue articulates the foundational structural definition of 客観 as the cognized-thing that stands over against the cognitive subject. The articulation institutionalizes the relational-dialectical structure of the Kantian Subjekt-Objekt pair within modern Japanese vocabulary, with 客観 stabilized as the externality-side of the cognitive relation. Second, the externality-articulation: '我ノ外二存スル一切ノ対象即チ客観ナリ' (the totality of objects that exist outside the I is precisely the objective) — Inoue articulates the externality-register of 客観 as that-which-is-outside-the-I, with 対象 (taishō, object as that-toward-which a cognitive act is directed, the operating Meiji rendering of Gegenstand) and 客観 standing in calibrated relation: 対象 names the directed-toward of any cognitive act, while 客観 names the broader category of objectivity as a register. The articulation institutionalizes within modern Japanese vocabulary the 対象 / 客観 distinction that the German philosophical tradition makes between Gegenstand (the object as the directed-toward of a particular cognitive act) and Objektivität (objectivity as the structural register). Third, the Kantian-constitutional articulation: 'Kant二於テハ客観ハ感性ノ多様ガ悟性ノ範疇ヲ以テ統一セラレタル時始メテ成立スル者ナリ' (in Kant, 客観 first comes to stand only when the manifold of sensibility is unified through the categories of the understanding) — Inoue articulates the strict Kantian register of the Objekt as constituted-by-categorial-synthesis, with 感性ノ多様 (kansei no tayō, the manifold of sensibility) supplying the operating Japanese rendering of das Mannigfaltige der Sinnlichkeit, 悟性ノ範疇 (gosei no hanchū, the categories of the understanding) supplying the rendering of die Kategorien des Verstandes, and the broader doctrinal apparatus articulating the Kantian transcendental constitution of objective experience. The passage exemplifies the Tetsugaku Jii's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the Kantian object-structure in modern Japanese philosophical translation, with 客観 stabilized as the operating rendering of Objekt and the broader cluster 対象 / 感性ノ多様 / 悟性ノ範疇 supplying the systematic doctrinal apparatus that the modern East Asian reception of Kant inherits.

passage: Concept 概念。多数ノ事物二共通ナル特徴ヲ抽出シ之ヲ統合シテ得タル抽象的観念ヲ謂フ。観念ノ中個物ヲ表象スル者ヲ表象 (representation) ト称シ普遍ヲ含ム者ヲ概念ト称ス。Kant二於テハ概念ハ悟性ノ働キニ依リテ成立スル統一形式ナリ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 概念 across three calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese concept-vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: 'Concept 概念。多数ノ事物二共通ナル特徴ヲ抽出シ之ヲ統合シテ得タル抽象的観念ヲ謂フ' (Concept — 概念. It signifies the abstract idea obtained by extracting the features common to many things and unifying them) — Inoue articulates the foundational structural definition of 概念 as the abstract-unified content arrived at through the operations of extraction (抽出, chūshutsu) and unification (統合, tōgō) across particulars. The articulation imports into modern Japanese vocabulary the post-Lockean and Kantian articulation of the concept as the abstract-general content arrived at through the operations of comparison and abstraction across multiplicities, with 抽象的観念 (chūshōteki kannen, abstract idea) supplying the operating broader category within which 概念 is the specifically generalizing-unifying register. Second, the disambiguating articulation: '観念ノ中個物ヲ表象スル者ヲ表象 (representation) ト称シ普遍ヲ含ム者ヲ概念ト称ス' (among ideas, those that represent individual things are called representations, those that contain the universal are called concepts) — Inoue articulates the foundational distinction within Meiji philosophical vocabulary between 表象 (hyōshō, representation / Vorstellung in the narrow sense) and 概念 (gainen, concept / Begriff), with the structural distinction operating along the individual / universal axis: representations carry the singular content of particular individuals, while concepts carry the universal content that subsumes a multiplicity of individuals. The articulation institutionalizes the distinction within modern Japanese philosophical vocabulary that subsequent Kantian and post-Kantian translation has presupposed. Third, the Kantian-categorial articulation: 'Kant二於テハ概念ハ悟性ノ働キニ依リテ成立スル統一形式ナリ' (in Kant, the concept is the unifying form that comes to stand through the activity of the understanding) — Inoue articulates the strict Kantian register of Begriff as the unifying form constituted through the activity of the Verstand, with 悟性ノ働キ (gosei no hataraki, the activity of the understanding) supplying the operating Japanese rendering of die Tätigkeit des Verstandes and 統一形式 (tōitsu keishiki, unifying form) supplying the foundational doctrinal articulation. The passage exemplifies the Tetsugaku Jii's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern philosophical concept in Japanese, with 概念 stabilized as the operating rendering of Begriff and the broader cluster 観念 / 表象 / 統一形式 articulating the doctrinal apparatus through which the Meiji reception of Kantian and post-Kantian philosophy proceeded.

passage: Reason 理性。悟性ノ上二位スル高等ナル認識能力ヲ謂フ。悟性ハ経験ノ範囲内二於テ概念ヲ構成シ判断ヲ下スノ能力ナルニ対シ理性ハ無条件ナル者ヲ求メ理念ヲ形成スル能力ナリ。Kant二於テハ理性ハ霊魂・世界・神ノ三大理念ヲ生ズルニ至ル。古来東方ノ学二於テ性即理ト謂フハ此ノ理性ノ義二近シ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 理性 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese reason-vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-definitional articulation: 'Reason 理性。悟性ノ上二位スル高等ナル認識能力ヲ謂フ' (Reason — 理性. It signifies the higher cognitive faculty positioned above the understanding) — Inoue articulates the foundational structural definition of 理性 as the higher cognitive faculty within the Kantian hierarchical articulation of cognitive powers, with the structural relation 悟性ノ上 (above the understanding) supplying the operating Japanese rendering of Kant's distinction between Vernunft and Verstand. The articulation imports into modern Japanese vocabulary the strict Kantian Vernunft / Verstand hierarchy that the broader post-Kantian tradition presupposes. Second, the functional-distinguishing articulation: '悟性ハ経験ノ範囲内二於テ概念ヲ構成シ判断ヲ下スノ能力ナルニ対シ理性ハ無条件ナル者ヲ求メ理念ヲ形成スル能力ナリ' (whereas the understanding is the faculty that constitutes concepts and renders judgments within the range of experience, reason is the faculty that seeks the unconditioned and forms ideals) — Inoue articulates the foundational functional distinction between Verstand and Vernunft, with 悟性 anchored to concept-formation and judgment within experience and 理性 anchored to the search for the unconditioned (無条件ナル者, mujōken naru mono — the operating Japanese rendering of Kant's das Unbedingte) and the formation of ideals (理念, rinen — the operating Japanese rendering of Kant's Ideen). The articulation institutionalizes within modern Japanese philosophical vocabulary the strict Kantian articulation of reason as the faculty that drives toward the unconditioned ground that lies beyond the range of possible experience. Third, the Kantian-transcendental-ideal articulation: 'Kant二於テハ理性ハ霊魂・世界・神ノ三大理念ヲ生ズルニ至ル' (in Kant, reason gives rise to the three great ideas of soul, world, and God) — Inoue articulates the strict Kantian register of the three transcendental ideas (die drei transzendentalen Ideen) that Kant's Critique of Pure Reason articulates as the products of reason's drive toward the unconditioned: the soul (Seele) as the unconditioned subject of inner experience, the world (Welt) as the unconditioned totality of outer experience, and God (Gott) as the unconditioned ground of all reality. Fourth, the cross-traditional articulation: '古来東方ノ学二於テ性即理ト謂フハ此ノ理性ノ義二近シ' (in the ancient learning of the East, the formula 'nature is principle' approximates the meaning of this 理性) — Inoue articulates the structural-conceptual continuity between the modern Kantian Vernunft and the Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucian doctrine of 性即理 (xìng jí lǐ, 'nature is principle'), gesturing toward the foundational Cheng-Zhu identification of human nature with universal principle that supplied the classical-philosophical horizon within which the Meiji Japanese rendering of Vernunft as 理性 acquires its doctrinal weight. The articulation marks the Meiji philosophical project's characteristic gesture of cross-traditional calibration: the modern Japanese rendering of Kantian terminology is calibrated explicitly against the inherited East Asian philosophical vocabulary, with 理性 carrying both the Kantian Vernunft and the Cheng-Zhu inheritance of 性即理 in productive tension. The passage exemplifies the Tetsugaku Jii's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of Kantian reason in modern Japanese, with 理性 stabilized as the operating rendering of Vernunft and the broader cluster 悟性 / 無条件 / 理念 / 三大理念 articulating the doctrinal apparatus through which the Meiji reception of Kant proceeded.

passage: 夫レ警察ハ国家ノ耳目手足ナリ。其ノ任タル人民ノ生命財産ヲ保護シ社会ノ安寧秩序ヲ維持スル二在リ。警察官タル者其ノ職務二臨ムニ当タリ威厳ヲ以テシ温和ヲ以テシ公平ヲ以テセザルベカラズ。決シテ私情ヲ以テ公務二干スベカラズ。一視同仁、貴賤貧富ノ別ナク法ノ前二平等ナラシムベシ。警察ノ要諦ハ犯罪ヲ未然二防グ二在リテ既然二罰スル二在ラズ。故二警察官ハ常二人民ノ間二在リテ其ノ動静ヲ察シ其ノ困苦ヲ知リ其ノ風俗ヲ察スルコト緊要ナリ。蓋シ警察ハ威服ヲ以テ立ツニ非ズシテ信服ヲ以テ立ツモノナリ。
notes: From Kawaji Toshiyoshi's 警察手眼 ('Essence of Police Work,' 1879), the foundational doctrinal-pedagogical text of the modern Japanese police institution. The passage stages the foundational articulation of 警察 across four calibrated moves through which the modern Japanese policing-as-institutional-function vocabulary was stabilized. First, the structural-institutional articulation: '夫レ警察ハ国家ノ耳目手足ナリ。其ノ任タル人民ノ生命財産ヲ保護シ社会ノ安寧秩序ヲ維持スル二在リ' (the police are the eyes-and-ears and the hands-and-feet of the state; their duty is to protect the life and property of the people and to maintain the peace and order of society) — Kawaji articulates the foundational structural-institutional definition of the modern police as the operative-instrumental apparatus of state-administered public-order maintenance, with the dual-function articulation 生命財産ノ保護 (the protection of life and property) and 安寧秩序ノ維持 (the maintenance of public peace and order) supplying the doctrinal foundation. The articulation imports into modern Japanese institutional vocabulary the continental Polizeiwissenschaft tradition's articulation of the police as the systematic state-welfare-and-order administrative apparatus, with the metaphor of 耳目手足 (eyes-ears-hands-feet, the sensory and operational organs of the state) calibrating the institutional articulation through a classical-Sino-Japanese figural register. Second, the comportment-and-impartiality articulation: '警察官タル者其ノ職務二臨ムニ当タリ威厳ヲ以テシ温和ヲ以テシ公平ヲ以テセザルベカラズ。決シテ私情ヲ以テ公務二干スベカラズ。一視同仁、貴賤貧富ノ別ナク法ノ前二平等ナラシムベシ' (the police officer in the discharge of his duty must conduct himself with dignity, with gentleness, and with impartiality; he must never let private feeling interfere with public duty; he shall regard all alike with equal benevolence, without distinction of high or low, rich or poor, and treat all as equal before the law) — Kawaji articulates the foundational principles of police comportment, impartiality, and equality-before-the-law that ground the modern Japanese policing institution. The articulation imports into modern Japanese institutional vocabulary the broader Meiji liberal-administrative principles of equal-treatment-by-state-authority that the Constitution of 1889 and the broader Meiji legal-administrative reforms institutionalized, with the classical Confucian articulation 一視同仁 ('regarding all alike with equal benevolence,' from Han Yu's 原人, articulating the universal-impartiality principle in the classical-Confucian register) supplying the figural-classical anchor for the modern administrative-equality principle. Third, the prevention-over-punishment articulation: '警察ノ要諦ハ犯罪ヲ未然二防グ二在リテ既然二罰スル二在ラズ。故二警察官ハ常二人民ノ間二在リテ其ノ動静ヲ察シ其ノ困苦ヲ知リ其ノ風俗ヲ察スルコト緊要ナリ' (the essential principle of policing lies in preventing crime before it occurs, not in punishing it after the fact; therefore, the police officer must always be among the people, observing their conduct, knowing their hardships, and discerning their customs) — Kawaji articulates the foundational principle of preventive policing that grounds the modern Japanese policing institution: the police function as the preventive-vigilant apparatus that operates through continuous community presence and discerning observation, rather than as a reactive-punitive apparatus that operates only after criminal occurrences. The articulation institutionalizes in modern Japanese institutional vocabulary the principle that would shape the distinctive Japanese institutional articulation of community-based policing through the 派出所 / 交番 (kōban, neighborhood police box) system that locates police presence within local communities as a structural feature of Japanese policing. The dual structure of the compound 警察 — 警 (vigilance / preventive watchfulness) and 察 (investigation / discerning observation) — receives in this articulation its operative-doctrinal calibration: the preventive function is exercised through the discerning observation of community life. Fourth, the legitimacy-through-trust articulation: '蓋シ警察ハ威服ヲ以テ立ツニ非ズシテ信服ヲ以テ立ツモノナリ' (truly, the police institution stands not by means of fear-induced submission but by means of trust-induced submission) — Kawaji articulates the foundational principle of the police-public relation as one of consent-and-trust rather than of coercion-and-fear, supplying the doctrinal foundation for the modern Japanese policing institution's articulation of its public legitimacy. The articulation, although Kawaji's institutional model was principally the French Préfecture de Police rather than the British Peelian model, articulates a principle structurally parallel to the Peelian Principles' articulation of policing-by-consent — the police as 'citizens in uniform' bound to public consent and minimal-force restraint — and supplies the operating doctrinal foundation for the modern Japanese policing institution's distinctive emphasis on community-trust-based legitimacy. The passage exemplifies Kawaji's articulation of the foundational vocabulary of the modern Japanese policing institution at its institutional-foundational moment, with 警察 stabilized as the operating term for the modern police institution and the broader cluster 警察官 / 公平 / 平等 / 未然二防グ / 信服 articulating the doctrinal apparatus of modern Japanese policing within the institutional framework that Kawaji established and that has substantially shaped the modern Japanese police institution across the 150 years of its institutional life.

passage: Abstraction 抽象。多数ノ事物ヨリ其ノ共通ナル性質ヲ抽キ出シ之ヲ別二取リテ思惟スルノ作用ヲ謂フ。其ノ反対ヲ具象ト称ス。論理学二於テ概念ハ此ノ抽象ノ作用二依リテ成立スル者ナリ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The entry stages the stabilization of 抽象 across three moves. First, the operational definition: '多数ノ事物ヨリ其ノ共通ナル性質ヲ抽キ出シ之ヲ別二取リテ思惟スルノ作用' (the operation of drawing out the property common to many things and considering it apart) — and the choice of verb is the whole point: Inoue glosses 抽 with 抽キ出シ (hikidashi, to draw out), so the definition performs the character's own etymology, abstraction defined as a drawing-out exactly as the Latin abs-trahere is a drawing-away. The compound thus arrives in Japanese already carrying the Western term's root metaphor, an unusually faithful calque. Second, the binary fix: '其ノ反対ヲ具象ト称ス' installs 具象 / 抽象 as a clean contrary pair, importing a tidy opposition the European tradition's quarrel over whether abstract ideas exist at all never resolved so neatly. Third, the systematic placement: tying 抽象 to the genesis of the 概念 (concept) within 論理学 locates the term inside the post-Lockean account of concept-formation, which is the doctrinal frame the modern East Asian reception of logic inherits from this dictionary.

passage: Ethics 倫理。人倫ノ道ヲ究メ善悪正邪ノ標準ヲ論ズル学ヲ謂フ。之ヲ倫理学ト称ス。倫トハ君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友ノ五倫ヲ謂ヒ理トハ其ノ当二循フベキ条理ヲ謂フ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The entry is doctrinally revealing precisely in its third clause, where Inoue does something he does not do for the more purely imported terms: he glosses the compound's two characters back into the Confucian tradition. '倫トハ君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友ノ五倫ヲ謂ヒ' explicitly identifies 倫 with the Five Relationships — ruler–minister, father–son, husband–wife, elder–younger, friend–friend — so that the rendering of Western Ethik is anchored, by the dictionary itself, in the relational architecture of Confucian moral order rather than in the Greek ēthos of individual character. '理トハ其ノ当二循フベキ条理ヲ謂フ' then defines 理 as the binding pattern those relations ought to follow, completing the framing of ethics as the principle of right relation. The first clause's '善悪正邪ノ標準ヲ論ズル学' (the discipline that argues the standard of good and evil, right and wrong) supplies the recognizably Western disciplinary scope, but the entry's order of exposition — disciplinary scope first, then a Confucian etymological anchoring — captures the structural friction the term carries into modern East Asian moral philosophy: an imported discipline named in a vocabulary whose root character already answers relationally the question the discipline poses about the individual.

passage: Logic 論理。思惟ノ法則ヲ論ジ正シキ推理ノ規則ヲ究ムル学ヲ謂フ。之ヲ論理学ト称ス。推理二演繹ト帰納ノ二アリ。演繹ハ普遍ヨリ特殊二及ボシ帰納ハ特殊ヨリ普遍二至ル。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The entry stabilizes 論理 across three moves. First, the disciplinary definition: '思惟ノ法則ヲ論ジ正シキ推理ノ規則ヲ究ムル学' (the discipline that argues the laws of thought and investigates the rules of correct inference) — and the verb 論ジ performs the compound's own first character, logic defined through 論 as the ordered marshalling of discourse rather than through the Greek logos as the structure of being. Second, the disciplinary naming: '之ヲ論理学ト称ス' fixes the institutional form 論理学 that Nishi Amane's coinage supplied and that this dictionary stabilized as the operating Japanese term. Third, the partition of inference: '演繹ト帰納' (deduction and induction), with the calibrated definitions '普遍ヨリ特殊二及ボシ' (proceeding from the universal to the particular) and '特殊ヨリ普遍二至ル' (arriving from the particular at the universal), installs in modern Japanese the universal / particular axis on which the European logic of the period turned. The entry is also a quiet monument to a fork in the road: 論理 entered Chinese but was there partly displaced by Yan Fu's transliteration 邏輯, so this dictionary records the moment the Japanese semantic calque was fixed in the very form that would, in China, lose ground to a phonetic rival.

passage: Phenomenon 現象。我ノ感官二現ハレテ知覚セラルル所ノ事象ヲ謂フ。其ノ背後二在リテ現象ヲ成立セシムル者ヲ本体 (Noumenon) ト称ス。Kant二於テハ現象ハ時空ノ形式及ビ悟性ノ範疇二依リテ構成セラルル者ニシテ物自体ハ終二知ラレ得ズ。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register of Meiji philosophical translation. The entry stabilizes 現象 across three moves. First, the definition by appearing-to-a-subject: '我ノ感官二現ハレテ知覚セラルル所ノ事象' (the matter that appears to my sense-organs and is perceived) — the gloss spells out 現 with 現ハレテ (arawarete, to appear / become manifest), performing the character's force, so that phenomenon is fixed as the manifest-image presented to a perceiver, the Greek phainomenon ('that which shows itself') tracked closely through the 現 + 象 compound. Second, the contrastive pair: '其ノ背後二在リテ現象ヲ成立セシムル者ヲ本体 (Noumenon) ト称ス' installs 現象 / 本体 as the Japanese rendering of Phänomen / Noumenon, and the phrase 其ノ背後二在リテ (lying behind it) discloses the representationalist tilt the compound carries — the appearing as image standing for something behind it, a framing congenial to Kant but in later tension with Husserl's recovery of the phenomenon as self-givenness. Third, the Kantian-transcendental articulation: '現象ハ時空ノ形式及ビ悟性ノ範疇二依リテ構成セラルル者ニシテ物自体ハ終二知ラレ得ズ' (the phenomenon is constituted by the forms of space and time and the categories of the understanding, while the thing-in-itself remains finally unknowable) supplies the operating Japanese rendering of die Formen von Raum und Zeit, die Kategorien des Verstandes, and das Ding an sich — the doctrinal apparatus through which the modern East Asian reception of Kant proceeds, fixed here in the dictionary that stabilized it.

passage: Consciousness 意識。心ガ自己及ビ其ノ対象ヲ知覚スル作用ヲ謂フ。我ノ諸表象ニ恒ニ伴フ所ノ「我思フ」ノ統一是ナリ。Kant 之ヲ統覚 (Apperception) ト称シ、一切ノ認識ノ成立スル根本ノ条件トナス。
notes: From the philosophical-vocabulary entry in Inoue Tetsujirō and Ariga Nagao's Tetsugaku Jii (1881), in the calibrated bungo register that fixed the modern Japanese rendering of Bewusstsein. The entry stabilizes 意識 by defining it through a doubled object — '心ガ自己及ビ其ノ対象ヲ知覚スル' (the mind's perceiving of both itself and its object) — which performs the work of the two characters: 識 supplies the perceiving-of-an-object (the Yogācāra discriminating cognition redirected to epistemology), and 意 the reflexive turn by which that perceiving is also a perceiving of itself. The second sentence, '我ノ諸表象ニ恒ニ伴フ所ノ「我思フ」ノ統一' (the unity of the "I think" that constantly accompanies all my representations), is a near-verbatim Japanese casting of Kant's das Ich denke muss alle meine Vorstellungen begleiten können, installing 意識 as the rendering of transcendental apperception. The closing identification with 統覚 (Apperception) and '一切ノ認識ノ成立スル根本ノ条件' (the fundamental condition for the constituting of all cognition) fixes the term inside the Kantian-transcendental architecture rather than the empiricist one, so that 意識 enters modern Japanese already weighted toward consciousness as the constituting unity of experience — the very framing through which the East Asian reception of Kant proceeds.

passage: Idea 観念。心中ニ現ハルル所ノ表象ヲ謂フ。Locke ニ於テハ凡ソ思惟ノ直接ノ対象タル者皆観念ニシテ、感覚ヨリ来ルト内省ヨリ来ルトノ二種アリ。Kant ニ於テハ観念 (Idee) ハ経験ノ範囲ヲ超エテ理性ノ要求スル所ノ統制的概念ニシテ、経験ノ中ニ其ノ対象ヲ見出スコト能ハズ。
notes: The Tetsugaku Jii entry stages exactly the doubleness that makes 観念 a difficult rendering: it must hold both the empiricist and the transcendental sense of "idea" in one term. The opening gloss — '心中ニ現ハルル所ノ表象' (the representation that appears within the mind) — leans on the contemplative force of 観 (the holding of a content before the inward view) and 念 (its mental persistence), so that the Buddhist genealogy of the compound is doing quiet definitional work. The Locke sentence renders "the immediate object of thought" as '思惟ノ直接ノ対象' and reproduces the sensation/reflection division ('感覚ヨリ来ルト内省ヨリ来ルト'), fixing the empiricist atomistic sense. The Kant sentence then pivots to the wholly different Idee — '経験ノ範囲ヲ超エテ理性ノ要求スル所ノ統制的概念' (a regulative concept demanded by reason beyond the bounds of experience) — and the entry makes no attempt to reconcile the two, simply recording that the single Japanese term 観念 must carry both, which is precisely the conceptual remainder the compound's contemplative origin leaves it equipped, but unevenly, to bear.

passage: 美学ハ美ノ理ヲ究ムルノ学ナリ。世ノ論者多ク美ヲ以テ理想ノ模倣ニ在リトナスモ、維氏 (Véron) ハ然ラズト為ス。曰ク、藝術ハ感情ノ発現ニシテ、作者ノ情ノ真ニ顕ハルル所、即チ美ノ存スル所ナリト。故ニ美学ノ務ハ定マレル美ノ典型ヲ説クニ非ズシテ、情ノ発現ノ法ヲ明ラカニスルニ在リ。
notes: The opening sentence — '美学ハ美ノ理ヲ究ムルノ学ナリ' (aesthetics is the discipline that investigates the principle of beauty) — is itself the lexicalizing act: Nakae Chōmin's translation is one of the texts through which 美学 was fixed, and here the compound is glossed by its own components, 美 (beauty) + 学 (the investigating discipline), the definitional move that cut aesthetics loose from its Baumgartenian root in aisthēsis (sense-perception) and re-founded it on its object. The body of the passage carries Véron's polemic: against the academic doctrine that locates beauty in '理想ノ模倣' (the imitation of an ideal), it asserts '藝術ハ感情ノ発現' — art is the manifestation of emotion, a direct casting of Véron's l'art est la manifestation de l'émotion. The final clause redefines the task of the new discipline as clarifying '情ノ発現ノ法' (the manner of emotion's expression) rather than prescribing fixed types of beauty, so that the very text stabilizing the word 美学 — the discipline named for 美, beauty — installs it with an expressivist content that displaces beauty from the centre, the irony noted in the term's conceptual remainder.

passage: 化学新書
notes: The coinage 化学 makes its standardizing appearance in the very title of Kawamoto Kōmin's treatise, displacing the Dutch-derived phonetic loan 舎密 (seimi) that earlier rangaku scholars had used. The title is itself the decisive lexical act: by naming the field 'transformation-study' rather than transliterating chemie, Kawamoto gives the discipline a self-explaining Sino-Japanese name a Confucian-educated reader can parse on sight. That this happens c. 1860, before the Restoration, shows the machinery of scientific calque already running in late-Edo Dutch learning. The choice of 化 over a phonetic loan is the same motivated-calque-beats-transliteration pattern that would later govern the great Meiji coinages.

passage: 物理階梯
notes: Katayama's 1872 primer fixes 物理 as the school-system term for physics through its title — literally 'the steps/ladder of physics,' a graded introduction for the new national curriculum. Placing the coinage in a mass-education textbook rather than a scholarly treatise is what standardizes it: a generation of students learns the discipline under this name, and the broader Edo umbrella 窮理 (kyūri) recedes accordingly. The title's pedagogical framing ('steps') quietly enacts the Neo-Confucian assumption folded into 物理 itself — that the principle of things is reached by a graded, cumulative investigation. The term's institutional victory is thus a curricular event, not a theoretical one.

passage: 電気は天地間に充満する気なり
notes: Electricity is a qi that fills all space between heaven and earth. Fukuzawa's 1868 popularization explains the new force to a mass readership precisely by leaning on the 気 of the coinage: electricity is presented as a pervading vital vapor, continuous with the cosmological qi the audience already understands. The sentence shows the conceptual remainder of 電気 doing real explanatory work — and real distortion — at the moment of transmission: the metaphor that made electricity intuitively graspable also recoded it as a vitalist plenum rather than a quantifiable charge. The phrase 天地間に充満する is lifted straight from the register of qi cosmology, naturalizing the import by dissolving it into an indigenous picture of the world.

passage: 東京横浜間電話交換業務開始
notes: The 1890 official designation of the inaugural Tokyo–Yokohama service is the bureaucratic act that fixes 電話 as the term, retiring the transliteration テレフォン and the rival calque 伝話器. The passage is documentary, not literary, and that is the point: the coinage is settled not by a writer's felicity but by an administrative decision that makes 電話 the institutional name of a public utility. Once the state attaches the word to the service, the alternatives have nowhere left to live. The phrase 電話交換 ('telephone exchange') also shows the term immediately generating the compounds (交換, 番号) that a working telephone system requires, confirming 電 as a productive technological prefix.

passage: 酸素は物を焼くを助け、生を養ふの気なり。其の名は酸を生ずるの義に取る。
notes: Here the term is introduced by its two functional signatures — it supports combustion and sustains respiration — and then, crucially, the passage glosses its own name: 'so called from the sense of generating acid.' That self-gloss is the giveaway. Udagawa is not merely translating a gas; he is transmitting Lavoisier's theoretical claim that this element is the principle of acidity, baking the 18th-century thesis into the Japanese word at the moment of coinage. The combustion-and-respiration description is observationally durable, but the etymological note fossilizes a doctrine that European chemistry was already preparing to abandon. The passage thus shows the calque doing two incompatible things at once: reporting what oxygen does and asserting why it was named, the second of which would not survive.

passage: 水素は最も軽き気にして、酸素と合して水を成す。故に水素と名づく。
notes: The naming logic is stated explicitly in the last clause: 'because it combines with oxygen to form water, it is called water-element.' This is the calque principle laid bare — the gas is defined by its synthetic product, exactly as Lavoisier's hydrogène had been. The passage also pairs 水素 with 酸素 in a single reaction sentence, so the two coinages enter the language already locked together referentially, the one literally making, with the other, the substance that names it. Unlike the oxygen entry, nothing here is theoretically unstable: 'lightest gas' and 'combines to form water' are both still true, which is why 水素 aged better than its sibling. The entry shows Udagawa's element series operating as a system, each name generated by the same rule from observed behaviour.

passage: 窒素は焔を消し、生を死せしむる気なり。故に窒の字を以て之を名づく。
notes: The passage defines nitrogen purely by negation — it extinguishes flame and kills what breathes it — and then justifies the character choice: 'therefore it is named with the graph 窒 (suffocate).' This is a direct calque of Lavoisier's azote, 'without life,' and the explicit reasoning makes 窒素 the single clearest piece of evidence that East Asia received the French privative name rather than the English nitrogen.
