The negative definition is empirically narrow: it captures what an experimenter at the bench observes but nothing of nitrogen's positive role as the atmosphere's bulk and a constituent of all proteins. The entry preserves, at the point of coinage, the decision to name an element by what it destroys — a decision the word has carried unrevised ever since.

passage: 草木の体を分かちて至微に至れば、細小の胞ありて相連なる。之を細胞と称す。
notes: The passage stages the microscopic descent that the term encodes: divide the body of a plant down to the most minute scale and one finds 'small sacs joined together,' which are then named 細胞. The phrasing 至微 ('reaching the minute') is doing the work of 細, and 胞 ('sac') is chosen over any room- or box-word, so the calque is built from an organic, enclosural metaphor rather than Hooke's architectural cellula. Read closely, the sentence is itself a miniature argument for cell theory — structure resolved by descent into bounded units that connect — composed decades before Schleiden and Schwann and on the Japanese side a generation before Meiji. It is also the moment a Japanese scientific calque enters the language in a form China and Korea would later adopt unchanged.

passage: 神経は、神気の経脈に行く所以なり。これ和蘭の所謂ゼニュウなり。
notes: The gloss does the coinage in the open: the new word 神経 is immediately unpacked as 'that whereby the vital spirit (神気) travels the channels (経脈),' and only then equated with the Dutch zenuw. The sentence is therefore not a definition of the nerve but a translation of it into the indigenous qi-and-channel physiology — the Western structure is admitted to the language by being re-described as a conduit for an animating pneuma. The explicit 'これ和蘭の所謂…なり' ('this is what the Dutch call…') marks the precise seam where rangaku anatomy is stitched onto Edo medical cosmology. It is the earliest instance in the atlas of a scientific concept entering Japanese by motivated contraction rather than phonetic loan, nearly a century before the Meiji wave, and in a form Chinese and Korean would adopt unchanged.

passage: 物を分析して、もはや分かつべからざるに至る。その本然の質を元素と名づく。
notes: The definition is built by descent and arrest: analyze a substance until one reaches what 'can no longer be divided,' and that residual 'inherent stuff' is named 元素. The phrase 分かつべからざる ('not further divisible') states Lavoisier's operational criterion exactly — element as the limit of analysis — but the naming clause then adds 本然 ('inherent, originary nature') and the morpheme 元, converting an analysis-relative status into a claim about primal essence. Read closely, the sentence shows the calque's surplus being introduced at the very moment of coinage: the Dutch source defines by what cannot be done, the Japanese term renames it as what fundamentally is. This is the entry that simultaneously fixes 元素 and licenses the productive 〜素 element-suffix the rest of the lexicon depends on.

passage: 物質を分かちて達し得る極限の微粒を原子と称し、原子相結びて成るものを分子と称す。
notes: The standardizing formula sets the pair in a single breath: the 'ultimate minute particle' reachable by division is the 原子, and what 原子 form by combining is the 分子. The opposition is engineered, not inherited — origin-particle against divided-particle, a clean 原/分 contrast bound by a shared 子 suffix — where the European atom/molecule pair is etymologically unrelated. Reading the sentence shows the calque system working on a relation rather than a word: the atom enters Japanese already positioned as the primal term of a manufactured polarity, and that polarity, not just the lexeme, is what passes intact into Chinese and Korean. The privative core of Greek atomos ('uncuttable') survives only as 極限 ('the limit'); the positive 原 silently supplies a metaphysics of primacy the etymon never asserted.

passage: 生物は不変のものに非ず。下等より高等に向かひて次第に進化す。
notes: The popularizing sentence states the thesis and, in doing so, exposes the calque's built-in slant: living things 'are not unchanging' but 'progressively 進化 from the lower toward the higher.' The directional phrase 下等より高等に向かひて ('from lower toward higher') is not Darwin's — descent with modification has no such axis — but it sits in perfect agreement with the morpheme 進, so the word and the gloss reinforce a progressivism the science disowns. This is the Spencerian-Morsean reception captured at its source: the term that would standardize 'evolution' for East Asia is introduced already meaning 'advancement up a scale.' The passage is the clearest demonstration that the choice of 進 over a neutral 変 was a doctrinal act, fixing a teleological reading that 進化論 has carried in Japanese, Chinese, and Korean ever since.

passage: 一身独立して一国独立す
notes: "When the single person stands independent, the single nation stands independent." Fukuzawa's famous formula prepares the conceptual ground on which 個人 would be coined: he does not yet have the stabilized compound, but the 一身 (the single body/self) here performs exactly the individuating abstraction 個 would later lexicalize — the lifting of the lone unit out of the relational web. Crucially, Fukuzawa subordinates the independent person to national independence, prefiguring the characteristic East Asian reception in which 個人 is weighted against 国家 rather than celebrated as an end in itself. The passage shows the concept arriving instrumentally — the individual mattering because the nation needs independent individuals — which is precisely the strategic charge the bare Western 'individual' did not carry and which the conceptual remainder of 個人 retains.

passage: Culture 文化、修養
notes: The Tetsugaku Jii's entry pairs the headword Culture with two Japanese renderings — 文化 and 修養 (self-cultivation) — and the doubling is diagnostic. By placing 文化 beside 修養 the lexicon registers exactly the unresolved freight the conceptual remainder identifies: culture as the German Bildung-inflected formation of the person (which 修養 captures) versus culture as an objective collective totality (which 文化 was being made to bear). The dictionary's act of stabilization is also an act of conflation, fixing 文化 as the standard equivalent while the gloss-pair preserves the trace of the Kultur/cultivation ambiguity. This is the reverse-flow mechanism at its most precise: a Meiji academic lexicon assigning a re-semanticized classical compound to a Western concept, and that assignment then radiating, via the Tetsugaku Jii's enormous authority, into the operating philosophical vocabulary of Japan, China, and Korea.

passage: 文明とは英語にてシウ゛ヰリゼーシオンと云ひ、即ち人の安楽と品位との進歩を指す
notes: "Civilization — in English, 'civilization' — refers to the progress of human comfort and dignity." Fukuzawa explicitly flags 文明 as the rendering of the English word, then defines it not as a static condition but as 進歩, progress — the decisive Meiji re-charging the conceptual remainder describes, by which a classical noun of radiant virtue becomes a developmental scale. The pairing of 安楽 (material comfort) with 品位 (dignity/refinement) shows Fukuzawa holding together the material and the moral within the single term, the very breadth that would later have to be split across 文明 and 文化. And by routing the definition through the English loanword spelled out in katakana, the passage stages the reverse-flow event itself: a foreign concept consciously installed into a Sino-Japanese vessel that then becomes the standard East Asian word.

passage: 我カ臣民克ク忠ニ克ク孝ニ億兆心ヲ一ニシテ世々厥ノ美ヲ済セルハ此レ我カ国体ノ精華ニシテ教育ノ淵源亦実ニ此ニ存ス
notes: "That Our subjects, ever loyal and filial, united in heart, have through the ages realized this beauty — this is the glory of our national essence (国体), and the very wellspring of 教育 lies herein." The Rescript performs the institutional resolution the conceptual remainder anticipates: it locates the source of 教育 not in the development of the learner (the 育 pole) but in loyalty and filial piety rooted in the 国体 — decisively foregrounding the 教 pole, education as the state's transmission of an authorized moral content. The word 教育, only two decades old as a rendering of Western schooling, is here annexed to a Confucian-loyalist program and bound to the imperial institution. Recited before the imperial portrait in every school until 1948, this single sentence did more than any lexicon to fix which of the compound's two warring metaphors would govern its modern East Asian career.

passage: Religion　宗教
notes: In the Tetsugaku Jii the English headword 'Religion' is set against the single fixed equivalent 宗教, and it is this lexicographic act — not any treatise — that does the decisive conceptual work. By entering 宗教 as the standing translation of a generic Western category, the dictionary retroactively constitutes a genus that classical Chinese never possessed: Buddhism, Christianity, and the rest become co-listed species of one abstract kind. The choice of 宗 (sect/lineage) plus 教 (teaching) is not neutral; it imports the Buddhist sectarian template, so that 'religion' is silently defined as an organized doctrinal school. The entry's very terseness is the point: a controversial Western abstraction is naturalized precisely by being made to look like a settled dictionary fact.

passage: 自由とは、一身の好むままに事を為して、窮屈なる思ひなきを云ふ。但し、self-government の意味なれば、決して我儘放盪の趣意にあらず。
notes: Fukuzawa's explanatory note on 'liberty' is doing damage control on its own vocabulary. Having rendered the English word with the ready binome 自由, he must immediately fence it off from the very sense it natively carries — 我儘放盪, willful licentious self-indulgence — by glossing it back through the untranslated English 'self-government.' The English term is left in roman script because the Sino-Japanese word cannot supply the missing element: liberty as self-rule bounded by law rather than as appetite unleashed. The passage is thus a visible seam in the reverse-flow process, the translator caught annotating against the connotations of the word he has just chosen, training 自由 toward a political ideal it did not yet mean.

passage: 今日の社会には、富める少数者の階級と、貧しき多数者の階級とありて、その間の懸隔は年と共に大なり。
notes: Kawakami uses 階級 to partition a single 社会 into two opposed economic strata — the wealthy few and the poor many — and the word is carrying weight its etymology does not supply. The graphic image inside 階級 is a graded ladder of station, but Kawakami needs it to name a structural relation and a widening antagonism ('the gap grows greater year by year'), so the conflictual content is borne by the surrounding clause rather than by the compound. The pairing of 階級 with 社会, both reverse-flow coinages, shows the imported sociological lexicon operating as a system: society is the whole, class the line of fracture within it. Bimbō Monogatari's huge popular readership helped move 階級 from technical vocabulary into the common language of social criticism, on the eve of its Marxist hardening.

passage: 荘子に衛生の語あるを憶ひ出し、文雅にして口調も悪しからず、遂にこれを健康保護の事務に用ふることとせり。
notes: Nagayo narrates the coinage as a deliberate act of lexical archaeology: faced with naming the European administrative domain of public health, he 'recalls that the phrase 衛生 occurs in the Zhuangzi,' judges it 'elegant and not ill-sounding,' and assigns it to the bureaucratic business of 'protecting health.' The justification offered is explicitly aesthetic and tonal (文雅, 口調) rather than semantic — he wants classical dignity, and accepts the semantic mismatch silently. The Zhuangzi's 衛生 was an inward art of nourishing one's own vitality; Nagayo redirects the guarding outward onto a population and upward into the state, so the memoir records the precise moment a Daoist self-cultivation phrase is conscripted for sanitary administration. It is one of the rare cases where the coiner himself documents both the source and the motive of a reverse-flow term.

passage: 演説とは英語にて「スピイチ」と云ひ、大勢の人を会して説を述べ、席上にて我思ふ所を人に伝ふるの法なり。
notes: "Enzetsu — in English called 'speech' — is the method whereby one gathers a great many people, sets forth one's exposition, and conveys what one thinks to others on the spot." The single most important sentence in the history of the term: Fukuzawa flags 演説 not as a name for something already present in Japan but as the rendering of an English word, spelled out in katakana, and proceeds to define the practice from scratch — a deliberate gathering, a sustained spoken exposition, a public conveyance of thought. The definition is procedural rather than substantive: it tells the reader how to do an enzetsu, because the activity itself is being installed. This is the reverse-flow event at its most visible — a Sino-Japanese compound coined to install a Western civic practice, with the English term left in roman script as the conceptual hinge until the new word can carry the weight on its own. The passage anchors the whole subsequent vocabulary of Meiji deliberative procedure (討論, 動議, 賛成) and made the speech hall and the speech society plausible Japanese institutions.

passage: 広告　本紙へ広告御掲載ノ向ハ料金別表ノ通リ／一行ニ付キ金何銭
notes: The bare masthead heading and rate notice — "Advertisements. Those wishing to place advertisements in this paper, see the schedule of rates: so many sen per line" — captures exactly what the conceptual remainder identifies. By the early 1880s the major Meiji dailies all carry this kind of standing column under the heading 広告, with a posted per-line rate that constitutes the new institutional category: a paid placement priced by length, sold to commercial parties, printed under a standardized header. The classical 'inform widely' kernel of the compound is preserved on the surface, but the entire economic apparatus that now sits behind the word — paid placement, rate schedule, advertising department, commercial competition for column space — is invisible in the characters and supplied by the newspaper's institutional context. The persistence of these mastheads across 横浜毎日新聞, 東京日日新聞, and 時事新報 is what stabilized 広告 as the standing East Asian word for commercial advertisement, distinct from the state's 公告 (official public announcement); the lexical bifurcation between the two compounds, both available in classical Chinese, is itself a Meiji institutional achievement.

passage: Ideal　理想
notes: The Tetsugaku Jii's terse entry — the English headword 'Ideal' set against the single Japanese equivalent 理想 — does the decisive conceptual work for what becomes one of the keywords of modern East Asian philosophical and literary discourse. By stabilizing 理想 as the standing translation of a Western philosophical category, the dictionary fixes a small family of paired distinctions that the language did not previously need to mark: 理想 (Ideal) against 観念 (Idea), against 概念 (Begriff), against 理念 (the later normative Idee), against 想念 (mental image). The choice of 理 + 想 — 'principle' joined to 'image-thought' — keeps the Western Ideal close to its Platonic-Kantian register as a rationally grounded exemplar held in mind rather than a bare logical concept, and the very dryness of the lexical entry is what makes it consequential: a contested Western abstraction is naturalized precisely by being recorded as a settled dictionary fact. From this entry 理想 flowed outward into Tsubouchi Shōyō's literary criticism, into 理想主義 as the standing name of philosophical and aesthetic idealism, and into the operating East Asian vocabulary of aspiration.

passage: 学問の要は活用に在るのみ。活用なき学問は無学に等し。…学問の目的は、活用にあるなり。
notes: "The essential of learning is in its active application alone. Learning without active application is equivalent to no learning at all. … The purpose (目的) of learning is application." Fukuzawa folds the new compound 目的 into the opening philosophical argument of Gakumon no Susume: the question 'what is learning for?' is posed and answered in terms that presuppose the Western category of purpose as the rational end-point of an activity. The passage is doing two things at once. Lexically, it normalizes 目的 — barely a decade old as a stable Meiji rendering of Western purpose / Zweck — by deploying it inside one of the most widely read sentences in modern Japanese, anchoring its meaning for a mass readership as the directed aim of a deliberate practice. Philosophically, it presses the imported category into a specifically Meiji utilitarian reframing: learning has a purpose, and that purpose is 活用 (active application) rather than self-cultivation, accomplishment, or moral perfection. The compound 目的 carries the Western teleological grammar (every serious activity has its end), while the immediate gloss 活用 swaps in a Meiji pragmatic content (the end is application to national life). It is a small but exact example of how a reverse-flow coinage and a programmatic redefinition arrive in the same sentence.

passage: 澳国博覧会出品ノ部類左ノ如シ。第一部 鉱業及冶金術。… 第二十二部 美術。即チ西洋ニテ「ビルデンデ・クンスト」ト称スル者ニシテ画図、彫像、雕刻、銅版、石版ノ類ヲ包含ス。
notes: From the Meiji exposition office's official Japanese rendering of the German exhibition regulations for the 1873 Vienna World Exposition. The translator enumerates the twenty-six exhibition classes and, at the twenty-second, introduces 美術 as the Japanese rendering of bildende Kunst — explicitly transliterating the German term in katakana (ビルデンデ・クンスト) alongside the new Sino-Japanese compound, and enumerating the constituent media (painting, sculpture, engraving, lithography) the Western category was understood to bound together. The bilingual presentation lays bare the conceptual labor: the German exhibition apparatus required Japan to nominate a single term that would bound off a specific set of practices from the surrounding categories of industry, mining, agriculture, and craft, and 美術 is minted to do precisely that institutional work. The passage is the documentary locus classicus of the coinage moment — the institutional event at which the Western category of 'fine art' was first imposed on Japanese practice as an organizing classification and a Japanese word was created to name the imposition. Nothing in the surrounding classical Japanese aesthetic vocabulary had had to do this kind of work, because the classical Japanese aesthetic apparatus had not bounded these practices as a single class against craft and industry; the Western exhibition category requires the new Japanese term, and the new Japanese term arrives the same day the German classification does.

passage: 小説の主脳は人情なり、世態風俗これに次ぐ。…されば文学を以て世を益するの効、亦尠少にあらざるなり。
notes: From the opening doctrinal articulation of the Shōsetsu Shinzui — Tsubouchi's foundational statement that the novel's principal concern is human emotion (人情), with social conditions and manners (世態風俗) as its secondary concern, followed by the argument that literature thus understood is of substantial public utility. The passage uses 文学 in precisely the modern academic-aesthetic sense the work is engaged in stabilizing — literature as the bounded aesthetic-imaginative category whose proper object is the truthful depiction of human emotional and social reality, freed from the Edo gesaku tradition's didactic-moralizing apparatus (the kanzen-chōaku 'rewarding virtue and punishing vice' formula). Three things are doing simultaneous work here. First, the compound 文学 is being deployed in its narrowed modern sense (literature as the imaginative-aesthetic discipline) rather than its broad classical Confucian sense (the cultivation of letters), and the deployment is performative: by using the term in the narrower sense and arguing for that sense, Tsubouchi is stabilizing the narrower sense as the operating modern meaning. Second, the argument is methodologically inaugural: the criterion of mimetic truth to human emotional and social reality (人情 and 世態) is being installed as the proper standard of literary value, displacing the Edo didactic criterion. Third, the closing claim of literary utility (世を益するの効) preserves an older Confucian register of literature-as-publicly-useful even as the substantive content has been redefined — literature serves the public not by moralizing but by truthful depiction. The Shōsetsu Shinzui is the inaugurating doctrinal moment of modern Japanese literary criticism, and this passage is its conceptual hinge.

passage: Art. 芸術。Fine Arts. 美術。
notes: From the first edition (1881) of the Tetsugaku Jii — the foundational dictionary of Meiji-coined philosophical vocabulary edited by Inoue Tetsujirō, Ariga Nagao, and Wadagaki Kenzō at Tokyo Imperial University. The two adjacent entries register the deliberate Meiji distinction between art-as-philosophical-category (Kunst, glossed as 芸術) and the institutional fine arts (bildende Kunst, glossed as 美術), a distinction the dictionary stabilizes as the operating Japanese disciplinary vocabulary. The compactness of the lexicographic entry conceals the conceptual labor it accomplishes: by listing the two compounds side by side as separate entries, the dictionary registers in print the position that art (the philosophical-aesthetic category) and the fine arts (the institutional-visual domain) are different conceptual objects requiring different Japanese terms — a position that aligns Japanese with the German Kunst / bildende Kunst distinction and against the English collapse of both into the single ambiguous word 'art.' The dictionary's status as the institutional reference work of Tokyo Imperial University philosophy made these renderings the operating academic vocabulary across subsequent Meiji and modern Japanese aesthetic-philosophical writing, and the 芸術 / 美術 pair has remained the standard Japanese disciplinary distinction in academic aesthetics, art history, and arts-institutional discourse ever since. The Tetsugaku Jii's stabilization moment is also the moment at which the broader philosophical-aesthetic register of 芸術 was institutionally bound to the Kantian-Hegelian Kunst tradition rather than to the institutional museum-and-academy apparatus of 美術 — a binding that subsequent Japanese academic aesthetics (Mori Ōgai's translation of Hartmann, Ōnishi Yoshinori's systematic Aesthetics, the Kyoto School aesthetic writings) would continue to exploit.

passage: 凡ソ歴史ヲ研究スルニハ其時代ヲ區分シテ各時代ノ事跡ヲ稽古シ其因果ヲ究明セザル可ラズ。今支那ノ歴史ヲ上古、中古、近古ノ三期ニ區分シ其各期ノ大勢ヲ叙述シテ以テ通史ノ體裁ヲ為サントス。
notes: From the methodological preface to Naka Michiyo's Shina Tsūshi (Comprehensive History of China, 1888) — the foundational work of modern Japanese academic historiography. Naka articulates the methodological program of the work: that the proper study of 歴史 requires the division of the past into periods, the investigation of the events of each period, and the elucidation of their causal relations; and that the work accordingly divides Chinese history into the three periods of antiquity (上古), the middle period (中古), and the recent past (近古), narrating the broad currents of each period to constitute a Comprehensive History (通史). The passage is methodologically inaugural in multiple registers. First, it deploys 歴史 in its modern academic-disciplinary sense — history as a scholarly practice governed by periodization, source-investigation, and causal explanation — rather than in any classical-chronicle or moral-evaluative register, performatively stabilizing the modern sense by using it. Second, it imports the European periodization schema (ancient / medieval / modern) into the East Asian historical material, an application that was at the time a substantive methodological innovation and that would become foundational for modern East Asian historical writing. Third, it articulates the demand for causal explanation (其因果ヲ究明) as the proper task of historical scholarship, distinguishing the modern discipline from the chronicle and standard-history genres that had organized the classical 史 tradition. The passage is the documentary locus classicus for the Meiji stabilization of 歴史 as the term for the modern academic discipline of history, and Naka's broader scholarly corpus is the principal vehicle through which the discipline-vocabulary cluster (歴史, 史学, 通史, 史料, 古代/中世/近代) was bound to Rankean methodological commitments. The compound 歴史 — the experienced sequence (歴) bound to the scribal record (史) — is here carrying the full weight of the modern academic discipline that the Meiji project of writing Japan and East Asia into world-historical narrative required.

passage: 心理学ハ精神ノ作用ヲ論究スル学ナリ。其作用ヲ大別シテ知・情・意ノ三ニ分ツ。
notes: From the opening definition of Nishi Amane's Shinrigaku (1875), his Japanese rendering of Joseph Haven's Mental Philosophy. "心理学 is the discipline that investigates the operations of the mind. These operations are broadly divided into three: intellect, feeling, and will." The sentence is doing the work of installation that all the foundational Meiji disciplinary translations do, but it is doing it with particular structural visibility. The compound 心理学 is being deployed in the act of being defined: Nishi names the discipline (心理学), specifies its object (精神ノ作用, 'the operations of the mind/spirit'), and offers the tripartite faculty division — 知 (intellect), 情 (feeling), 意 (will) — that organized Haven's American Scottish-common-sense-tradition mental philosophy. The choice of 精神 rather than 心 for the discipline's object in the definitional sentence is itself terminologically careful: 精神 (seishin) names the broader spirit-mind register, distinct from the bounded 心 of the discipline-title, and the slight terminological gap between the title and the defined object marks the compound's stake in carrying a register that the bare 心 would not exhaust. The tripartite faculty division (知情意 chi-jō-i) imported from Haven became one of the most pedagogically productive Meiji compounds, organizing the operating Japanese psychological-and-educational vocabulary for the rest of the nineteenth century and into the twentieth. The passage is the documentary locus classicus for the stabilization of 心理学 as the operating Japanese word for psychology as an academic discipline, and the act of definition-by-deployment is the precise reverse-flow mechanism by which the imported Western disciplinary category becomes a Sino-Japanese word.

passage: Tragedy. 悲劇。Comedy. 喜劇。
notes: From the first edition (1881) of the Tetsugaku Jii, edited by Inoue Tetsujirō, Ariga Nagao, and Wadagaki Kenzō at Tokyo Imperial University. The two adjacent entries register the deliberate Meiji installation of the Western tragedy / comedy dramatic-genre distinction as a paired Sino-Japanese compound-couple. The compactness of the lexicographic entry conceals the conceptual labor it accomplishes. By listing 悲劇 and 喜劇 side by side as adjacent paired entries, the dictionary registers in print the position that tragedy and comedy form a structural genre-pair in Western dramatic theory — a position alien to the classical East Asian theatrical traditions, which had no such binary genre-axis organizing their indigenous dramatic categories. The pairing of 悲 (sorrow) with 喜 (joy) as the two affective categories that organize the dramatic genre-pair is precisely calibrated against the German Trauerspiel / Lustspiel pair (the 'sorrow-play' / 'joy-play' literal renderings of the Western genres that German preserves alongside the loanwords Tragödie / Komödie), and the compound-pair is built to render the structural symmetry of the Western pair in compact Sino-Japanese form. The dictionary's status as the institutional reference work of Tokyo Imperial University philosophy made these renderings the operating academic vocabulary across subsequent Meiji and modern Japanese dramatic-aesthetic writing, and the 悲劇 / 喜劇 pair has remained the standard Japanese theatrical-genre distinction in dramatic theory, theatrical criticism, and the broader reception of European dramatic literature ever since.

passage: Comedy. 喜劇。
notes: From the same first-edition Tetsugaku Jii (1881) entry-pair as the higeki instance. The terse lexical entry — the English headword 'Comedy' set against the single Japanese equivalent 喜劇 — performs the same kind of stabilization-by-listing that the dictionary performed for the broader Meiji philosophical-aesthetic vocabulary. What is being installed is not merely a lexical equivalent but a genre-category: by entering 喜劇 as the standard rendering of 'comedy,' the dictionary fixes the position that the Western comic genre is a bounded theatrical category requiring a single Japanese compound to name it, rather than a phenomenon that the indigenous Japanese theatrical vocabulary (狂言 kyōgen, 笑い waraji and the comic registers of kabuki and rakugo) could carry through its existing categories. The structural pairing with the adjacent 悲劇 entry is doctrinally consequential: the two compounds are installed not as independent renderings but as a paired couple that together names the structural binary of Western dramatic theory. The choice of 喜 (joy) as the affective marker is precisely calibrated against the structural symmetry of 悲 in 悲劇 — the dictionary deliberately mirrors the affective taxonomy 喜怒哀楽 of classical Confucian moral psychology in the genre-vocabulary it stabilizes, drawing on the deepest Sino-Japanese affective register to bind the Western dramatic genres to the structural-affective categories already available in the language. The lexicographic entry's brevity is the point: a contested Western genre-category is naturalized precisely by being recorded as a settled dictionary equivalence.
